LIFE—IN SIX ACTS. MANHOOD. Cooing, wooing, Future wife; Gushing, blushing, Tied for life.
Sighing, crying -Night and day; Winking blinking, Full of play. BOY.
Fooling, schooling, Getting tall; growing, rowing, • Playing ball. YOUTH. fussing, mussing, Over a tie ; larking, sparking, Cu the sly.
MIDDLE AGE. Slaving, craving, FLarding wealth; Driving, striving, Broken health.
OLD AGE. Ailing, failing, Day by day; The undertaker Ends the play.
THE FUNERAL. BY WILL CARLETON. I was walking in Savannah, past a church decayed and
dim, _ When there slowly through the window came a plaintive

funeral hymn; And a sympathy awakened, and a wonder quickly grew, -ran found myself environed in a little negro pew. Out at front a coloured couple sat in sorrow, nearly wild; On the altar was a coffin, in the coffin was a child. I could picture him when living—curly hair, protruding lip— And had seen perhaps a thousand in my hurried Southern trip. But no baby ever rested in the soothing arms of Death That had fanned more flames of sorrow with his little
Buttering,. breath; And no funeral ever glistened with more sympathy pro-
found 'Than was in the chain of tear-drops that enclasped those mourners round. Rose a sad old coloured preacher at the little wooden desk— With a manner grandly awkward, with a,:countenance
grotesque ; With simplicity and shrewdness on his Ethiopian face; With the ignorance and wisdom of a crushed, undying race.

And he said, -‘ Now don' be weepin' for dis pretty bit o' clay— For de little boy who lived dere, he done gone an' run away! He was doin' very finely, an' he 'predate your love; But sure n'uff his Father want him in de large house up above.
Now he didn't give you dat baby, by a hundred _thou- san' mile ! He just think you need some sunshine, and Ho lend it for awhile! An' He let you keep an' love it, till your hearts was big-
ger grown; And dese silver tears you're sheddin's jest de interest on de loan.

"Here yer oder pretty chilrun :—dont be making it appear Dat your love got sort: o"nop'llized by dis little fellow here-, Don' pile up too much your sorrow on deir little mental shelves, -So's to kind o' set 'em wonderin' if dey're no account demselves ! 4‘ Just you think, you poor deal: mounahs, creepin"long o'er Sorrow's way, What a blessed little picnic dis vere baby's got to-day! Your good faders and good raoders crowd de little fellow round In de angel-tended garden of de Big Plantation Ground. -1' An' dey ask him, Was your feet sore?' an take off his little shoes, An' dey wash him, an' dey kiss him, and dey say, Now what's de news?' An' de Lawd done cut his tongue loose; den de little fellow say, All our folk down in de valley tries to keep de hebbenly way.'

-"An his eyes dey brightly sparkle at de pretty things dey view; Den a tear come, an' he whisper, Tut I want my paryents, too!' But de Angel Chief Musician teach dat boy a little song, Says, 'lf only dey be faieful dey will soon be 'comin' 'long.' "An he'll get an education clat will proberbly be worth Seberal times as much as any you could buy for him on earth; He'll be in de Lawd's big school-house, widout no con- tempt or fear; While dere's no end to de bad tings might have happened to him here.

'So, my pooah dejected mounahs, let your hearts wid Jesus rest, An' don't go to critercisin' dat ar One w'at knows de best? He have sent us many comforts—He have right to take away— 'To de Lawd be praise an' glory now an' ever !—Let us pray !"

"Why do you mutter that way when you read ?" asked an old man of a negro who sat mumbling over a news- paper. "How ought Ito read, sah ?" "Why read with- out moving your lips." "What good would dat sorter readin7 do torrie, for I couldn't heah it. When I read I wanster 'read so I can heah what I'se readin"bout." THE POETICAL URCHIN.—A little urchin, seven or eight years old, in a school where a Miss Blodgett was teacher, composed the following, and wrote it on his slate at prayer time, to the great amusement of the boys:— A little mouse ran up the stairs To hear Miss Blodgett say her prayers. The teacher discovered the rhyme, and called out the culprit. For a punishment she gave him his choice to make another rhyme in five minutes or be caned. So, after-thinking, and blinking, and scratching his head till his time was nearly out, and the te,icher was lifting the cane in a threatening manner, at the last moment he exclaimed : Here I stand before Miss Blodgett; She's going to strike, and I'm going to dodge it. A certain noble Scottish lord used to go about Naples attended by a large ferocious bull-dog. Having decided upon going to Rome, he proceeded to the station and took his place in a first-class carriage, his " dauf,r" taking up a position on the seat opposite his master. The platform inspector, with many gesticulations, declared that the bull-dog should not travel in a passenger carriage. "Very well, then, take him out," was Lord X.'s quiet re- joinder. In vain the official expostulated; Lord X. merely reiterated his former reply—a piece of advice which was not followed; and, apparently master of the situation, he threw himself back in his seat and calmly lighted a cigar: but the Italians were not to be outdone, and, quietly detaching the carriage in which the "Eng- lish millor" was seated, they made up the train with another baggage car, and started it off. Lord X. sat I quietly smoking for a quarter of an hour, and then, sur- prised at the delay, thrust his head out of the window and demanded when the train was going to start. His feelings, when the situation was described to him, may be imagined. BOYS WANTED.—What kind of boys are wanted in counting-rooms and offices to take the place, in time, of the merchants and ship-masters who are so active to-day? Let us see :—First, boys that know how to obey orders. It is said that the famous General Havelock set

out for a walk in London one morning, taking with him his son Henry, about 12 years old. On his return his wife exclaimed, "General, where is Henry ?" "I left him on Thames bridge this morning, telling him to await my return," he replied. Hurrying back to the bridge, the boy was found walking up and down, up and down, waiting as he had been told. All the long day the boys had jeered at him, called him names, pointed at him, and now, touching his hat to his father, he was ready for home. During a famous battle between the French and English, the British commander gave orders to an officer, with his regiment, to guard a certain bridge and remain there till Ordered to march. The battle raged fiercely, now one army retreating, and then the other forced back, till the officer could wait no longer, but gave orders to "march," and joined in the thickest of the fight. He was brave and did good service, but Napoleon crossed that bridge and escaped. After the battle the commander called the officer into his presence, and, breaking his sword, stripping him of his honour, disgraced him. Severe was it? He should have remained upon the bridge till the timbers fell into the river, unless ordered away. The kind of boys needed must learn to obey. Secondly, boys must be able to say "No," and mean it. Nine out of ten boys who fail to rise in the world lack the will power to brave a sneer, and to resist temptation. In the third place, boys need help. They ought to be Christians, and not fear to let their companions know it. Twenty years ago a boy in Boston had a good situation, with ex- cellent prospects, but gave it up because he would not do wrong to please his employer, though there were several dependent upon him at home. He was desirous of pleasing the merchant, but he served and trusted in a better Master. To-day he is respected and wealthy, and occupies several positions of honour. Boys are needed everywhere who are prompt, honest, faithful, Christian. All such will find favour here and a crown hereafter. A ZEALOUS "MINISTER'S MAN."—The minister's man I was in former times a person sui generis, and whether the office was combined with that of beadle, which in coun- try parishes was almost invariably the case, he was marked by many peculiarities and singularities. As, with the change of times and manners, the olden type , has all but disappeared, it may not be uninteresting to present a few specimens of the order. Dr. Paterson, in the appendix to his "Manse Garden," remarks that even then they were dying out, and gives a graphic descrip- tion of the "minister's boy," who was beginning to supersede them. One of these important functionaries, a long time in my father's service, was Walter Brydone, nearly related to Patrick Bryclone, author of "Travels in Sicily." Many stories lingered long in the neighbour- hood of his peculiarities. One anecdote my father was fond of relating. He had been in a distant part of the parish on some duty, and was astonished to hear on his way home that Duke Henry of Buccleuch had, through the overzeal of his factotum, been taken prisoner on his own ground. The particulars were these :—Wat, who ' was not over-burdened with work, was standing with j his hands in his pockets, looking. about him, when he saw a lady and gentleman in a light gig, followed by a rider, approaching. The roads not being in the best state of repair, they turned aside and passed along a strip of grass by tile river side, rented by his reverence from his Grace. Wat, thinking they were people going to Moffat Wellwhom he might not see again, overlooked the devia- tion. Ere long, however, the party returned, and took the same route as before. He then thought it right to interfere, and sang out in no/ mellowed or measured tone, "What sort o' road is that ye're takin' ? " The elderly gentleman on the pony became spokesman. "Your roads here are not very good, my lad." "That's nae business o' mine; if ye re no' pleased with the roads ye should apply to them that hae the charge o' them." "Who may these be ? " replied the rider, feigning ignor- ance. "There is Pringle o' Yak-, and Pringle o' Tor- woodlee, and Pringle o' Haining—ye may gang to them and compleen o' the bad roads; but that's no reason for treadin' down the minister's grass, and that's eneuch." "What's your name, my lad ? ' " I'm no' obliged to tell ye my name; but if ye're very anxious to have it ye'll find it in the session register o' Selkirk. I think lam mak entitled to hae your name," and, suiting the action to the word, he made a bolt and seized the bridle of the pony. The Duke, entering into the joke, said, "I see, my lad, we are yourprisoners," and, taking out the back of a letter, with his pencil wrote on the front of the saddle, "The Duke of Buccleuch, the Countess of Dal- keith (mother of the present Duke), and Colonel Ruther- ford of Edgerston," and then handed it to his neighbour. The ratter, at once perceiving his awkward mistake, relaxed his hold of the rein, and with great cunning and naïveté, but with somewhat of a hang-dog look, stam- mered out—" I canna read." "I am not surprised at that," remarked the Duke; "I've often been told by my friends that lam a bad scribe. But take that slip to your master; he'll know where to find us if he is dis- posed to prosecute."—Remigiseenees of Yarrow. Public Analysts have submitted CA DBURT'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved Its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

Yachtsman surveying a friend's yacht, through his binocular: "They have dropped their anchor." Lady Friend, on her first trip: "Serves them right ! It has seen hanging over the side all day long." Gentleman of Colour—A painter.—Burglar's Advertisement—Goods carefully removed.—Why should tailors always be able to please their customers ---Because it is their especial duty to _suit people. A Parisian photographic artist was the other day en- gaged in securing a new view of the Arc de Triomphe, and he presently became quite absorbed in his task, so much so, in fact, that he in due course, much to the amusement of the crowd gathered round, cried out in the niechanical voice which phctographic artists affect— * Now, please, keep quite still/. One, two, three! Thank you very much!" It is scarcely necessary to add that the arch, thus appealed to, did not move. When once Dr. Vincent introduced Dr. Henderson, who was to lecture on "Fools," he said," We are now to have a lecture on fools by one" (long pause and loud laugh- ter from the audience, when the president concluded with the clause) "of the wisest men in the country." The lecturer advanced to the desk, and responded, "I am mot half so big a fool as Dr. Vincent" (another very long pause, and still more hearty laughter from the audience) "would have you suppose." Tam THREE STErTrERERS.—A gentleman afflicted with an impediment in his speech, sat down to dinner at a tavern, and calling to a waiter addressed him thus " We-w-waiter, gi-give me s-s-some r-r-roast b-b-beef." The waiter stammered out in reply, " We-w-we a-a-ain't g-g-got a-a-any." At which the gentleman, highly en- raged, supposing the servant was mocking him, sprang from his seat, and was proceeding to knock him down, when a third person arrested his arm, and cried out not to strike, saying, He s-s-stutters s-s-same as w-w-we

• How HE &mum A Jon.—On a North-Western train was a sallow-faced, red-haired man, with a pair of spec- tacles onshis nose and an annual pass in his pocket. In the west seat was a smooth-faced young man, who said he was looking for a job. "I want a young man to clerk in.my office," said the sollow-faced man, "and if you can fill the bill I'll take you. lam an editor up in Wisconsin. Now, s'pose I was sitting at my desk and a big man with his fists all doubled up and a wild look in his eyes should come up the stairs and inquire for the editor, what would you tell him?" "ru tell him the editor wasn't in," re- plied the young man; "but that if he'd sit down and wait a few minutes you'd probably be back from the gun store, where you had gone to get a new seven-shooter and a knife 13 inches long to cut up rollers and things with." "Consider yourself engaged. Salary, 4 dols. a week and board, with one-third of all the big water melons that come into the office."—Chicago FIRST QUARRELS.—A young couple had passed the first few weeks of:their marriage at the house of a friend. Having at length ;occupied their new home, they were taking their first breakfast, when the following scene took place :—The young husband was innocently open- ing a boiled egg in an egg cup. The bride observed that he was breaking the shell at what she thought was the wrong end. "How strange it looks," said she, "to see you break your egg at the small end, my dear. No one else does so, and it looks so odd." "Oh, I think it is quite as good, in fact better, than breaking it at the large end, my love, for when the large end is opened the egg runs over the top," replied the husband. "But it looks very odd when no one else does so," replied the wife. "Well, now, I really do think it is not a nice way of eating an egg. That dipping of strips of bread and butter into an egg certainly is not tidy. But I do not object to your doing as you please if you will let me break my egg at the small end," retorted he. "I am sure my way is not so bad as eating fruit pie with a knife, as you do, instead of using a fork; and you always eat the syrup as if you were not accustomed to have such things. You really do not see how bad it looks, or lam sure you would not do so," added the wife. "The syrup is made to be eaten with the pie, and why should I send it away in the plate?" asked he. "No well-bred persons clear up their plates as if they were starved," said the young bride, with a contemptuous toss of her pretty head. "Well, then, I am not a well-bred person," re- plied the husband angrily. "But you must be if we are to live comfortably together," was the sharp answer. 'Well, I must break my egg at the small end, so it does not signify; and I must also eat the syrup." "Then I will not have either eggs or fruit pie at the table." "But / will have them," he petulantly exclaimed. '"then I wish I had not been married to you," cried the young wife, bursting into tears. "And so do I," added the now incensed husband, as -he arose and walked out of the room. This domestic quarrel was followed by others equally triffina in their origin and disgraceful in tfitir character, until the silly couple made themselves so disagreeable to each other ithat their home I?eca.rae unbearable and they separated- OES,APEST HOUSE in the city for Glass, China, Oriental Wares, and Fancy Goods.-175, Oxford-street, Mallet-ester.— ..doter.

One of the most successful of Illinois dairymen keeps I 100 cows, but he never raises a pound of clover hay. He feeds his cattle on maize hay. It is cut when in blos- som, bound and set up until cured, or until winter, when it is removed to the barn. He gets seven tons of this dry fodder to the acre, and claims it is as good as the best of hay. Prime butter should cut or break like wax. The knife cuts smoothly through the print or lump, leaving but a slight dampness on the blade. Such is the result of judicious feeding combined with proper dairy manage- ment. Causes, apparently insignificant, as the change in feeding late-cut and over-ripe hay, where previously the aromatic, succulent, soft, early-cut grass formed the principal part of the ration, reduces the quality of the product. The successful dairyman watches and guards against such changes in the cow's ration. It is estimated that last year not less than 100,000,000 lb. of oleomargarine were manufactured in the United States. It cost, perhaps, 8 cents a lb.-8,000,000 dols.; and, sold as butter at 25 cents per lb., would bring 25,000,000 dols. Allowing a profit of 20 per cent., which would be 1,600,000 dols., it leaves a clean swindle of 15,500,000 dols.' as a commercial transaction, to say nothing of the fact that the entire sum was made by misrepresentation and downright cheating selling it as pure butter instead of as oleomargarine, and at a price commensurate with its real value. SALT FOR SHEEP.—It is certain that little snails act as bearers or intermediaries of the liver fluke, which pro- duces rot in sheep. They render pastures hitherto deemed safe for sheep to be hazardous in a wet season. It seams tolerably well established that even if the sheep swallow the cysts, these will not pass into the fertile stage, provided there be a certain amount of saline pre- sent in the sheep's stomach. This fact points to its being a wise precaution at once to begin giving sheep a por- tion of salt daily. Fasciola hepatica is so terrible a scourge when it. does get possession of a flock that every care should be taken to keep it out. A daily dose of salt has been proved to be a safeguard. The next three months will be anxious ones for many flockmasters. FEEDING CALVES.—Professor W. A. Henry, of the University of Wisconsin, who has been conducting elaborate experiments in calf feeding, says :—" We have had both good and poor results from feeding skim-milk, and as a summary of experience .offer the following hints :—Feed skim-milk lightly. Eight to nine quarts in three feeds is sufficient to make a thrifty calf gain from 12 to 14 lb. a week. More calves are killed by over-feed- ing than under-feeding. Feed three times a day if you wish good relults. Never let the milk go into the calf's stomach colder than 98 deg. Fahr. Use the thermometer regularly in determining the warmth of the milk. Make lime-water by putting a lump of lime the size of a hen's egg into a jug of water and shaking. When the water is clear it is ready for use. Keep the jug corked tight at all times. A tablespoonful of the clear lime-water may be given with each feed if the calf shows any kind of scour. If scouring occurs reduce the amount of milk at once. An egg stirred in the milk and parched flour are both excellent remedies. Over-feeding, not feeding often enough, irregularity, and cold milk are the principal causes of scouring. Teach the calf tb eat crushed oats by the time it is three weeks or a month old by slipping a few small handfuls into its mouth just after it has drunk milk. When it has learned to eat them keep a supply before it in a little box. If you have not oats enough both for the horses and calves, let the horses go without rather than the calves. Bran, oil meal, and other articles are good, but oats are the most satisfactory of all. I never knew of a calf eating too many. While young, keep each calf tied by itself, and if the flies are troublesome darken the stable. Do not put the young things out into the hot sun with the idea that the little grass they may eat will compensate for the blood sucked by the myriads of flies that pester them. We have had less trouble and better results with winter calves than with those that come in the spring. Dismiss all prejudice that a skim-milk calf must be a stunted, unsightly thing. We are making as great advancement in calf-rearing as in butter or cheese making, and old ideas must be put ' away:" THE MIGRATION OF TER SPARROW.—Mr. W. B. Teget- meier writes :—" As bearing on the question of the in- jurious character of the common sparrow in our gardens and cornfields, I am desirous of calling attention to a circumstance which is so common and universal that it appears to have escaped general notice; at least, I do not find any account of it in the ordinary volumes of British ornithology, and the public at large, who are not practised in the art of seeing, are usually perfectly igno- rant of it until their attention is directed to: it, when they generally reply, "Yes, now you mention it, I have not seen any sparrows in my garden for some time, but I did not think anything of it." To give a single instance of the facts to which I wish to direct attention, I will relate my own experience this season. My residence at North Finchley,within a quarter of a mile of the high road to Barnet, is perfectly open to the country on the west side. The gardens of the houses, which are fairly nu- merous, are infested with sparrows, that fly from the seed beds and ripening peas during the summer in flocks of fifty or more. Amongst other offences that these avian rats perpetrate, they appropriate the nests of the martins, turning out the rightful owners; they stop the water pipes, and defile the rain water; in the early spring they pull up the crocuses; in summer they eat the bush fruit, destroy the peas, and levy heavy toll on the seed beds that are not protected by wire-work. But in August they disappear, and scarcely a sparrow is to be seen—not more than one in fifty of the previous num- ber, the very few that remain being apparently young birds of the present season. On making inquiry of my neighbours, I find this migration is general in the neigh- bourhood. Now, the question to be answered is, what has become of the pests? This, I believe, admits. of but one reply—they have. gone to the cornfields to levy blackmail upon the farmer. But, as far as lam aware, there is not a single cornfield of any description within two and a half or three miles from my house; but this distance has not interfered with the partial migration of the sparrows. Of the amount of damage done in the cornfields by the thousands of these birds that leave the neighbourhood I need say nothing. It did not need the conclusive treatise recently published by Messrs. Gurney and Russell to convince farmers of the evil, and no words of mine or of anyone else would convince the silly sentimentalists who gush about subjects on which they are profoundly ignorant. But I may mention that my next neighbour, a large land holder, who formerly i grew corn n this district, informs me that he has for some years given up the practice, finding that the spar- rows were too destructive to allow of its profitable cultivation." RIPENING TTIFI Cnr.Ax.—A Wisconsin woman writes : Ripening the cream for churning has never been given the importance it deserves in any lecture,. newspaper, article, or book I have read upon the subject. Cer- tainly it is one of the most important and troublesome operations of butter-making. By the old way the cream often remains on the milk too long, and then again is skimmed too soon. No matter how hard the over-worked farmer's wife may try our variable climate will be sure to upset all her calculations. Some of her cream will be just ripe enough to churn when she skims it, some not ripe enough; she must either let some get too ripe or lose much of that not ripe enough, must either make poor butter or less good butter. Either way makes sad havoc of her profits. Were she to stand over it all her waking moments, I do not believe she could make a tub of uni- form quality. By the submerged system the cream is dipped off sweet and cold, of even consistency, not leathery and tough. It can be set away in a cold place until enough has accumulated for a churni.ng, then all brought out, warmed, and ripened together. Before we contrived our cream closet, we had awful troublesome times to get it to the right temperature, perhaps had to move it from one place to another a dozen times, had to set it in warm or cold water; and with all our bother could seldom get it just right, and when we did it took a great deal of attention to keep it right long enough to ripen. Now, our cream closet saves us most of that trouble, and it is a very simple affair too, not patented. Long and slim like our cans, it is about 13ins. square on the inside, and about 5-1-ft. high, with close-fitting door the whole length, and open work movable shelves every 6ins., except it is 16ins. between the bottom and the first shelf, where sits a large tin can of water. In

winter this closet is let in a warm corner with its back to the chimney; in Ammer in as cool a place as we can find. In winter we put crocks of cream enough for one churning in this closet, take out the can of water and heat it as hot as we think will warm the cream to 62 degs. ; in very cold weather we may have to heat it up two or three times, in summer may have to put the can of water on top and use ice; but when once the cream has got 'warmed through, the water will keep it just about right for the thirty-six hours it ought to stay there to ripen. You must not forget to stir it frequently until it gets warmed through, because you know the scientific folks tell us cream is a very poor conductor of heat, and I really believe it would bake on the outside before it would warm the inside a particle, and it is of the greatest importance your cream should ripen evenly or it will not all come to butter at the same time; is very apt to be full of white specks and all sorts of flavours. If too ripe the desired aroma is destroyed, if not ripe enough it will not be developed, and you do not get as good or as much butter. It is very hard to tell on paper just how to do it, it needs lots of watchful experience; but one thing I am sure of, you must have a good ther- mometor and learn to use it with great exactness, or you cannot make Al butter. Watch your cream carefully, and as soon as it shows signs of acicity put it in the churn and churn it. • '__

It is distinguished by a portiOn of the intestines coming down at the vent, and unless the hen is relieved she will soon die. The remedy is to gently return the part whenever it protrudes, afterwards inject,- ing a little cold water, in which some alum has been dis- solved. This treatment must be accompanied by a low diet, and the absence of stimulating food. But it is also necessary to observe that fowls with a tendency to this complaint should be carefully and somewhat sparingly fed at all times.

div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

A Blackburn correspondent informs us. that on the morning of the 23rd inst. the frost was so severe as to affect French Beans and other tender plants in his gar- den.—Gardening World this week has an illustration of the " Black Champion" Currant, with the following re- marks :—" It was brought into notice by Mr. Dunnet, partner in the Holborn firm (James Carter and Co.), in whose garden, in the centre of the famous seed farm at Dedham, in Essex, it is a subject of considerable interest to visitors in August and September—aye, September, for among its other sterling qualities is that of retaining its freshness until long after other sorts are shrivelled up. We have more than once seen the fine bushes in Mr. Dennet's garden, and have no hesitation in saving that it has no rival, and well deserves the most extensive cultivation. In habit it is a robust grower and a most abundant bearer, and produces long bunches of jet black berries measuring nearly three-quarters of an inch in ' diameter, and which are particularly delicate and plea- sant in flavour."—Strawberries : Young plantations or beds must be attended to, and after the runners are cut rtin the hoe between the rows to destroy weeds and break the surface in order to prevent the still from crack- ing. Camomile: The flowers of this useful herb should be picked about twice a week and spread on a sheet of paper in a dry airy room, and when they are thoroughly I dried they should be enclosed in a paper bag and sus- ' pended from the kitchen ceiling or placed in a dry drawer. If not stored in a dry state they are liable to become mouldy and consequently unfit for a decoction. THE FRONT GARDEN.—One of the most striking plants in flower at present is Anemone Japonica, and the white variety Honorine Jobart. They usually grow from two to three feet high, but some plants we have seen this year were nearly four feet, and covered with rose- coloured and white flowers. When the autumn is not very severe they continue to flower until Christmas. Our experience of these plants is that they never do well for a year or two after they are planted, but then they improve amazingly, and commence to throw up nu- merous suckers, which may be moved altogether or left on one side to spread, so that in time the old plant may be chopped up and the hole filled up with good soil and manure. The plant is a native of Japan, as the specific name indicates. Annuals: Where there is ample space, and the ground not too heavy, many annuals sown now withstand the winter, and flower early next year, or from the end of April onwards, If the front garden is not favourable for the purpose, then a square yard in the vegetable plot might be set apart, and the plants in spring transplanted into the front garden. They will do equally well in this way, only their flowering period may be slightly delayed. For sowing a poor piece of ground should be preferred to that which is rich, as the latter is conducive to succulence, which predisposes the plants to the destructive energy of frost. Leaving the plants too thick, or not timely thinning them, exposes them to the same danger, and must be obviated by com- mencing to thin as soon as the seedlings are well above ground, and follow it up until not a plant encroaches on its neighbour. The following varieties usually de well treated as above :—Collinsia bicolor, Nemophilla insignis, Candytuft crimson and white, Gilia tricolor, Lupinus Nanus, and red and white Virginian Stocks. Tins WINDOW.—If Pelargoniums were pruned as pre- viously advised they will have made half an inch of new growth and be in a suitable state for potting. The pots should be new or well washed, and have a large crock or oyster shell over the hole in the bottom, and on this broken pieces of crocks, but not China or hard earthen- ware, should be placed. Gardeners generally use the broken pieces of flower pots, and we find the clinkers from furnaces broken small answer very well. A 4-inch pot should have rather better than half-an-inch in depth of them, and for larger pots the quantity should be pro- portionately increased. To prevent the small particles of soil mingling with the crocks and interfering with the free egress of water, they should be covered over with dry moss, half decayed leaves, or fibry portions of loam. The soil should be composed of three parts loam and one leaf mould, and about one-eighth of the whole of gritty sand. Turn the plantsi out of the pots they. are in and press the ball of earth between the hands in order to break it and disentangle the roots from the soil, which should be gradually worked away until it is reduced one-half; then cut most of the strong roots off, and shorten others about half their length, so that they can be placed in pots about two inches less than those they were in. In potting avoid cramping the roots altogether, but take time to work the compost well in amongst them, and be careful to have some between all the roots and the sides of the pot! Whatever soil may be neces- sary underneath the roots should be slightly pressed and a few sharp taps of the bottom of the pot on the potting table will settle the other. To prevent the plant sinking too deep clasp the pot with the fingers and bring the thumbs to press on each side of the stem whilst tapping is being done. Should any more soil be required press it down with the hand. Give a good watering in two or three days after potting.

div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

THE MODERN POULTRY INTEREST (Continued). England may be termed the home of breeders, and it appears to be part of the British nature wherever it may be found to endeavour to improve the quality of the animals, birds, or plants that are around. In no other country is there to be found the same proportion of high class stock as in this "tight little island." It is to Britain that stock buyers turn for the wherewithal to

improve their stock. nature is shown in almost all sections of society. for earnest and skilful breeders are to be found in large numbers not only amongst those who have wealth and space at their disposal, but amongst the very poor, and this spirit of stock breeding permeates all classes, from the Queen down to her poorest subjects. It is, in fact, a part of the British nature, and will find an outlet in one way or another. The wealthy breed their race horses or their pedigree cattle, with the farmer, as far as his means will allow, following in their wake; the suburban residents breed dogs or poultry, and cottagers take up poultry or gar- dening, whilst the denizens of our crowded towns make cage birds or rabbits their bets, unless they are more favoured than usual and can manage to breed a few fowls or pigeons. Nearly every one of these, whatever is the animal or bird they breed, desire to improve them in one way or another, and, be it noted, the object is not a mere mercenary one. It is for the pleasure derived from the fact that this improvement will give. To this spirit we owe the vast improvement in the quality of our domestic animals, and but for it we should not be in the position we now are occupying as the breeding centre of the world. There is another factor in the business, namely, that the very limitation of space which cannot but be the case with the majority of British breeders has had a direct effect upon the quality of the stock pro- duced. Few are there who can keep all the birds or animals they breed, and they have very speedily to kill off a portion, which, being naturally the worst, eliminate such as would have the tendency to reduce the stan- dard. For instance, if a poultry breeder only has suffi- cent room for twenty fowls, he is almost certain to breed a hundred, and he must get rid of eighty per cont. some of which will be killed and consumed, and others of which may be sold. Naturally, he kills off all those that are "halt, lame, and blind," and the worst in the special qualities for which he is breeding, reserving the best for himself. In this way the process of improvement goes on steadily, and in a few years the stock assumes a high character. Some there are who believe apparently in mongrels rather than pure breeds, but we are not of that number, for we contlnd that all the success we have had as a nation in breeding has been due to the individual races of animals and birds we have produced or im- proved.

The amounts received at the door were this year larger than during previous years, v.ith one excep- tion, which was a good sign. It was to be regretted that their efforts had failed to create that taste for better class music, which was the first and greatest object of the society, but they must not be discour- aged. To create that taste was a matter of time. The frequent visits to the town of travelling com- panies, no doubt, was an attraction that absorbed money that might otherwise be expended on the society; Efforts that had been made, he mentioned, to get up a good orchestral band, had failed, and during the past year they had spent £42 odd to pro- vide professional instrumentalists for one concert. —The report and balance sheet were adopted. THE OFFICERS.7-31r. John Rylands was unani- mously re-elected president of the society, and the following gentlemen were re-elected vice-presidents: Messrs. James Marson, W. I3eamont, J. White, C. Broadbent, F. Monks, C. White, and P. Pearse. The former committee were re-appointed without alte- ration. Mr. W. Reynolds again consented to act as secretary and treasurer, and Mr. Seotson was re-ap- pointed assistant secretary. NEXT -SEASON'S WORK.—It VCRS resolved to re- commend the committee to consider the desirability of giving an extra concert, open to the public, but not included in the subscriptions, the solos to be en- tirely taken by the members, and that the commit- tee report to a meeting of the members on the matter. It was also decided that the oratorio -" Judas Maccabeus " be given during next season, the fixing of the date being referred to the com- mittee. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the proceedings.

DISCOVERY oF AN AN(IIENT BRITISH GRAVE AND BURIAL URN. Mr. Tattersall Wilkinson, who recently discovered an ancient grave on the summit of the brow overlooking "Hell Clough," on the south side of Thursden Valley, con- tinued his examination on Saturday week, when the Burn- ley Literary and Scientific Club was represented by one member; there were also present two members of the Ladies' Literary Branch of the Young Women's Chris- tian Association, Mr. Crooke and others from :Nelson. Mr. Wilkinson was rewarded with the discovery of a

beautiful specimen of a cinery urn found about six inches below the surface of a stone wall grave, and was covered with a debris of charcoal mixed with calcined bones, which yielded a very fragrant smell. Upon Mr. Tattersall laying bare the rim of the vase the interest of those looking on was increased, and it was a matter of intense anxiety that the urn should be removed as per- fect as possible. Owing to it be: • firml "Ided

_ig to r. ing ly embed& .in the clay Mr. Kippax, the tenant of the farm, at this stage of the proceedings took Mr. Wilkinson's place, and with great care removed the clay upon the western side until he had laid that portion bare. There the proportions and shape of the urn could be distinctly perceived and the nature of the find to a certain extent estimated. It took some time, however, to relieve it from the superin- cumbent mass, evecially on the northern side, where the greatest caution had to be exercised. The operation, however, was happily successful, and just before dusk fell this interesting receptacle of a cremated interment was eventually lifted on to the turf from the grave where for nearly 2,000 years it must have reposed. Here it was swathed with haybancls, placed in a hamper, and carried to Mr. Wilkinson's residence. The cursory examination which was able to be made showed that it was an urn formed of coarse baked clay, not dissimilar to that up to late years manufactured at the pottery works at Cliviger. The inside was of a darker colour than the outside, as if it had been burnt, thus giving the idea that the bones were transferred to it when they were glowing with heat. These particulars are gathered from the fragments of the urn picked up in the grave, which was evidently broken by a stroke of the pick. It is not cer- tain whether there was a lid to the urn. It may be ob- served that another ancient British burial urn was found upon the same property (belonging to T. Parker, Esq., Of Cuerdale) in 1858, and the present urn bears a striking resemblance to that one, although it is much larger. The further examination of this most interest- ing find is looked forward to with interest, and the greatest credit is due to Mr. Wilkinson and to Mr. Crook, of Nelson, together with Mr. Kippax, son of the tenant of the farm, for their perseverance in excavating. It may be stated that outside the grave, near the circle of stones on the north side, Mr. Wilkinson came across a debris of a body and funeral pyre, which appeared to have been consigned to earth without the protection of urn or coffin of any kind. So far as could be ascertained, the pottery is of a very primitive character, and there does not seem to be any ornamentation upon the out- side. It resembles to some extent the pottery of the early Pagan Anglo-Saxons resident in Britain after the Roman occupation, although it must be admitted the contour of the urn is slightly in favour of it being a Ro- find The dis

them belonged to the Roman occupation somewhere between A.D. 78 when that part of Britain was first occupied by the Romans and the sth century when fly) Romans evacuated Britain,—possibly the later portion of that period. Any other remains found upon the samS site would be accessory evidence. Certainly some ot the remains upon those hill sides were Roman; for where they had the square encampments it was pretty Plaall that the Romans had military posts, if they had not a settled colony. They had a colony at Colne; Roman roads traversed those moors, and there were places in the neighbourhood where they had their camps and posts of outlook. His idea was that the lower and lesg- exposed portion of that hill-side had been at one time a British village, probably a Roman upland camp as well! but the British villages clustered round the Roman camps there was another at Darwen, and a third at Black- ; burn, at both of .which places urns had been found. Urn burial extended over a considerable period, and the only point that would occur to his mind would be whether it was British or Anglo-Saxon. But under all tY3 circumstances he considered it more likely to be a British than an Anglo-Saxon interment, and tliat it belonged to the Romano-British period. So that it might hav° been 1,500 or 1,600 years since the interment took plaef• It was only distinguished persons who were buried _Alrt that way. If all the natives for hundreds of years h' been so buried they would have met with ;cores and hundreds of urns. • If the remains were those of woman and child, as the doctors seemed to think, Iu must have been the interment of a wife and daughter, or wife and son, of some prominent British notability (?! the district in that period. They might rely upon that it represented son-IC person of note. (Applause:)--, Mr. Tattersall Wilkinson explained the circumstances 1:"• the find. In digging, about three weeks ago, a few' yards from where he found the urn he discovered a carbonised mass about three feet below the surface. had been a burial without an Urn, and considering u urn was so near he thought it was a "barrow," vibler was far anterior to Roman times. Outside the grave ,O` the urn he found a quantity of charcoal, which 113.11 apparently been used to burn the body.—Dr. March sal!-5 he agreed with Mr. Abram in everything, except that might be older than he had estimated because of tho bronze pin being there. He agreed that it was nc4 Anglo-Saxon. it was a question that no one would WO to dogmatise on, but possibly it could be settled by more careful examination of the remains. What Nvouia settle it would be the discovery- of some implement Or, ornament. They had found no beads or anything 0- that kind.—Dr. Dean had been much interested in the fact that the urn had been found two feet beneath the surface, and showed that there had not been an accre- tion of soil, that the place was bare, and not a forest ag they had always been given to understand. There bad been no forest there. It was bare 1,500 years ago, or whatever the date might be, and it was the same now. -- The party then adjourned to the site of the grave, and afterwards, under the guidance of Mr. T. Wilkinson, visited several Roman encampments, making one or two interesting discoveries on the way, which may be expected to find work for the field-antiquary for some time to come.

SHOCKING I) I S ASTER IN SCOTLAND. EIGHT PERSONS SUFFOCATED. On Saturday, at Craree Quarries, Lochfyneeide, Soar land, a blasting operation on an unusually large scale Wei announced to take place at the quarries, when a large area of solid rock was to be displaced preparatory to being trimmed for paving purposes. To witness this operation about 1000 people left Glasgow in the forenoon in the steamer Lord of the Isles, which arrived off the quarries about half-past one. The charge was fired by electricitYs and consisted of 61. tons of gunpowder is two chambers. The blasting was successfully carried out, and nearly 80,000 tons of granite were dislodged. When the immense masa had been rolled down, a number of the exeursionists, curiouS to inspect the effects of so extensive a disruption of the rock, left the steamer and climbed up aver the freshly' broken granite. They appeared to have divided into tWO large parties, and one party climbed over a portion of the quarry without experietacing any ill effect. The other---" about 50 or 60 ladies, gentlemen, and boys—entered the quarry by a different path, and had been there about fist(' minutes when one of the workmen shouted out that there was danger from the sulphurous smoke, and called upon them all to clear out. There was immediately a rush for the outside; but the choking afterdamp overtook them, and rendered them insensible, some falling on their backs on the ground, and others on their faces. A few recovered in a minute or two, and were assisted out ty those who bad not ventured far into the quarry; but several of the rescuers were caught by the deadly atmosphere and fainted away. Men staggered about as if drunk, boys were lying on the roadside in convulsions, and loud screams wese uttered by women who had come to their senses. The repre- sentatives of Edinburgh and Glasgow papers were amonget those who had penetrated furthest into the quarry, to take notes of the experimentseand when the alarm was raised Mr. Paterson and Mr. Stewart. two Glasgow journalists, rushed to the road and escaped; but Mr. Temple: of Glasgow; hire Harvie and Mr. Young, of Edinburgh, were thrown down. Mr. Temple was thrown on his back into a pool of water, but recovered consciousness in a few minutes, and was assis- ted away. The case of Mr. Harvey was apparently the most serious of the party, and he and Mr. Young, while in- sensible, were carried with other sufferers on to the deck of the steamer. A search among those who were lying around soon revealed the fact, however, that these were not the worst sufferers. Out of the whole party six were dead. All the dead, iusensible, and other sufferers were conveyed on board the steamer, which proceeded with all possible des- patch to Greenock, where they were taken to the infirmarit and every means employed to restore them, but in one case the efforts were unavailing. The condition of Mr. Young, the reporter, was also, according to latest accounts, very critical, and it was even reported that be had died. The party on board the Lord of the Isles included the members of the Statute Labour Committee of the Glasgow Town Council, and a number of other prominent citizens of Glas- gow, Paisley, Greenock, and other towns on the west coasts who had attended at the invitation ef the quarrymasters to ' see the monstre blasting operations. An eye-witness of the catastrophe says that before the steamer reached Crams pier she stopped, and her whistle was blown to acquaint the man in charge of the electric battery on shore that the passengers were ready to see the explosion. Instantly the hillside seemed to crack and open up, and an immense quantity of granite rolled down to the water's edge, and there was a tremendous detonation. The vessel then steamed to Crade pier, and about 100 persons landed, and proceeded to inspect the debris. Before this the volume of smoke from the exploded powder had not commenced to issue from the chambers of the quarry, but when the visitors were climbing on the heaps of fallen granite, a quarryman called out, "Halt, there; don't you go near the quarry. The sulphurous gases will poison you." Many, however, did not hear the warning, and before word could be -passed round ladies and gentlemen were dropping down, first on their hands, and then on their faces. Great consternation ensued upon the cry which arose of "We are choking; help, help." The narrator was so overcome that he dropped. but by the assistance of those near him he recovered sufficiently to get away. He esti- mated that there were at least 40 persons thrown on the ground and rendered insensible. The boys who were in- jured appeared to suffer worse than the men, and did not recover for several hours. The disaster was entirely attribu- table to the sulphurous gases emitted from the quarry. The effects of the gas on these who survived was for a time most curious. Those who were able to vomit recov- ered soonest. Dr. Taylor, medical officer of health, Port Glasgow, who was in the quarry at the time, thus describes his experi- ences :—I was standing on a lot of stones, looking at a mass of rock that had been dislodged. In about five minutes I perceived a peculiar pungent odour, and on stepping down from the stones, lat once recognised the danger to which the people were exposed. I cried to them to rnn, and I got out into the road very much exhausted, The first sensation felt by the people was a pungent taste and smell. This was followed by a sense of constriction and oppression of of breathing, succeeded by a feeling of giddiness and ner- vous apprehension. In some cases a peculiar contraction of the muscles of the face was observable, like convulsive spasms. The Flatterers reeled and fell as if in a fit. Others made a struggle to reach the road, reeling like drunken men. In slight cases the insefsibility passed off quickly, but in severe cases the first symptoms were followed by convul- sions affecting the whole body. Many of the delicate sufferers were seized with uncontrollable nervousness, laughing, crying, and shouting as if suffering from hysteria. This, in many cases, was succeeded by vomiting, and when that passed away the sufferers became calm and fell asleep. it is supposed that sulphur and carbonic gas had escaped from the bottom of the dislodged mass of stone, and there being no wind to carry it away was present in great volume. Before the firing of the mine an incident of a somewhat amusing kind is said to have occurred, and even afterwards the action of the person concerned was not without its grimly comic side, althoagh those who witnessed it then could not help feeling rather shocked at hie seeming callous- ness. A phetographer, presumably from Glasgow, went down some time before the mine was fired, and fixed his camera at a point along the jetty not above 150 yards dis- tant from the Quarry face. Across the entrance a barrier of heavy blocks of granite had been rudely formed to arrest the progress of any stones which might be ejected by the blast. He seemed to imagine that be would be quite safe. At any rate he got his camera all right, and made arrange- ments to " take " the scene while the disruptive force of the-gunpowder was in active operation. He asked some of the quarrymen what they thought of his position, and was told by one of them that he would not occupy it even if be were to be promised the whole of Crarae as a reward. no man of likenesses, not to be balked of his purpose, set the camera, and when the signal to fire was given retired to a place of safety, and after the blast was over ran out and placed the cap over the lens. He subsequently informed the son of the person with whom he had lodged in the vil- lage during the night that be had secured a good plate. But the grimmest part of the affair has yet to come. When be saw the calamity which bad befallen the excursionists.be seized his camera, it is alleged, and running forward, with great professional rapidity continued taking scene whilst the people were dropping down under the in- fluence of the noxious gasses and the work of rescue and re- suscitation from the quarry was going on. views of the

THE TRUE TEST. The true test of any religion is the effect it pro- duces upon the lives of those who profess it. And, indeed, the test of real merit everywhere must be the power it possesses of accomplishing desirable results. In this age of the world. men are not judged by what they claim to be able to do, but by what they can do; not by what they are reputed to he, but by what they are. Here is where the re- ligion of our own country rises superior to the faith of Mohammedan or Hindoo lands ; for while there is much hypocrisy in the church, and far too much worldliness, there is vet an absence of those • sensual and brutal elements which characterise the religions of Arabia and the Ganges. This principle is equally true in all departments of life. The same rule which applies to persons is also applicable te things. Unquestioned merit must characterise them all, or they cannot be acceptable, Much less popular. These prefatory remarks are called forth by rea,- San of certain investigations which have recently been made concerning an article at present being ex- tensively advertised throughout the United Kingdom. The statements published in the papew were so Strong, and the claims made so marvellous, that both were discredited. Of the many statements * given to the press, the one which attracted our par- ticular attention was announced as coming from the Rev. George Waterman, of Berwyn Lodge, Broadstone, Wimbortie. Among other things, the rev, gentleman is made to say :—" I owe my pre- Sent health, and even my life, under Providence, to the use of Warner's SAFE Cure.' About Christ- mas, 1882, I became aware, for the first time, of the existence of the remedy named. I had been suffer- ing for nearly two years previously from disease of the kidney's and urinary organs. During nearly the whole of that time I had been under the treatment of one of the most celebrated of our London physi- dans. At first I derived great benefit from his skill in treatment, but at last he gave me to understand that he could do nothing more for me. The state- ment of J. B. Henion, *ID., of Rochester, ICY., coming under my notice in Warner's Pam- phlet, induced me to try Warner's SAFE Cure.' After using one or two bottles I had a full analysis made, by a professional analyst, of the fluid I was passing, that I might compare it with subsequent analyses, and thus determine whether the medicine Was doing me any real good or not. The first analysis by heat test, showed, "'Albumen abundant. Sugar considerable.' "I continued the use of the medicine, having a fresh analysis made after each half dozen bottles used. When I had taken 26 bottles, the last analy- sis showed : "No trace of either albumen or sugar by the severest tests.' • "Its other words, I was cured. Since then I have recommended Warner's SAFE Cure' to several per- sons where I thought it would prove beneficial, and I have not been disappointed in a single ease." In answer to the letter of inquiry as to the truth of the above statement, the following communica- tion was received from Mr. R. W. Kirkus, of 46, Baldwin-street, Bristol :—" I am writing on behalf of my father-in-law, Rev. George Waterman, who received your letter of the 22nd inst. In reply. he is very pleased to say that the statement made by him is true in: every respect, and, furthermore, that it is now more than three years since he took the Warner's Safe Cure, and he has had no return what- ever of the albumen, and considers his as a per- manent cure." Satisfied there had been no imposition in the case of the Rev. Mr. Waterman, we wrote to several other persons whose statements regarding Warner's Safe Cure we had notices' in the papers, with the following results:— Rev. Thomas Bryant, of 1, Myrtle-place, London- road, Bognor, Sussex, writes :—" Replying to your favour, I have pleasure in informing you that I can without scruple or hesitation recommend Warner's Safe Cure to any of my countrymen who may be suffering from any of the diseases this remedy is Calculated to relieve and cure. I cannot speak-of it too highly, as it has been of great benefit to myself and family." Mrs. C. Gnawing, of 29, Sydney Buildings, Bath- Wick, Bath, says :—" Whatever I have written con- cerning Warner's Safe Remedies is true. The half has not been told. I shall be happy to write fully to any one wishing further details, and tell them of the excellent effect the medicine has had in my case." The result of our investigations was so totally different from what we had expected, that out of justice to the proprietors, Messrs. H. H. Warner & Co., 47, Farringdon-street, E.C., and for the sake of suffering humanity we have decided to lay the mat- ter before our readers. We are led to do this be- cause we believe that the press should be as ready and willing to commend that which is discovered to be meritorious and worthy, as to condemn and denounce that which is wrong and misleading. The result of our inquiries proves two things: First, that the testimonials published by Messrs. 11. IT. Warner & Co. are genuine and bona fide, and se- cond, that Warner's Safe Cure has a most marvel- lous power over all diseases of the kidneys, liver, and urinary organs.—CHRISTIAN UNION, August:6th, 1886.

THE BULGARIAN QUESTION. RECEPTION Oir GENERAL KAULBARS. VIENNA, SATURDAY.—It is stated that Lord Iddesieigh is endeavouring to bring about a close rapprochment be- tween Sarnia, Bulgaria, Greece, and Turkey, and hopes that Austria will be favoura6ly disposed towards such a combination. SOFIA, SUNDAY —Gnoral KialhirS wee met yesterday some six miles outaide Soda by the Prefect of the city and the members of the Zankoff party. The Prefect bade him welcome and then one of the partisans of M. Z tnkoff ad- dressed the General, stating that the nation was happy to see him. The people had the greatest confidence in Russia, who alone could take Bulgaria under her protection and satisfy the national aspirations. General Kaulhars answered that he would he happy to telegraph to the Cztr what kind of a reception he had had la Bulgaria, especially as he knew it was not a tribute to him personally, but to the re- presentative of the Czar, who would certainly give full pro- tection te Bulgaria, on condition, however, that Bulgaria should place fall confidence in him. The General empha- sised this by repeatiug Do not forget the fullest confi- dence, for during the late events the Ru.ssian Government did not possess this cobflience." som, Mowfoas.—lt is stated on good authority that the Bulgarian Government will resist the delnande of General Saulbars, and the utmost conce-sion will probably be that at the conclusion of the judicial inquiry the persons impli- cated in the coup d'etat will simply be banished. SOFIA, WEDNESDAY, 1.5 P.M—General Kaulbars yester- day issued a circular to the Russian Consuls in Bulgaria, asking them to make known its contents to the population. The document, which is couched in violent terms, contains twelve poinV, several of which the Bulgarian Government declares Russia must know to be false. It commences by stating that the time for mere words is at end, and that the Majesty oif.e- the country internal and exter- nal can now only be convinced by acts, adding that only then-will His protection. The Bulgarians are also accused of having burnt the flags, a proceeding which General Kaulbars char- acterises as an act of indiscipline, and of having burnt eerge with the colours. This, ,however, the insignia of St. G is denied.

AFFAIRS IN BURMAH. RANGOON, suNDAs.—A Government steam launch was proceeding from Tounghoo to Ningyan with Mr. Henry Gladstone the newly-apPointed del)uty Commissioner, on board, and was attaced by 1,400 insurgents. The launch fought its way through the rebels. Of the armed guard on board one policeman was killed and several were wounded. An expedition will start immediately from Mandalay for the ruby mines. Much discontent is expressed at the secrecy observed by the Government of India as to the terms on which the ruby mines are let on lease without having been offered to public competition. The local Government is ignorant of the exict terms. It is announced, however, on good authority that no stipulations have been made that the mines shall be worked through native agency. If this course, which is opposed to the advice of Sir C. Bernard and the local Government, has been adopted serious troubles ma" be anticipated in the district PESTS, TIITIRSDAY.—In the Lower House of the Hun- garian Diet to-day, M. Tisza delivered his reply to the inter- pellations on the Bulgarian question. Ti-e House presented a most lively appearance. every seat being occupied, and the galleries being also crowded. The Premier commenced by refuting the assumption that the Austrian Foreign Office had planned the deposition of Prince Alesander, or had received any previous intimation of the plot against His Highness, or had under any conditions expressed approval of tbe coup de main. The Foreign Office was little in a position to know of these events and those which followed, as Prince Alexander, as appeared from his telegram to the Czar, regarded his crown as received direct from the Bus-

sian Emperor, and made his stay in Bulgaria dependent upon his Majesty's consent. "There exists," pro- ceeded M. TISZI, "no agreement whatever between our Government and Russia regarding the exertion of influence in either the Western or Eastern portion of the Balkan Peninsula, and such an understanding cannot there- fore be connected with any conditions. The positions ac- quired by the Monarchy through the Berlin Treaty, to which we firmly adhere, corresponds, as long as that treater is upheld, quite sufficiently with our interests. The Pre- mier then continue,d :—" I now come to my promised decla- ration. When I first had the opportunity, in 1868, to make a statement with reference to the Eastern question, I stated as my private opinion that, as regarded future events, in case of any change occurring in the East, our interests would require that the nations inhabiting that portion of Europe should form themselves into independent States corresponding to separate in- dividualities. I share the opinion of the Foreign Ministry that this view best answers to the interests of the Monarchy. and that Austria-Hungary, repudiating all de- sire of aggrandisement and conquest, should concentrate all her efforts to promote the independent development of those States and to prevent the establishment of any protectorate not provided for in treaties, or the assertion over these coun- tries of the permanent influence of any one foreign Power." This statement was preeted with loud and prolonged cheers by the Ministerialists. M. Tisza proceeded next to deal with the Austro-German alliance. He declared that there had been no change in the relations between Austria and foreign Powers, but that they remained as defined by Count Kalnokv before the delegates. 'With Germany," continued the Premier, "we stand upon the old basis!' The Government adhered firmly to its repeatedly declared opinion that in case Turkey should claim the right accorded to her in the Balkan Peninsula, no Power would be entitled to resort to armed intervention or to establish a protectorate there, and also that no chanee in the constitutional and ter- ritorial relations of the Balkan countries could be effected without the consent of the signatory Powers." The Pre- mier resumed his seat amid loud cheers from all parts of the House. SOFIA, WEDNESDAY EvENINO.—A deputation of citizens waited upon General Kaulbars to-day to present to him the opinions of the Bulgarian population. Upon being told that the nation was confident that no other Ministry than that now in authority could extricate the country from its pre- sent crisis. General Kaulbars remarked that the Czar had the prosperity of the Bulgarians at heart, but they must have confidence in his Majesty and carry out his wishes. The interview thereupon had an abrupt termination, the leader of the deputation exclaiming," If that is all you have to say, then we will retire." EARTHQUAKE IN TURKEY. CONSTANTINOPLE, SUNDAY.—A somewhat sharp shock of earthquake occurred at half-past four this morning, but no damage was done. Serraeta, SUNDAY.-1 we sharp shocks of earthquake in rapid succession were felt in this city and neighbourhood at about a quarter to five this morning. Little damage was done.

THE REVOLT IN SPAIN. MADRID, MONDAY.—On Saturday morning 38 armed men, led by a well-known Republican named Startus, rose at Espinabell, in the province of Gerona. The only troops near the scene of the rising was a small garrison of 30 men and one officer, who at once started in pursuit of the in- surgents. Coming up with them a smart engagement en- sued, in which the insaraents were routed after an boar and a halt's fighting. There were Imes on both sides. During their retreat the insurgents attacked a small military post defended by five soldiers and a sergeant. They killed the sergeant and one soldier, and afterwards crossed the frontier into France. The daughter of General Villacampa, the leader of the rising, has been with some difficulty dis- suaded by the civil authorities from going on the road to cast herself at the feet of Royalty and implore mercy for her father. The untortunate girl rushes aboat all day from one Ministerial department to another, in several instances creating harrowing scenes. The aathorities show her much deference, and allow her to spend several hours daily in her father's cell, but she is given little ground for hope. Her aunt, cousins and uncle, himself a general officer, accom- pany the girl, and the Bishop of Madrid also intercedes on her behalf, though understanding how difficult it is for the Government to grant the petition. VOLCANIC ERUPTION IN NEW ZEALAND. VVNLLINGTON, SUNDAY.—The White Island volcano in the Bay of Plenty, off the North Island coast, is in active eruption, and sanding forth a vast column of flame and smoke, rising to a height of one hundred feet. ANOTHER EARTHQUAKE AT CHARLESTON. NEW YORK, TTIESDAY.—A. fresh shock of earthquake was felt at Charleston and other places in the south at five o'clock yesterday afternoon. The inhabitants are in a state of the greatest terror, and especially the negroes, owing to the predictions of a general great earthquake to-morrow. The negroes are to be seen constantly elagazed in their de- votions, and some of the white population are suffering from nervous prostration. The persons who prophesied the oc- CUrrenee of disasters are severely denounced. THE SALVATION AII.MY IN CANADA. TORONTO, SEPT. 29m.—General Booth, of the Salvation Army, has arrived here, and was received by about a thou- sand members of the army. THE PROPOSED IMPERIAL INSTITUTE. OTTAWA, WEDNESDAY.—The Canadian Government has decided, on the re-assembling of Parliament, to apply for a vote of £20,000 as a oontribution to the proposed Imperial Institute to be established in celebration of the jubilee of Queen Victoria. Sir George Stephen and Sir Donald A. Smith have each contributed £5,000 each to the same object.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—SATURDAY On Saturday the first session of the Twelfth Parliament of Queen Victoria was prorogued. The Lord Chancellor entered the house shortly before twelve o'clock, and an- nounced that her Majesty had been pleased to grant two Conimissions—one for the purpose of giving the Royal Assent to several bills, and the other for proroguing Parlia- ment. The Prince of Wales and other peers were named as Commissioners. The Lord Chancellor then retired to the robing room, and after the lapse of a few minutes returned with the Earl of Iddesleigh, Lord Stanley of Preston, the Earl of Kintore. and Viscount Barrington, all in their peers' rubes. They took their seats on a bench in front of the throne as Lords Commissioners. The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod was at once sent to the House of Commons to request the attendaeca of the Speaker and members. The Royal Assent was given in the usual form to the Appropria- tion Act, Secret Service Money (Repeal) Act, Submarine Telegraph Act, Belfast Contruission Act, Expiring Laws Con- tinuance Act, and a number of local Acts agreed upon by both Houses of Parliament. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. The LORD CHANCELLOR said—MY lords and gentlemen, we are commanded by her Majesty to deliver you her Majesty's Speech, in her Majesty's own words. He then read the Queen's Speech, as follows : MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,—I am glad to be able to release you from your arduous duties. My relations with foreign Powers ecntind% to be friendly. The mutiny of a portien of the Bulgarian army has led to the abdication of Prince Alexander. A Regency has been established, which is now administering the affairs of the Principality, and preparations are hing made for the election of his successor in accordance with the provisions of the Treaty of Berlin. In answer to a communication addressed by the Porte to the signatory Powers, parties to that Treaty, I have stated that so far as this country is concerned there will be no in- fraction of the conditions guaranteed by Treaties to Bul- garia. Assurances to the same effect have been given by other Powers. The demarcation of the Afghan frontier Bas advanced to within a few miles of the Oxus. In view of the approach- ing of winter my Commission has been withdrawn, but the information which they have obtained will be sufficient for the determination, by direct negotiation between the two Courts, of the portion of frontier which still remains un- marked. GENTLEMEN' OF THE HOU3E OF COMMONS,—I thank you for the supplies which you have voted for the require- ments of the public service. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN.—I have directed the issue of a Commission to inquire into the circemstances which appear to have prevented the anticipated operation of re- cent Acts dealing with the tenure and purchase of land in• Ireland. I have observed with much satisfaction the interest which in an increasing degree is evinced by the people of this country in the welfare of their Colonial and Indian fellow- subjects, and I am led to the conviction that there is on all sides a growing desire to draw closer in every practicable way the bonds which unite the various portions of the Em- pire. I have authorised communications to be entered into with the principal Colonial Governments with a view tc the fuller consideration of matters of common interest. I pray that the blessing of Almighty God may be with you. The Clerk read the Royal Commission proroguing Parlia- ment to Thursday, Nov. 11th, and the LORD CHANCELLOR declared Parliament prorogued accordingly. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—SATURDAY. The Speaker toek the chair at 1-50. NOTICES AND QUESTIONS.—Several notices for next see- I sion were given and a number of questions asked.—Sir J. FERoussoN, replying to Mr. Shirley, said there was an ex- tradition treaty with Spain, concluding on the 4th June, 1578, and it was still in force. In answer to a question as to the part gevernment would take in the Queen's Jubilee C elebrations, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said it woeuit M dbe a matter of great interest to her ajesty's Govern- ment that celebrations should take place next year, and the Government will consider the question, but all celebrations of that kind will probably possess a far greater value in so far as they arise from the spontaneous action of the people. While he was speaking Black Rod was announced, and the hon. member had to resume his seat amid laughter without having completed his qaes- tion. THE PROROGATION.—AdmiraI Sir J.
