div.head: NEWTON ADJOURNED LICENSING
div.p: NEWTON ADJOURNED LICENSING
SESSIONS.

The adjourned licensing sessions for the Newton Petty Session Division were held on Saturday. The magistrates on the bench were Mr. R. Houghton, Mr. T. J. Gillespie, Mr. C. Pilkington, and Mr. W. F. Gooch. The only application was one by Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, who appeared on behalf of Stephen Auckland, for an off beer license, for a shop at 247, Winwick-road, Warrington. Mr. Browne stated that the circumstances were very peculiar. The shop was formerly licensed, but the license was refused three or four years age owing to the conviction of the then tenant for permitting drunkenness and selling during prohibited boars. The present applicant was the owner of the property, which had been leased to a certain gentleman in Warrington, and under the lease his (Mr. Browne's) client had no power whatever to control the license until the lapse of the lease. It seemed hard that that license, which was the first in the neighbourhood, should be lost through the wilful miscon- duct of a tenant overwhom his client load no power what- ever. The nearest public-house was 250 yards away, the Horse and Jockey, and there were four off licensed houses within a circle of 300 yards. Superintendent Weir said he had not a word to say against the character of the appli- cant, but there were only 205 houses, four of which were unoccupied, in the immediate locality, and it was for their worships to consider whether the requirements of the neigh- bourhood were not sufficiently provided for without increas- ing the number of licensed houses.—The Bench, after a short consultation, said the application would be refused.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND. MORE RIOTING IN BELFA.ST.-MANIFESTO OF MR. PARNELL.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND. MORE RIOTING IN BELFA.ST.-MANIFESTO OF MR. PARNELL.

Serious rioting broke out in Belfast on Sunday, resulting lin David Moore being shot through the body by the police. He is not expected to recover. Many of the police have been seriously injured by stones. Shortly after noon a dis- orderly crowd, composed chiefly of young people, assembled in Hopewell-street, which is situated between the Shankhill land Old Lodge roads, and, after challenging the police at the IShankhill-road end, and using a good deal of derisive lan- guage, some stones were thrown. The constables, to the number of eight or ten, stood this treatment for some time, but as the stones—with which all the streets in this neigh- beurhood are paved—were beginning to come so thick and fast that it was impossible for them to keep their position, one of the number hastened to Peter's Hill Barracks for reinforcements for the purpose of dispersing the rioters. These were quickly upon the scene and at once a strong charge was made up the street, the stone-throwers being dispersed in all directions. Driven out of one street, how- ever, the mob ran down another, on to the Shanklin-road, where the attack was immediately renewed, half a dozen policemen, who had been left at the corner of Hopewell. street, being the marks at which the stones were thrown. Some of them were knocked down by large pavers, one man received a dangerous scalp wound, the stone cutting right through his helmet. Realising the serious position in which they were placed, the constables who were still on their feet fired upon the mob. As stated, the young man Moore received the contents of one of the rifles while rushing into Christoper-street, the ballet, whick struck kim below the shoulder blade, entering one of his lungs. The firing of the police had the desired effect upon the rioters, who were driven off the Shankhill and adjoining streets by other bodies of police. Moore was carried into Dr. M'Mullin's surgery, where his wound was dressed, and from thence he was conveyed to the Royal Hospital. Altogether about a dozen constables have sustained serious injuries, many of them having to be taken to their respective barracks. In some of the streets between North Queen-street and York- street disturbances broke out about the same hour, but they were not serious. The police made six arrests. At night there was a good deal of excitement in the districts in which the rioting took place, but strong bodies of military and con- stabulary had been drafted into these districts. On Friday a sharp attack was made upon a patrol of con- stabulary near Ardfert, a few miles from Tralee. The patrol were attracted by what appeared to he an incendiary fire, and on proceeding to the place found two men setting fire to the furze. They arrested the men, and when they were corwayihg them to the station an attack was made upon them by a number of men and women who attempted a rescue. A free fight ensued, but the police beat off their assailants and conveyed their prisoners to the barrack. The fire was intended as a bonfire to celebrate the release from prison of a man named Healy. The two men, Mahony and Griffin. arrested in the "moon- light" affray in county Kerry on Thursday night, were charged at Liseowel on Saturday, with four other young men. with being concerned in firing on a police patrol. Constable Power stated that he and two constables, having overheard a party of men arranging to attack Mangan's public-house, concealed themselves, and confronted the party when they demanded admittance. The police summoned them to surrender; but two shots were fired, and the police then discharged their rifles and witness fired his revolver. The Moonlighters returned the fire and retreated. Witness followed and captured Griffin, who resisted. Another con- stable saw Mahony fall, and they took him to the police hut in a donkey cart. Mahony was disguised, and had a revolver. Corroborative evidence having been given, Mr. Rastray, steward of Mr. Mahoney, M.P., proved that a gun and holster like that produced were recently taken from his lodge by Moonlighters. Griffin and Mahony were com- mitted for trial, and the other prisoners were remanded. About ten o'clock on Sunday night five men, having their faces disguised, but who were not armed, were arrested by Sergeant O'Donnell and several constables as they were leaving the backyaid of Mrs Elonora Hickey's public-house at Castleisland. After conveying the men to the police station, the police returned to the place, and found a bag full of all sorts of disguises, as well as three revolvers and a sword, believed to belong to the party. Early on Monday morning a party of eight men were arrested between Farranfor and Currans, a few miles from Killarney, while in the act of carrying off a threshing machine from the premises of a farmer named Horan. The men, who were arrested by a police patrol, were conveyed to the county gaol. The farmers of county Waterford have decided not te allow any hunting to take place on their lands during the imprisonment of Father Fay. Speaking in Liverpool on Monday night, Father Sheehy said there would be no crime in Ireland during the coming winter, for the Irish people were prepared to suffer. At present special commissions were the only remedy promised to Ireland. These commissions were like the animal the Jews selected to carry their sins into the desert—the goat. Before next spring he could tell Lord Salisbury and his Cabinet there would be universal insolvency among Irish tenant farmers, and he apprehended the farmeri would clear their farms of their cattle and their houses of their chattels, and offer passive resistance to the landlords.—Mrs Parnell, who received a most enthusiastic reception, also spoke. She said Americans looked to Irishmen to uphold democratic principle in demand for Home Rule. Ireland's chance must come if they only stayed their time. England now was in the arms of Ireland, and America as well as Ireland rejoiced over this fact. Mr. Parnell has addressed the following to Mr. Fitzgerald, the President of the Irish Natioaal League of America : " The rejection of the Tenants Relief Bill, the scarcely- veiled threats of the Irish Secretary, and the alarming in- crease in the number of evictions, clearly indicate the com- mencement of a combined movement of extermation against the tenant farmers of Ireland by the English Government and the Irish landlords. I lose no time in advising you of the imminence of a crisis and peril which has seldom been equalled even in the troubled history of Ireland. I know that it will be the highest duty and the most honpurable task which can engage the attention of my countrymen in free America to do what in them 11. is to frustrate the attempts of those who would assassinate our nation and to alleviate the sufferings of those who, unhappily, must be the numerous victims of the social war which has been preached by the powerful and rich Government of England against our people. In sending us that moral and material assistance which has never been wanted, never been stinted, from your side of the Atlantic, you will perform two most important and valuable functions; you will encourage the weak to resist and bear oppression, you will also lessen and alleviate these feelings of despair in the minds of the evicted which have so often and so unhappily stimul ted these victims to a recourse to the wild justice of, revenge. In doing so you will assist in preserving for our movement that peaceable character which has enabled it to win its most re- cent and at most crowning triumph,while you will strengthen it to bear oppression and encourage our people until the final goal of legislative dependence has been won." At a meeting of the National League in a)oistn, on Toes- day, Mr. Dillon, M.P., who presided, said Mr. Par- nell's Bill was brought forward with a honest desire to tide over the winter. It was rejected, and if Parliament would not redress the grievances of the people. then the people must win by organisation and lawful resistance the neces- sary concession, just as they had done in 1880. There was some disturbance on Wednesday, in North Howard-street. The emplovei in Messrs. Combs, Barbour, and Combe's foundry stoned each other. Soon large mobs collected from the adjoining Shankhill-road and Falls-road districts. A large force of constabulary proceeded to the place, and were severely stoned. The police charged the rioters. Afterwards the mobs were dispersed by infantry and cavalry, and matters quieted down, but there was a good deal of excitement up to a late hour. Three arrests were made.

PAWNING A MEDAL.-At Greenwich, on Tuesday, John D. Urry, pawnbroker, was charged with taking in pledge a silver medal of the Egyptian War of 1882, which had been sent to the pawnshop by a drunken soldier of the Shrop- shire Regiment. The defendant was fined £3 and treble the value of the medal. CoNnissioN or MURDER.—A man named Edward Bren- nan, who is in the custody of the Glossop police on cnarges of assault and vagrancy, has made a statement to the effect that be committed a murder at Middlesbrough two years ago. In June, 1884, the body of a little girl named Cooper was found in the park at Middlesbrough, and it was clear that she had been brutally outraged and afterwards mur- dered. A reward was offered for the discovery of the cul- prit, but nothing more was heard of the matter until Bren- nan made his confession. The Middlesbrough police are inquiring into the truth of hie story.

div.p: TME SCHOOLS COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee stated that the superinten- tendent of the schools at Padgate had reported the general health of the children to be excellent. The committee having considered the report of the sub-committee as to the purchasing of shoemaking machinery for the use of the school, recommended that the necessary plant be got from Messrs. Pearson and Bennion, Leicester, at a coat of 44 Is. —On the motion of the CHAIRMAN the minutes of the com- mittee were pas,.ed.

THE ESTIMATES, The CLERK read a statement with regard to the estimates as follows :—The estimates of contributions required from the varieue townships in the Union for the half year ending at March, 1887, has formally been laid before your Board. The call made at Lady Day last was for £12;343, making with a balance then in hand of £743, a total capital for the half year ending tbis week of £13,086. The estimated ex- penditure to the close of the same half year is as follows: Separate charges, 118; common charges, £8,108; county rates, £2,677; total, £10,973 ; leaving in the treasurer's hands a probable balance of £2113. The esti.nates your Board are now therefore invited to approve provides £lBB for separate charges, £8,364 common charges, £2,290 county rates, and £1,394 the usual propertion to meet expenditure before another call can be made, the total probable outlay for the half year ending March, 1887, thus being £12.236. Deducting £2,113 from this sum, leaves the actual contribu- tion to be fixed to-day at £10,123. The cost of " mainten- ance " in the correspondini, half of last year was £2,323 us 4d, and a sum of £2,300 under that head is now pro- vided. "Out relief" in the same period amounted to £2,047 105 3d, and, contrary te our usual experience, the expenditure under that head will it is estimated have risen in the expiring summer half year to £2,110 4s 4d, it has therefore been deemed prudent now to provide £2,300. For lunatic account £LIOO is fixed, compared to an expenditure in the same corresponding half of last year of £1,149 135 3d. Under other heads the actual expenditure in the same period was so approximative with the present estimates as not to require exceptional reference to the figures, and it is only desirable to say that it is confidently anticipated that the capital to be provided will amply cover all the demands, and it may also be hoped that a liberal balance will remain at the close of the financial year.—Mr. JOLLEY moved, and Mr. HELTON seconded, that the estimates be approved, and that the calls be made on the various townships in accord- ance therewith.—Tbe motion was carried. THE EARLESTOWN VACCINATION OFFICER The CLERK mentioned that some time ago in ac- cordance with a promise mide to Mr. Cooper, the Board, considering the work which he had done for which he had not been paid, such as • at- tendance at Petty Sessions, Jac., allowed him £lO. The matter went to the Local Government Board for their ap- proval, and he (the clerk) had not been able to understand why there shouU have been so long a delay before the allowance was sanctioned. He now had a letter from the Local Government Board referring to his communication, and the matter had probably been before the law officers, because the Local Government Board stated that they found it was doubtful whether in such a case as that they could allow the £lO, and therefore in order to meet the difficulty they proposed to amend the regulations so far as that Union was concerned, so that the allowance might be made. It would be necessary for the Board to repeat their resolution when the amendment had been made.

div.head: GRAPPENHA.LL ELECTION.
div.p: THE GRAPPENHA.LL ELECTION.

The CLERK announced that the result of the cerrespon- dance on the subject of the Grappenhall election was that on Monday next, the 4th October, Mr. Stephens, Local Government Boaid Inspector, would hold a final inquiry, when he would take into consideration the last cases that could be objected to by Mr. Woods and Mr. Derbyshire. "BLIND JOE." The CLERK read a letter from the Rey. W. R. Parry, bringing before the Board the case of the blind lad, Joseph Finch, who is best known in Warrington by the name of "Blind Joe," and asking them to use their influence to get the lad admitted to a school for the blind. An accompany- ing note in supnort of Mr. Parry's application was also read from the Rev. J. Yonge.—Some discussion took place with regard to the case, the CHAIRMAN .nentioning that it had been before them twice or thrice already, and Mr. Heaton bad kindly taken an interest in the case and made inquiries. —Mr. lis,vrox said he had called at the Liverpool institu- tion for the blind, and after some conversation with the manager he was told that under no circumstances could they take Ow lad in there. With regard to the Old Trafford in- stitution, he was afraid there was no prospect of his teeing taken in there.—lt was also mentioned that Finch was by no means a pauper, and had, in fact, got money in a bank, and it was decided that this was a case the Board could not deal with.
SCHOOL FEES. The School Fees Committee rewirted that fees had been allowed in 70 cases, 47 of which were old and 23 new cases.

THE WINTER'S PROSPECT. The CHAIRMAN said they bad not yet reached the end of September, yet the workhouse on the women's side, was already filled, while OR the other side there was room for only 18 more. He was, therefore, afraid that daring the coming winter they would require more accommodation to meet the cases—Mr. JOHN HOUGHTON asked if tin school buildings could not be utilised.—The Clamx re- marked that this was a matter for the special consideration of the House Committee. If they found that the house was already full in the month of September they should at once act; they should suggest some means whereby the difficulty was to be met. In the estimates he had provided £3OO more under the head of out-relief than in the corre- sponding period of last year.—The CHAIRMAN said that the want of accommodation in the house disarmed them in giv- ing relief ; they could not then offer people an order for the workhouse.—The CLERK: I was going to say that £3OO would never do unless you could give orders for the house. —Mr. JOLLEY was under the impression that without much structural alterations a larger portion of the house might be used for the inmates, and they might, perhaps, tide over the difficulty in that way.—Dr. MACKIE suggested that, before expending any serious sum of money, they should consider whether it would net be much better to gather together all their offices in one place in the town. That could be done without absolutely incurring any extra expenditure, and it would enable them to add the offices they now meet in to the workhouse. He believed that they paid as much rental in the town for offices as would enable a proper building, devoted entirely to themselves, to be erected. —The CHAIRMAN had no doubt that in the event of their being compelled to make additions to the workhouse some such steps as those suggested by Dr. Mackie would be taken. At present, however, he thought it was premature to discuss the matter.—The discussion then dropped.

An address has been issued to the trades of the United Kingdom, inviting subscriptions towards the proposed testi- monial to Mr. John Burnett, late treasurer to the Parliamen- tary Committee of the Trades Union Congress. SIR M. HICKS-BEACH AND IRELAND.—A London corres- pondent writes :—Six Michael Hicks-Beach intends to spend some time in Ireland, and ascertain as far as he can what 'is the real position of affairs. The Chief Secretary is an honest, though not a brilliant, official, and I do not believe that be would willingly support or countenance injustice. It is to be hoped that he will not restrict his inquiries to landlords, magistrates, and police. If he wants to learn what is the real condition of the country, be should consult men who have the confidence of the people, like the Catholic bishops and the better class of priests, and who know something of their real condition. Many of the mis- takes of the Executive in Ireland have arisen from its de- voting itself too exclusively to one interest or party. If the Chief Secretary really endeavours to obtain from the best sources information as to the true condition of the country, he must avoid this serious mistake. I believe that the Land Commission will begin its inquiries about the latter part of October.

div.head: RUGBIL RULES.
div.p: RUGBIL RULES.

/ TRUE BLUES V. SAXON OLD BOTS.—A, match was played on Satueday between Warrington True Blues and Sixon Old Boys, and at(the call of time the score stood—Old Boys, ona goal, three minors; Blues, nil. Lowa HOUSE 'IRUE BLUES V. WARRINGTON HORNETS.— On Saturday these teams met on the ground of the Hornets, at Warrington, and although it rained during the whole of the afternoon a very interesting game was gone through. The Hornets only scored one minor during the whole of the ' game, while the Blues' score was two goals and twelve minor points. For the Blues, Unsworth and Baines, at three-quarter, played a splendid game, an the whole of the forwards, without any exception, played in grand form. For the Hornets, Mason, Marwood, and Litherland played exceedingly well. WIDNES V. ST. HELENS RECREATION. The Widnes team turned out for the first time on Saturday, when they encountered St. Helens recreation at Widnes. The home team were attired in the new jerseys adopted by the club, and their appearance was much smarter than for. The weather was very unfavourable for the sport, and militated against good play. Morris and Harding made several capital runs for Widnes, who had rather the best of the play. The game resulted, however, in a draw, each team scoring one try and one minor point. The try for Widnes was gained by Parkinson from a pass by Bing- ham, who made a capital run. The following were the teams :—Widnes : Full back, F Plumpton ; three-quarter backs, S Morris, D Harding, and 8 Bingham ; half-backs, R Barker and J Parkinson ; forwards, Kiddie, Smith, J Bingham, Pervin, Wilkinson, Fogg, Spencer, Hughes, and Hardman. St Helens Recreation: Full back, Taylor; three-quarter hacks, Doyle, Hodgkinson, and Pike ; half- backs, Rankin and Roberts ; forwards, R Twist, W Dean, J Gaskell, J Fletcher, H Gregson, Albert Smith, Harry Ash- ton, J Gabbitas, andJ Hankinson. Mr J J Latham was umpire for Widnes, and Mr Whhaveats, of Runcorn, officia- ted as referee.

COCKREDGE MISSION STAR OF HOPE T. WIDNES TRUES BLUES.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday in the presence of a goodly number of spectators. The home captain won the toss and elected to play against the wind. Clare kicked off for the visitors, who were the first to draw blood, as soon after the start the home team were forced to save. From the drop out Whalley got possession and put in a short run and kick to witch. After the line-out corns tight scrimmages took place, the home team having rather the advantage. Jest before half-time Whalley got hold from a scrimmage, but being pressed, transferred to Lin- gard, who kicked the ball over the line, and Shaw follow- ing well up gained a try. Adcroft was entrusted with the place kick and put the ball over the centre of the loAr in a neat fashion. Tne home team tried hard to equalise, and after a nice bit of play their efforts were rewarded with a try, but the kick at goal failed. Half-time having been , called the home team kicked off with the wind and ground in their favour. The home forwards came with a deter- mined dribble, but Habberley saved nicely by a screw into touch. Nothing more of interest was noted, as scrimmages were the order for the rest of the afternoon. At the call of time the visitors were declared the winners of a hard game by one goal and two minors to one try and three minors. Star of Hope Team: Full back, Lemax ; three-quarter backs, Lingard, Whalley, and Habberley ; half-backs, Black- more and Shaw; forwards, Whittaker, Phoenix, Hope, Kirkham. Ratlabone, Clare. Harrop, Adcroft, and a stMti- tute ; umpire, Mr. J. Todd. WARRINGTON (A TRAM) v. HIGHPIELD.—The A team journeyed to Highfield, on Saturday, in very boisterous weather, which, however, did not damp the spirits of these players, as will be seen by the result of the game. The kick-off was effected by H. Pennington for Highfield at four p.m. Ashurst returned by a good high kick, and Molyneux, in following well up, prevented the opposing full back from returning. From the scrimmage which fol- lowed Appleton obtained possession, and after making a smart ran passed to Walsh, the latter having very hard lines in not scoring. The home team strongly resented this conduct, and took the ball a few yards; but all to no effect, for immediately afterwards the Warrington forwards en masse cleared everything before them to the goal line, and Walsh, securing the ball, passed smartly to Appleton, the latter obtaining a capital try. The try at goal was practically useless, on account of the soft state ef the ball; nevertheless, the attempt by Walsh nearly succeeded. The ball was no sooner brought into play than it was rushed over again, and Pennington was compelled to touchdown. The play at this point of the game was very sharp on both sides, and was assuming an even character when Whittle obtained possession and secured a try after a splendid run, Walsh failing at goal after another capital attempt. Some good loose play followed, until the home team were again overpowered by the sweeping manner in which the visitors' forwards played, and Hill was frequently compelled to touch down till the call of half-time. On resuming the game the visitors again were the first to score by a touch down. The home team now made another effort to mend matters, and commenced operations by accidentally mal- treating their umpire, who, by the way, had the misfortune , to get entangled in a scrimmage, and looked a most pitiful obisct when rescued. Jones afterwards obtained possession, and finally deposited the leather over the goal line, but the attempt at goal was fruitless. Highfield was at last enabled to score by compelling the home team to touch down, and from the kick out Forster obtained the only try for their side. When time was called Warrington was left victorious by three tries and four minors to one try and one minor. Teams:—Warrington: Full back, Hewitt; three-quarter backs, Massey, Appleton, and Randal's; half-backs, Whittle (captain) and Walsh; forwards, Molyneux, Jones, Nevins, , Littlewood, Nicossoraßigby, AshnrA, Antrobus, and Cragan. ' Highfield: Full back, Tipping; three-quarter backs, Hill, P Forster, and T Forster; half backs, H Pennington and W Pennington; forwards' r S Pennington, Waterworth, Mell- ing, Bryan, T Walsh, Wood, Beardsmore, W Forster, and J Forster.

div.head: RUNCORN V. CASTLEFORD.
div.p: RUNCORN V. CASTLEFORD.

Castleford sent a strong team on Saturday to Runcorn, to oppose the local fifteen, when a stubbornly contested game was witnessed by nearly two thousand enectators. When the teams entered the field rain was fallir. ; heavily, and the ground was quickly soaked, and its slipp, 'y condition, mili- tated against good play amongst the backs. Runcorn placed a strong combination in the field. In the forward division were W 'Hughes, W 0 right, G Wainwright, J Lewis, W H Broady, J Dean, J Barns, J Clarke, and J Faulkner. On the arrival of Broady, who made his first appearance, he re- ceived an ovation. By his sterling work later on he justi- fied the compliment. H Hughes l(captain) and U Andrews occupied their old positions as half backs, while the three- quarter places were filled by H C Speakman, E Lunt. and T Davies. The goal was protected by T Woods. On the Castleford side were—Hanson, full back; G H Jones, Ham- mond, and Moreton,three-quarter backs; Scott and Clarkson, half backs ; Phillips, Cockcroft, Chappell, Abquith, Jones, Brooke, J H Brooke, Tate, and Adams composed the forward division. An even and stubbornly contested game resulted in a draw—Castleford, 3 minor points; Runcorn, 2 minor points.

WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON RANGERS. This match was played on the ground of the former, off Wilderspool-causeway, on Saturday. The weather was very unfavourable for football, there being a heavy downpour of rain, but at the time of starting some 3,000 spectators had assembled round the rapes to witness the encounter. The Rangers set the ball in motion, the first scrimmage taking place in the visitors' 25. Some very good scrimmages were next the order ef the day, until Simpson obtained posses- sion, and gained a lot of ground, but was well collared by Barnes. again scrimmages were the order of the day, and the Broughton forwards coming through seemed to be dan- gerous, but Boardman was equal to the occasion, and saved grandly. Play was now confined to the visitors' 25, but; bard as they tried, the Warringtonians could not score. Robertson next showed prominently, but was tackled by Barnes before being dangerous. The little centre three- quarter next made an excellent run, and gained a lot of around. At this period of the game an amusing incident took place. Speakman, on the ball emerging from a scrim- mage, passed very nicely, the ball falling into the hands of Barnes, the umpire, who looked as if he would have liked to have run a try in for his side. Barnes again obtained pos- session, and by s splendid dodgy run, cleverly eluding the vigilance of Robertson, the celebrated county three-quarter, got over the line, thus scoring the first try for Warrington amidst the applause of the spectators, Sneakman did the needful in the shape of goal kicking. Shortly afterwards half time was called, with the ball in the home 25, the Ringers' forwards, after the centre three-quarter had got over, seeming to play with more energy. After the usual interval Frank Turner kicked off for Warrington, and the forwards, following well up, prevented its return. Scrimmages were again the order of the day, but Ashton eventually came through, and took the ball close to the line. Heyes was next conspicuous by stopping a splendid rush of the Rangers' forwards. After they had taken the ball from the visitors' 25 to the home quarter, a good scrimmage took place. The ball going over the hue a maul ensued between Unsworth and Farrar, the Rangers' forward having the best of it, thus scoring a try for the visitors. The kick at goal was unsuccessful. From now until the end of the game the Warringtonians vemed to have the best of it, but by a lucky loose scrimmage on the part of the Rangers' forwards the ball was taken over the line. This was owing to a mistake on the part of Bux- ton, which the Rangers took advantage of. Buxton should have touched down, but instead kicked out, and the kick teitag weak the Rangers rushed the ball over, and one of them fell upon it. The kick at goal proved fail!, and Warrington thus won the match by one goal and a minor to two tries. On behalf of Warrington Barnes was the best in the back department, his splendid runs and kicks arous- ing the enthusiasm of the spectators, and his good judgment and play was too much for his opponent on'the opposite , side. Gilbert and Speakman at half back played a good game, but had not many chances of passing to the three- quarters, the collaring of the former being of the best des- cription. In the ranks of the forwards iFair Turner, Frank Turner, Heyes, Rigby, Ashton, and Hughes—the latter of whom played excellently—did their utmost to beat the cele- brated team. Simpson and RohPrtson were the two shining lights in the back department ef the Ringers' team, while W. Teggin, Farrar, and Atkinson were the best in the front ranks. Teams :—Warrington; Full back, Buxton; three- quarter backs, Boardman, Barnes, and Unsworth ; half backs, Gilbert and Speakman; forwards, Fair Turner, Frank Tur- ner, Ashton, Heyes, Rigby, Hughes, Hough, Davies, and Povey. Broughton Rangers: Goal, Jackson; three-quarter

backs, Farrar, Robertson, and J. Todd; half backs, S. Simp- qpn and A. Moxon ; forwards, Atkinson, Smith, Royle, A. G. Harrison, Squires, Powell. Bradson. W. Teir:r.in, and Wall. Umpires, Messrs. Barnes and McNiel ; referee. Mr, Parry, Liverpool.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.
Bootle, Wavertree, Tuebrook, Southport Olympic, St. Helens, St. Helens Recreation, Widnes, and Runcorn have arranged fixtures similar to those of last season.

"To the goals," as was Tom Brown of old, we are enthu- siastically called, and as enthusiastically we wend our way to the arenas where our nineteenth-century gladiators engage in friendly and bloodless combat. Are our local Associa- tionists more energetic, more zealous, or more speculative than their Rugby confreres, that they have been so long afield? We fear, indeed, that the dribbling game is taking a firmer bold of the football-loving public, and Rugby play- ers must look to their laurels if they desire their number of admirers to wane not. Two clubs of honourable repute in I our midst have entirely failed to keep their heads above , water, and must now be associated only with the past. Far I from weakening the cause of football, however, such acci- dents often tend to its strength, for the more ardent spirits of the deceased add to the ranks of the existing. We have in our midst several widely-known clubs, the locus .standi of each of which is of the highest class, who are still doing their best to foster the Rugby game in the district, whilst the young but flourishing West Lancashire Union will again do its utmost to show us how well it deserves the support it has been accorded.—" Liver- pool Mercury." In the National competition. Queen's Park are drawn against Preston North End. In the Lancashire Senior Cup ties, North End are drawn against Blackburn Rovers. In the Birmingham district. Aston Villa have to meet West Bromwich Albion; whilst in the local Cup competition, Bootle and Everton came out as the last "draw." _

In the Lancashire Senior Challenge Cup competition Fishwick Ramblers and Higher Walton dechled their tie in the first round at Walton Brow. Mather scored for Higher Walton in four minutes, and at half time the home team were three goals to none. On crossing over Higher Walton added a fouth goal, when the Ramblers scored three in suc- oession. They, however, were not able to equalise the scare, and lost the game by four goals to three. Broughton met Wigan on Saturday when the game re- sulted in a victory for Broughton by one goal, one try, and four minors to four minors. Salford and Bradford met on Satyay, when a pleasant game ended in a draw.

div.head: PR ESCOT-
div.p: PR ESCOT-

CONSERVATIVE CLUB.-- On Saturday last the above club had their annual excursion to Belle Vue. Between three and four hundred psrsons availed themselves of the oppor- tunity of visiting this popular resort. ZION SIIND&Y Scaom.—Sermons were preached in the new Assembly Hall, on Sunday, by Mr. W. Sanderson, of Liverpool. In the afternoon an address was delivered to Sunday scholars by Miss Ellen Robinson, of Blundell Sands, a member of the Society of Friends. Collections were made after each service in aid of the Sunday School.

PARISH CHURCH. - The harvest 'thanksgiving services were continued on Sunday last, when sermons were preached morning and evening by the Right Rev. the Bishop of Soder and Man. In the afternoon an address was delivered to the children by the Rev. H. S. Bolton, vicar of Raven' head.

DAMAGING TELEGRAPH WIRE INSULATORS.-At the Pros- cot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Colonel W. W. Pil- kington, and Mr. W. L. Evans, James Wilson and Edward INl'Manus, two rough-looking young men, were brought up charged with doing wilful damage to certain telegraph wire insulators. Police-constable 1,152 proved that he saw the prisoners throw stones at the insulators on some telegraph wire poles on Sunday afternoon, on the Liverpool-road, Huyton, and do damage to the extent of is. The inspector of the postal telegraph department stated that a great amount of damage to similar insulators in the district bad been done recently. The Bench imposed a fine of 203 and costs, or one month's imprisonment with hard labour in de- fault.

SCENE AT PEESCOT LICENSING COURT—The adjourned Licensing Sessions for the Preecot Petty Sessional Division were held on Tuesday, in the Court-house, Derby-street, before Mr. W. L. Evans and Colonel W. Pilkington. At eleven o'clock, the time announced for the business of the court to commence, only Mr. Evans had arrived. After waiting for some time, and the second resident magistrate not appearing, a telephone communicatiou was sent to the St. Helens Police Station. At twenty-five minutes to ene o'clock, after a delay of an hour and thirty-five minutes, Colonel W. W. Pilkington arrived from St. Helens as a sub- stitute. The delay ceased by the non-attendance of the second justice on the bench caused considerable inconveni- ence to those in court. After the preliminary business bad been disposed of, Mr. F. W. Hartley, solicitor, made an ap- plication to the bench for a temporary transfer on behalf of a Mr. Bennett, who resides at Morecambe, the owner of a house 16, Waterloo-road, Widnes. Unfortunately, through no fasilt of his (Mr. Hartley's), the person in whose posses- ' sion the license was which was granted at the last annual licensing meeting was not present. He was present at eleven o'clock that morning, but had since had to leave. He (Mr. Hartley) would ask for an adjournment till next Tuesday.—The Clerk to the bench (Mr. C Spencely) saki he had no case at present on which the bench could ad- journ.—Mr. Hartley said there appeared to be some dispute as to whether this license had been granted or not.—The Clerk again said there was no Case to adjourn.—Mr. Hart- ley: The clerk cannot deny that the gentleman who has the license has been here this morning.—The Clerk: Do not you see you are not making an application to the magistrates. If you want the magistrates to grant something you must tell what it is.—Mr. Hartley: I am making an application now for a license which is now in force, and which does not expire till the 10th of October.—The Clerk: Had not you better tell the bench what it is P—Mr. Hartley: It is for a license to sell beer off the premises. It is a temporary transfer, or in other words a permit.—The Clem: Would you be good enough to make the application properly—if Mr. Bennett lives in Widnes or in the moon? You have not described the license.—Mr. Hartley: The license is made out in the name of a person named Laurie Miller. of Waterloo-road, Widnes.—The Clerk: Is he the occupier ? Mr. Hartley: Ido not know. Mr. Hartley explained that be had not the license in his possession at court.—The Clerk: Then you have no case.—The Chairman: Then we decline to hear you.—Mr. Hartley: Upon what grounds?— The Chairman : You have no authority for this.—Mr. Hart- ley: And that is the ground on which you decline to hear me ?—The Chairman: You are oat of order now.—Mr. Hartley: lam not out of order.—The Chairman: You are out of order, and you will obey the ruling of the court.—Mr. Hartley: I am not out of order, and I will repeat it.—The court then rose.

VVESLEYAN BIND or HOPE.—A miscellaneous entertain- ment was given OR Tuesday evening, when Mr. Bradburn, of Liverpool, gave an address. The chair was occupied by Mr. John Jones. Recitations, &c., were given by J. McGre- gor Gore, William Jandrill, Mr. H. Connah, Eliz. Atherton, Lo....isa Crites.lev, and Mr. John C. Leadbetter. A collec- tion was made to defray expenses.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The forthigt.tly meeting of the Prescst Board of Guar- dians was held on Thursday at the Whiston Workhouse. Mr. J. Lowe, the chairman, piesided, and there were also present the Revs. C. W. Wool, and T. Finegan; Messrs. J. W. Wareing, E. Syder, J. Wkalley, J. Fisher, J. Griffiths, J. Kenwright, C. B. Johnson, J. Matthews, J. Jackson, J. Ranson, J. Buckley, W. Swift, H. Hulme, T. Eatock, J. Burchall, P. Middlehurst, J. Ellison, W. Middlehurst, P. Longton, W. Birchall, W. Gerrard, and S. H. Hartley, (clerk). RELIEF RETURNS —The Workhouse Master reported that there were 495 inmates of the house this week, against 489 last week, and 401 in the corresponding week of last year. DISCHARGE OF FEMALE PATYPERS.—From the minutes of a special meeting of the Board it appeared that a consider- able number of women and children had been discharged from the Workhouse, and the Rev. Father Finegan said he would like to know if the women were widows or deserted wives. a they were women with children and with no means ef support he did not see what was the use of dis- charging them.—Mr. W. Burchall said some of them were deserted women, who had been in the house over the proper term of three years, and some were able-bodied women with one child, some of whom had been in the house over four or five years. All the women were capable of getting their own living.—The matter dropped. MEDICAL OFFICER FOR WIDNES.—The Local Govern- ment Board wrote sanctioning the appointment of Dr. Cooper as the medical officer of the Union for the Widnes (Lower) Division at a salary of £7O per annum. APPLICATION FOR INCREASE OF SALARY.—Dr. Casey, medical officer for the Parr and Sutton districts of St. Helens, applied for an increase of salary. The matter was referred to the Finance Committee. THE WATER SUPPLY.—A letter was read from Mr. Coun- cillor William Longton, of Ecclesten Grange, the owner of a quarry from which the water supply of the Workhouse is derived, stating that he was about to sell the quarry, and giving the Guardians the first opportunity of purchasing it. A committee of the whole Board was appointed to consider the question. PAUPER PATIENTS.—The Clerk submitted a reply be bad prepared regarding the negotiations with the' St. Helens Corporation au the admission of pauper patients into the St. Helens Infectious Diseases Hospital. The Chairman considered the circumetances were justly described, and it was decided to forward the reply to the Local Government Board.

THE TesK-MISTRESS.—Mr. W. Birchall moved the ap- pointment of Miss F. McCulloch as task-mistress at the workhouse.—The Rev. Thomas Finegan moved an amend- ment that the question be considerod two months hence. —The amendment was carried by fourteen votes to eight. It was decided to remunerate Miss McCulloch for the time she had been on trial in the house. A WIDNES ASSESSMENT.-Mr. Wareing, said that as an individual member of the Board of Guardians he had re- ceived a communication from Mr. Richard White, manager of the Widnes Limestone Co, informing him that if the Guardians did not take steps to lower the existing assess- ment upon those works they would be compelled to close them.—The Clerk remarked that the Guardians had nothing to do with the assessments, and the matter entirely lay in the hands of the Assessment Committee. Mr. White had previously appeared before the committee and knew very well how to go about the method of getting the assessment reduced. This was the principal business.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.
Mr. A

Aneus Sutherland, M.P., leaves for America next week to lecture on the Crofter question. THE REVENUES.—The revenue returns for the quarter just expired show a net increase of receipts to the amount of £487,466 on the corresponding quarter of last year. In Customs there wss an increase of £478,000, and in pro- perty and income tax an increase of £170,000. • ANOTHER Mier, Fuse—Fire broke out on Wednesday evening in the Providence Mill, Hyde, thepropertyof Messrs. Walker and Sons, cotton spinners. The main portion of the building was destroyed, but other parts of the mill were saved. Damage estimated at £30,000 was caused, and a large number of operatives will be deprived of employment. The fire is supposed to have originated through friction in the machinery. A CLOWN'S "BENEFIT"—The Newport (Monmouth) magistrates have tined a professional clown, named James Bosiv, 10s, for extraordinary vagaries by way of advertising his benefit. The defendant perambulated the main thoroughfares on stilts nearly 20ft. high. He unhooked a pair of boots hanging over one shop window and slung them across a sk,nboard on the opposite side of the road. He peered into sevsral bedrooms,to the aneoyance of several females, and indulged in other freaks. A GIRL BURNT TO DEATH.—A fatal fire occurred OR Monday in the dwelling .house of Mr. Israel Sugarman, tailor, Strangewsys, Manchester. Mr. Sugarman's daugh- ter. a eel about seven years of age, took a light into the cellar, and accidentally set fire to some shavings and rags. Her father rushed into the cellar, and found his daughter lying helpless in the flames. He snatched her up, and she was at once tak-n to the Infirmary, bat died on the way. Mr. Sugarman was also burnt about the hands and face. EXCITING SCENE IN A POLICH COURT.—At Oldham, on Saturday, James Inman was charged with disorderly con- duct, and was led into the deck by two constables. He started wildly, and the chief constable said the prisoner was suffering from delirium tremens. The prisoner made a spring, endeavouring to jump over the dock rail, and a number of police held him down. Some female prisoners screamed, and rushed round the dock. The prisoner was remanded, and a struegle took place between him and a number of constables. MIRACULOUS ESCAPE FROM DEATH —As an express train was leaving Carmarthen railway station on Saturday a coun- try farmer hurried on the platform and made a rush at the train, when he slipped beneath the carriage, and was sus- pended between the footbard and the iron work of the car- riage. Piercing cries were raised by people on the platform, and after the train bed proceeded several hundred yards it was brought to a stand-still, when it was discovered that the man was wedged tightly in the framework ef the carriage, and was apparently unhurt. THE ASSAULT 0% AN ELDER BY A PRESBYTERIAN MINIS,. TER.—At Manchester City Police-court, on Monday, the hearing of the charge of assault preferred againet the Rey. J. Mackie, minister of the Scotch National Church, Blooms- bury, by Mr. John Carswell, an elder of that church, was resumed before Mr. Headlam (stipendiary), Mr. J. A. Beith, and Mr. Fisher. Among the spectators in ceurt were many members of Mr. MAckiet's congregation. Mr. Mackie was then committed for trial to the sessions, bail being allowed him on producing one surety of £lO. A DANGEROUS PLAYTIIING.—On Saturday morning, shortly after ten o'clock, a boy named Samuel Hughes, liv- ing with his parents at 47, Mazzini-street, Liverpool, was playing with a canister of gunpowder in the house, when it Accidentally fell on the hearth where a piece of paper was burning. The gunpowder exploded with a loud report, burning the lad in a shocking manner on the body, arms, and face. He was at once removed to the East Dispensary, where he was attended to by Dr. Campbell. and from thenee - he was taken to the Royal Inflrmary,where he lies in a cried+ oil state. TERRIBLE TRAPrZB ACCIDENT —A painful accident ec- curred on Thursday in the hippodrome at Lille. Two sisters were performing on the flying trapeze under the cupola of the establishment, when the ropes broke, and they were precipitated to the floor—a terrible distance. The eldest sister, Ile'ke Aragon, had her thigh broken and a wriet put out of joint. The other sister fell on the netting placed below to receive the trapezists after their leaps from the ceiling, and rebounded from it to the ground. She WU unhurt, although, like her injured sister, she was totally in- sensible. GREAT MILL FIRE.—A fire broke out on Tuesday afto. noon in the upper portion of a large mill in Heywood, owned and worked by the Roach Mills Spinning and Manu- facturing Company, Limited. The flames spread with great rapidity, assisted by the strong breeze, and befog* long the toot of the building fell in. The warehouse, in which was a large stock of raw and manufactured cotton and machinery, was also destroyed. A man named Whittaker was severely injured by the fall of a stone from the roof. The damage which is partially covereel by insurance, is estimated at be- tween £15,000 and £20,000. EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDINGS AT PICKMERE very unusual scenes have been witnessed at Pickmere, near Knutsford, this week. Lord de Tabley end the other riparian owners had required all owners of pleasure boats to remove them f?om the Mere, and in default of compliance bailiffs were sent to seize the boats. They were set upon by a mob with sticks and stones, and were obliged to retreat. The boat owners, provided with blankets and provisions, put off to the centre of the Mere, where they intend to stay SO long as eeizure is threatened. Their livelihood depends I upon letting the boats to excursionists, and they claim an immemorial right. ' A RUNAWAY FIRE ENGINE—FOUR MEN INJURED.— On Friday night, about eight o'clock, the Farowo:-th Fire Brigade turned out to a false alarm of a mill fire. Whilst returning from the scene the horses attached to the hose car took fright and bolted. In the terrible ride which fol- lowed through the crowle I streets four firemen, named res- pectively Fernworth, Schofield, Shorrocks, and Howarth, were hurled from their seats on the car and received most serious injuries, mostly about the head and legs, the last named being the worse hurt. The affrighted horses were run into a tram car when stopped. Great excite- ment prevailed, and many pedestrians narrowly escaped being run over. IRISH Evicrreeers.—NovEr. ExHinrrecre.—ln the event of the Irish landlords turning out a great many of their tenants, the Irish party intend to have an exhibitioe of evic- ted tenants in Great Britain. One of the mud cabins from the West of Ireland, dismantled by the crowbar brigade, will be placed upon a waggon, and accompanying it will be a, number of tenants, men, women, and children, in the exact condition in which they were when they were ex- pelled from their !Tomes. It is believed that an exhiNtien of this kind, bringing home to the minds ot the people of Great Britain the kind of cabins in which the peasants of the West of Ireland live and the position and dress of these , poor people, would be more effective than a thousand speeches. RELIGIOUS INTOLERANCE.—At Madrid, Spain, on Sunday evening last, &Protestant congregation -were in the midst of service in a chapel established there 12 years ago in a house which is the domicile of British subjects, when suddenly the Alcalde or Mayor, followed by several policemen and other persons, knocked loudly at the door with his baton of office, entered the courtyard and the chapel, and summoned the clergyman to leave the pulpit, threatening him with im- prisonment if be disobeyed. He also ordered the congrega- tion to disperse. When the clergyman protested and asked ' the meaning of such an interference, the Alcalde replied evasively, pretending that the singing disturbed the neigh- bours. It is to be remarked, however, that the neighbours had never complained before. The same Alcalde persistently refuses to allow the Protestant schools to be re-opened. LORD R. CHURCHILL AND THE PCOTTISH PROTESTANT ' ALLIANCE —The committee of the Manchester branch of the Church Association on Friday forwarded the following resolution to Lord Randolph Churchill :—" This com- mittee desires to expiess its'astonishment and deep pain at the reply Lord Randolph Churchill sent to the resolu- tion forwarded by the committee of the Scottish Protes- taet Alliance protesting against the appointment of a Roman Catholic Secretary of State for the Home Office— a reply evidently arising from his lordship's utter want - of knowledge of the system of Romanism and of its aims and objects in this country, which are the subversion of the Protestant Constitution of the realm and its subju- gation to the despotism of the Papacy, from which we were so mercifully delivered at the glorious Reformatien ; and this committee further deplores the alliance evidently in force bettveen the Conservative party and Roman Catholicism." MR. GLADSTONE AND WELSH POLITICS.—At Caaergwrle Eisteddfod, Flintshire, on Monday, the following letter was received by Mr. Morgan Jones, in reply to an invitatien to Mr. Gladstone to attend the eisteddfod :—" I have con- sidered with care the request made to •me in your letter. I think there is ground for believing that we have arrived at a period likely to be marked by something of new develop- ment in the political life of Wales. I have alluded to this subject briefly in a pamphlet which I have lately published on the Irish question, but I do not think it is well for me to take part at this early stage in giving any particular direction to this development. I think this function be- longs to persons whose connection with Wales is more special and exclusive than my own. I must, therefore,. be content at present to watch the course of political feeling and action in Wales with that interest which attaches, in my mind, to all the concerns of the principality.—l remain viiur very faithful servant. W. E. Geenseoem " - CAUGHT IN THE QUICKSANDS AT NEW Birmerr9Na—On Thursday morning Mr. Heinson, bete! keeper, Liverpool, was walking along the sands at New Brighton, towards the Red Noses, during which he busied himself in collecting cockles for his matitudinal meal, when. he suddenly found himself in one of those quicksands which are frequently to be found in this neighbourhood dui-113.g spring tides. Ap- preciating at once his dangerous position he made every effort to get out of the quicksand, but the mere he struggled the deeper he sank in the treacherous footway, until he was submerged to the waist. Feeling himself in terrible danger Mr. Hamson shouted loudly for help, and his cries were fortunately beard by several fishermen in the vicinity, who promptly went to his assistance, and by means of planks and ropes succeeded in dragging him from his perilous position. He was afterwarns conveyed to his hotel at l'ssew Brighton, and on reaching it was found to be in a very ex- hausted state. Prompt restoratives were applied with satis- factory result, and in the course of the forenoon Mr, Hamson was able to return to his home at Liverpool. div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, OCTOBER 2, 1886.

GENERAL KAVLBARS has begun well. To enter an independent country as the diplo- matic representative of a foreign and friendly Power, and to address the people as if their own Government either had no existence or were entirely beneath contempt, is a pretty achievement even for a Russian. The readi- ness with which General KAULBARS accepted the rude remark of a Russian lady in the crowd, who thought the occasion a good opportunity for insulting "the vagabond Re- gent," was an excellent illustration of the single-minded solitude of Russia for Bul- garian freedom. To put the matter bluntly, Europe has not since the days of the first NAPOLEON witnessed anything so cynically audacious as this disregard for the most ele- mentary principles of liberty. It Would appear that the CZAR is convinced by. Prince Brs- MARCK'S support that he has nothing what- ever to dread from the other Powers, and that he may carry matters in Bulgaria with as high a hand as he pleases. The demands which General KAULBARS has apparently been instructed to make are quite in keeping with this policy. They show that Russia is in a hurry to recover the ground which she lost when Prince ALEXANDER united the two Bulgarias without her leave, and when he ' was victorious in the war into which she in- cited Servia to plunge. The mortification of the CZAR, personal and political, was at that time severe. No Sovereign had probably so much reason to chafe and fume as this autocrat, who saw his darling schemes frus- trated by a petty Prince for whom he had always -felt the strongest aversion. There was no measure in the bitterness of his chagrin, and there is none in his victorious exultation. Only a man mortified so deeply as to be incapable of the most ordinary re- gard for the usages of civilisation could have sanctioned the plot against Prince ALEXAN- DER by the ruffians who seemed to be within art ace of murdering him. There are people who will always believe that Russia was perfectly innocent of complicity in this plot, and that the ample funds with which the conspirators were provided came from any other source except the Russian Treasury. Madame de NOVIKOFF is, no doubt, sincerely convinced that " our Emperor" is quite incapable of such detestable meanness as to be a party to a plot of this character. But the world has made up its mind on this point, and certainly nothing that Russiehas done since tends to confirm the reasoning of Madame de NOVIKOFF'S simple mind. General KAULBARS is stated to have demanded, amongst other things, the release of the prisoners who were implicated in the conspiracy against Prince ALEXANDER. !Rus- sia objects strongly to any trial whatever, and her agents are always anxiously asking what stage the inquiry has reached. This Is not exactly the temper of innocence; and the attitude of the conspirators shows that they expect great things from their august patron. M. ZANKOFF, if he had his deserts, would be shot as a traitor ; but he modestly demands that his party shall be admitted to
the Government, and shall have some of the most important portfolios. No doubt M. ZANKOFF has excellent reason for believing that General KAULDARS will furtlier his in—

terests to the utmost of his capacity. Russia is not ungrateful to her instruments, and the man who pocketed a considerable sum in roubles for organising the gang who carried off Prince ALEXANDER in the middle of the

night, certainly deserves further proof of the- Czar's distinguished esteem. Another of General KAULBARS'S reasonable suggestions is that the convocation of the Grand Sobranje should be adjourned sine die. This manoeuvre is intelligible enough, for Russia knows quite well that if the Grand.So- branje were to meet now, its deliberations would be far from favourable to Russian policy. The CZAR wants time ; so does M. ZANKOFF. That estimable patriot has doubt- less received another consignment of roubles with which he hopes to create a public opinion in Bulgaria that shall overturn thC• " vagabond Regents," and make the So- branje completely Russian. This cannot co.e done all once. M. ZANKOFF may find it necessary for the interests of morality and peace to have M. STAAIBOULOFF carried off in' the miadle of the night; but, apart from some ennobling coup of that kind, the task of per- meating the Bulgarian mind with the idea that Bulgaria must never be anything but a province of Russia, and an advanced post of the Russian march to .Constantinople, must be accomplished gradually. At present the Bulgarians are in anything but the humour to comply cheerfully with General KAULBARS'S demands. T,he conspirators will undoubtedly be released, but they will notfind themselves the idols of the ponulace. The convocation of the Grand Sobranje may be postponed, but the Regents will be able to plead with some force that, so far from tran- - quilising the popular mind, this step is the. very thing to increase the excitement. The popular feeling wants a vent, and the safest vent is the national assembly. If the Grand Sobranje does not meet, and Russian roubles fail to produce the anticipated effect, the condition of Bulgaria may suggest to some of the Powers the propriety of proposing a dif- ferent treatment. It cannot be pretended that Russia has any right under the treaty of Berlin to prohibit the convocation of the Bul- garian Assembly at her own will and pleasure. Prince Bismarck's journals solemnly proclaint that nothing will be done except in confor- • mity with treaty engagements. Speaking of the policy of Germany and Austria, the "North German Gazette" says: "Germany's present policy is dictated by existing treaties and her own interests and sympathies. For- tunately for both nations the existence of in- ternational treaties depends neither upon newspaper editors nor upon Parliamentary disputants who, in their speeches, use pre- texts for moral exasperations. Our foreign relations and the stipulations contained in. existing treaties upon which they rest, stand upon a firm basis, which has procured for them the well-considered sanction of the countries concerned." This diligent harping on treaties is suspicious, for the most flagrant- violation of a treaty is generally heralded by almost pious assurances that it will be observed to the letter. But all this will not persuade the Hungarians that to allow Russia to pursue her policy in Bulgaria with brutal energy, and without the slightest let or hindrance, is con- sistent either with the Berlin Treaty or with the understanding, more or less formal and exact, between Germany and Austria. The Austrian Foreign Office is greatly disturbed by the inconvenient eagerness of members of the Hungarian Parliament to have explicit information about the views of the dual Gov- ernment. If Austria approves the course of events in Bulgaria she will offend the most active and energetic section of her anomalous Empire. If she disapproves, she will get into difficulties both with Prince Bismarck and the Czar. It is not a comfortable posi- tion, and we are inclined to think that,though Prince Bismarck may have his own way, it will not be for long.

THE advantages and disadvantages of mothers-in-law are too well known to need description here. Society has decided that the latter much outweigh the former, but society is not always kindly disposed to elderly females. Another not less serious subject is the legal power of mothers-in-law. Mothers-in-law have, of course, the legal rights which pertain to all free citizens. A mother-in-law is not to be placed outside the pale of civilisation because her sons-in-law regard her as superfluous, not to say incon- venient. Because she has her opinions on dress, on household expenses, on morals, and on that great "hours' question" which has troubled the peace of more than one house- hold where business—of the strictest and most unimpeachable character—detains the husband somewhat beyond tea-time—because we say, she has a soul to feel and a mind to think on all these questions, she is not for that reason to be treated as a female Yahoo. I But though we are, therefore, inclined to hold a brief for the mother-in-law, we are not in- clined to favour her claims without reserve. For instance, we are disposed on mature consideration to hold that a mother-in-law has no power to say whether her daughter and son-in-law shall go abroad or no. The other day a respectably-dressed man attended atThames police-court, London,and asked Mr. LUSHINGTON if his motlier-in-law could prevent him and his wife from going abroad. He de- clared that his mother-in-law, with whom he was living, had prevented him from obtaining two or three situations, and had also dared him to leave the house. He had now an op- portunity of getting an appointment abroad, and he and his wife wished to go, but his mother-in-law said they should not, and would not let him make any arrangements to go. MI. LUSHINGTON'S reply was simple: "I can't," he said, "see what legal power your mother- in-law has to prevent your going abroad." The applicant, however, was still unsatisfied. "She says I shan't go," was his Piteous complaint. Mr. LUSHINGTON could add nothing to his bare statement of the law, and the anonymous person in Thames-street, with the mother-in-law, retired to have it out ' with her, and judging from his application and demeanour, to get very much the worst of it. So far as we can see, there is nothing for him to do but to relapse into the ancient slavery, and do his mother-in-law's bidding. For we are afraid that even the dis- covery that his mother-in law has no right to prevent him going to Switzerland or France will not greatly affect his position to- wards her.

Hereditary bondmen, know ye not, Who would be free, themselves must strike the blow. And we feel tolerably sure that the Tharne,s- , , street gentleman will never strike the blovv. We stspect that the relations between him and his mother-in-law must in some degree resemble those between poor CLIVE NEW COME and that awful Mrs. MACKENZIE. It. is possible that the Thames-street mother-in-

div.p: law holds the purse strings. It is certain that she rules the roost in the Thames-street home. It is to be feared that the continental trip will never come off. Legal powers the mother-in-law may not have, but her moral powers who shall deny or gainsay?

IT is not often that a Coroner is called upon in the discharge of his duty to pass . such severe censure as that which was in- flicted, on Thursday last, on MARY PoWELL, the landlady of the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Antro- bus. He described her conduct as "inhuman in the last degree " in refusing to allow a boy of five years of age to be carried into the Inn when he had met with a terrible ac dent through falling off a lurry. When Dr. WILLETT came on the scene, he found the poor little fellow lying on the pavement, out- side the Inn, and it was stated in evidence that he had been lying there for nearly an hour, the landlady refusing to have him in the house. The doctor insisted on the lad being taken indoors, and, as he died afterwards, it became a question for a jury to consider whether the unnecessary exposure had acce- lerated death. Fortunately for [TARY PoivELL, the medical evidence was to the effect that the lad's injuries were from the first of a fatal character. Had it been stated that the boy would have recovered if he had escaped exposure, it need hardly be said that the jury Y;ould have been bound to bring in a verdict , against the landlady of the " Wheat Sheaf." It was urged ou her behalf that ' the lad was not left on the pavement for any- thing like an hour; but• we hold that the offence was in the refusal ; it was not merely a question of time. When SHYLOCK," bent on having his pound of flesh, was entreated to provide a surgeon, lest the victim should bleed to death, he exclaimed—" I cannot find it; 'tis not in the bond." But the land- lady of the "Wheat Sheaf" had no such plea for it was in her bond ; it is one of the con- ditions upon which she holds her license that she shall receive all who apply to be admitted as guests—that is so long as she has room for them. She has been guilty, therefore, of a breach of the law of the laud, as well as of the higher law of humanity, and may con- sider herself fortunate in having escaped with nothing worse than a public censure as a "heartless creature."

div.p: LOCAL NEWS.

iIifITRIN CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH, WIDNES.--Tbe re- 'Opening services were continued on Sunday, when special sermons were preached by the Rev. C. H. Bradbury, of Peasley Cross. The collections in aid of the funds of the church were very satisfactory. CAMDEN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN.— At the weekly meeting of this class held on Friday even- ing, Mr. A Higgins read a paper en "dreams." Mr. H. Randle presided, and there was a good attendance. Messrs. Randle, Kitte, Moulton, Patin, and J. David Jones took part In the discussion that ensued. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT WESTON POINT.—The annual harvest thanksgiving service was held on Thursday even- ing at Christ Church, Weston Point. The edifice was prettily decorated with fruits and flowers. The pulpit was occupied by the Rev. George London, vicar of St. George's, Altrincham, who preached to a good congregation. TONIC SOL-FA CLASSES AT RUNCORN.—Mr. John Ho!- ford, whose tonic sol-fa classes have been attended with much success during the past few years, inaugurated the fifth session on Wednesday night by giving an open re- ' hearsal. Mr. F. J. Norman presided, and there was a crowded audience. The pupils went through a most clever and pleasing performance. RUNCORN THEATRE ROYAL —The boards of this theatre have this week been occupied by Messrs. Williams and Bowyer's Company in the comedy drama of "Self," and they have been favoured with good and enthusiastic houses. The company include several actors and actresses of more than average metit, and in the comic characters Mr. Brien McCullough displays exceptional ability. RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH CHORAL SOCIETY.—This is the title under which the Runcorn Parish Church Glee Class will in future be known. Under the lcadership of Mr. Warharn the society had a most successful season last win- ter, and increased prosperity is anticipated for the coming year. Unfortunately Mr. Warham. who was the recipient of a token of esteem and regard from the members a few months ago, has left the town to take charge of a school in Yorkshire, and his departure is regretted by a wide circle of

friends. ST. AMBROSE Canto", WIDNES.—ThiS edifice presented a pleasing appearance on Friday evening last, on the OCCA- • sin of the annual harvat thanksgiving service. Flowers, fruits, and cereals, tasbefally arranged, formed a pretty adornment. The Rev. G. H. Spooner, vicar of Woolton, occupied the pulpit, and preached an appropriate sermon to a large congregation. The services were continued on Sun- day, when the Rev. B. B. Prescot, of Latchford, preached in the morning, and the vicar (the Rev. S. A. Spooner) in the evening. FUNERAL or THE LATE DR. BAGNALL —The body of the late Dr. Bagnall, who died at the age of 43, at his residence, Dunham Massey, on Wednesday week, was interred on Saturday afternoon at the Bowdon Parish Church. The mourners, who were conveyed to the church in three coaches, were the deceased's only child, Mr. Knight (brother-in-law), Rev. E. Marsden, M.A., vicar of Aston, Mr. Noseworthy, Dr. McDougall, Dr. Carruthers, Dr. Cole, Mr. R. Clarke, and Mr. Green (from the office of Messrs. Robert Davies and Co.) The coffin was covered with a number of very beauti- ful wreaths and floral crosses. The funeral service was con ducted by the Rev. A. Anderson, vicar of St. Mark's, Dunham

Massey. Wenerns SCHOOL BOUM ELECTION.—The Nonconfor- mists of Widnes held a meeting on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. R. Fogg, to consider what action should be taken at the forthcoming School Board election. Mr. P. Glover intimated his intention not to stand again, and it was decided to nominate the chairman, who is manag- ing cashier at Messrs. Hall Bros. and Shaw, in hie stead. The other retiring members, Messrs. R. H. Davis and Joseph Robinson, will be again nominated. The Church party have made no further move than that recently reported, and it is understood that .the Rev. George Bond still adheres to his expressed intention to be an independent candidate. The Catholics, in the event of a contest, will ran five candidates. They at present bold four seats on the Board. PRP:MITE METHODIST FRUIT BANQUET, WIDNES.—The annual harvest thanksgiving services in connection with Simm's Cross Primitive Methodist Chapel were held on Sunday. The building had been tastefully decorated with the fruits of the earth, and appropriate mottoes, and pre- sented a pleasing appearance. There were crowded con- gregations at both morning and evening services, and Miss Griffiths, of West Bromwich, preached two sermons. The collections in aid of the trust funds amounted to nearly £5. On Monday evening a fruit .banquet was held, under the presidency of Mr. J. H. Lea. Addresses were delivered by Miss Griffiths. Messrs. David Lewis, Albert Calvert, and S. Owen, and the choir rendered specially selected music in good style. Readings were also given, and a pleasant even- ing was spent. ST. BEDE'S IrpUNG MEN'S SOCIETY, WIDNES.—The Mem- bers of this society had their annual supper and entertain- ment on Tuesdae7 After the tables had been cleared the Rev Father Finegan took the chair, and in the ' emirs° of the evening made a speech. He referred to the disadvantages Tinder which 'Catholics laboured with regard to education, and said be wanted the help of the members in the School Board Election, which would perhaps take place next month, and probably be a contested one. He beped it iniglat. They (the Catholics) had their plans arranged, they bad their candidates selected, and each one was willing to stand and to fight the battle over again that they fought so well nine years ago, when the four Catholics were at the head of the poll by hundreds over the other candidates. If there was a contest next month the • Catholics would run five candidates. An entertainment follewed in which Dr. McCernbridge and Messrs. F. Heyes, J. S. Hunt, Rafferty, Finn, and A. B. hope took part. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES.—Oh Sun- day Mr. Brongh, of Warrington, preached two sermons in this church in connectian with the &lapel harvest thanks- giving service. In the afterooon a musical service, entitled " Harvest Thantiseivine." was performed by the choir and scholars, the narrative being read by the Rev. E. Hall, the pastor. The chapel was beautifully decorated with a pro- fusion of fruits, flowers, and wheat, and appropriate texts adorned the walls. On Menday evening a fruit banquet wag held, and there was a good atiendance. In the absence of Mr. Emery Mr. Robert Wright presided, and delivered an addreas. The Rev. E. Hall also made a speech. Fruit was distributed amongst the audience at intervals, and the pro- ceedings were rendered mere enjoyable by the musical performances of the choir under the leade,ship of Mr. J. Betney. At the close the fruit, dr.c., was sold, Mr. J. Birken- head officiating as auctioneer. Donations were receiviel from the following :—Mr. H. Wade Deacon (E 5 Mr. T. C. :Edwards-Moss, M.P., Colonel J. Ireland Blackburne, Mr. Bolton, Mrs. Wateie, Mrs. oodward, Mrs. Margaret Long- ten. Mrs. Corns, Mrs. Major;Riessrs. M. A. Forest, R. Mercer, T. Sadler, J. Rule?, W. Hall, Pownall, H. Cromp- ton, R. Turton, R. Wright, Lister, Emery, Fletcher, Houghton, Smith, Sutton, Hitchmouah, Ford, i'rescot, Cal- lan., Bridge, Edwardson, P. Ireland, and Greig. The chapel had been decorated by Mrs. Birkenhead, Mrs. Greig, Mrs. Burgess, Mrs. Wilcox. Mrs. Lock, Mrs. Hoyle, Mrs. Savage. and Misses Har isen, Bet. Greig, Rimmer, .e and Glendenning. Ihe collectons will be devoted to the elee* reboot fund.
