div.p: ' House AND DONKEY ASTRAY.—At Widnes PetiV Ses- sions on Thursday, Robert Boyle, labourer, was fined 10e and costs for allowing his horse and donkey to stray in Tan- house-lane. PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.--MiSS Gentles, of South Bank Terrace, Runtorn, was the recipient of a beautiful present Irons her pupils on the occasion of her birthday on Tuesday. The gift consisted of a set of prettily panted jugs, a handsome black and gold teapot, a tastefully em- Oroiciered tea cosey, a braided apron, a valuable book, and several cards. RUNCORN POLICE COURT.—fla Thursday, before Mr. James Reynolds and Mr. James Handley, Phillip Handley, a young mau, was charged with trespassing in search of Yams upon land in the occupation of Wm. Bradburv, of! Norton. The case was proved by George,Rigby,gamekeener to Sir Richard Brooke, and a fine of 5s and costs was im- posed. ASSAULT ON A WIFE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty? Ses- sions; on Thursday. Richard Tansey, a labourer, who lives I at Moss Bank, was charged with assaulting his wife, Terence ! Tansey. The woman, whose face bore marks of severe ill- I id not wish to press the case, and asked for her bus.- 1 sand to be hound over. He ha 4 given her two black eves on Saturday and again assaulted her on Monday. l'he I prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was bound over to keep the! peace for three months, in two sureties of .£5 each. STONING WIDNES POLICEMEN.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, Lawrence KeaVng and Frederick I McLoughlin, youths, were charged with assaulting P.C. ! Holbrook and P.C. Coates. On Sunday, the 19th Septem- ber, the constables were taking a p,lsoner to the pelice station. In Victeria-road the defendants threw' stones and I apples at the constables, several of the missiles striking them. Sui,erintendent Barker read a long list against Keat- I ing, who was fined 40s and costs, or a month. McLoughlin- I whose character was not so bed, was fined 20s and coeree AN OnsetnePeaous RAILWAY TRAVELLER—At Widne,! Petty Sessions on Thursday, Sarah Geeratty, of Ditton, was ! summened to answer a charge of attempting to defraud the ! Londen and North-Western Railway Company. Mr. Pres- ton, junr , prosecuted, and stated that on the fifteenth of September the defendant entered a second-class cempart- ment at Widnes. As she had only a third-class ticket, she ! was rcqu.sted to cfan,, out, but she refused, and the train ! was despatched. At Ditton the difference in the fare was! f demanded, but the defendant, who was excited with drink, ! declined to pay it —The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was 1' fined 2s 6d and costs. ROBBERY BY A WIDNES CARTER.—SamoeI Iligginson, of Carlton-street, was brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions. on I Thursday, charged with stealing two spad s, the property ! of the Widnes Alkali Company. The defendant was em- ployed to cart rubbish Away from the works. On the 2Sth September Joseph Collier, the watchman who lives at 23, Lacey-street, saw the defendant hide the spades behind a gate, and when he drove oat with his cart Collier followed him and found the spades on his cart. Tney were con- cealed under a horse cloth. The defendant said he only borrowed the spades, and had no intention of keeping them.l A fine of 40a was imposed. A ViotExr CUSTOMER AT WlDNES.—Be#cre Captain H. I De Willis and Mr. J. Brock, at the Widnes Petty Sessions,' on Thursday, Timothy Leach, described as a tramp, was I charged with doing wilful demage to the Stanley Arms Hotel to the extent of a 15s. About ten o'clock on Tues- day night the prisoner went to the hoer and asked for a gill 1 of Cl bees; He, however: wonted the beer out of the best tap, and when it was dtawn retu.sed to pay more than 111-4. The empty jug was therefore given him, and then ha used ' " cheek " to tke landlord, Thomas Whittaker, who put him out. The prisoner then threw the jug through a plate glass window. A fine of 10s, and costs 7s 6d, or 14 days' hard labour was imposed. The prisoner was also ordered to pay the damage. A WIDNES PUBLICAN FINED.—Mark YOUtigi oi the Horse and Jockey Inn, Appleton, appeared. before the Widnes magistrates, on Thursdiy. and pleaded guilty to selling liquor during prohibited hours. Mr. Knowles ap- peared for the defendant. At a quarter-past twelve noon on Sunday, the 19th September, P.C. Almond saw a young woman named Tickle ge to the front window of the de- fendant's house. Mrs. Young motioned her to go round to the back, and she did so. The constable followed, and saw Mrs. Young give a jug of beer to Tickle. When Tickle saw the officer she ran home. Mrs. Young stated the liquor was a pint of vinegar, but a taste showed it to be fresh drawn beer. Mr. Knowles handed in a letter from the Rev. G. Bond, vicar of Farnworth, giving the defendant a good character, and Mr. Knowles pointed out that he had kept a public-house ten years without a complaint. A fine of lOs and costs, 12s, was imposed. DOGS AT LARGE IT RUNCORN.—Before Mr. Henry Rey- nolds and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, John Warburton, farmer, Kingsley, was charged with contravening an order of the justices by allowing two dogs to be at large at Sutton on the 15th September.— P.C. Fryer and P.S. Parrott proved the case. The defendant said the dogs were used to " work" cattle and sheep, and both animals were so quiet they could be worked to a yard. —The defendant's son was called, and said he was only using one of the dogs to drive the cattle. The other dog had followed him without his knowledge. Mr. Reynelds said it was quite clear that the dog being used to drive the Cattle would be under control. In respect to the other, which was not employed, a fine of Is and 9s 6d costs would be imposed. John Ormesher, Halton-road, was charged under two summonses for allowing a dog to be at large on the 17th and 19th September.—The defendant said the clog belonged to a man named William French, of Warrington, and the case was adjourned for a week in order that be might call that person. On the evidence of P.C. Milling- ton, Arthur Hough, of Church-street, was fined is and costs for allowing his dog to be at large. For a like offence, Joseph Richardson, of Devonshire•square, was mulcted in a similar penalty. TRAP ACCIDENT,—OH Friday evening last week Mr. William Lazenby, baker and flour dealer, Bewsey-road, was driving up Bridge-street, when his turnout came into collision with one driven by Mr. White, builder, of Runcorn. Mr. Lazenby's horse was killed by the shafts of Mr. White's trap penetrating it. NEW ISLE OF MAN NAVIGATION COXPANY.—It will be seen from our advertising columns that the New Isle of Man Steam Navigation Company, Limited, offers special facilities for shareholders. In order to give additional interest to the members the directors have decided to grant to original share- holders a non-transferable ticket entitling them to travel twice to and from the island each summer, and once during each winter. It is also intended to promote the pecuniary interest of the share- holders by constructing first-class swift triple ex- pansion screw steamers. THE LATE Samum, MORLEY.—A movement is on foot by the members of the National Thrift Society to erect a Thrift Hall as a memorial to the late pre- sident of the Society, Mr. Samuel Morley. It is proposed to erect the hall in as central a position as possible, so as to make it a centre of thrift and tem- perance work, and of other social movements for the welfare of the industrial classes. In addition to a large and small hall for meetings and confer- ences, it is intended to have a number of rooms set apart, at a moderate rental, for approved societies and philanthropic institutions. RAFFLING AT BAZAARS.—The Accrington magis- trates on Wednesday gave their decision in a case which possesses considerable interest for those who promote and manage bazaars. Messrs. J. Cunliffe, F. W. Kenyon, and William Foulds, officials of the Church Conservative Club, were summoned for a breach of an Act passed in the reign of George 111. and directed against the holding of lotteries. The defendants had assisted at a " raffle," which, the magistrates held, was an unlawful operation; but they pleaded that as their object was not to acquire personal benefit by defrauding the public, but merely to raise money for a charitable object, they were without the statute. This plea was rejected by the justices, who imposed a nominal fine upon each of the defendants. STRANGE BEHAVIOUR OF A BOY.—A singular and in some respects a dramatic incident occurred at the meeting of the Warrington Rural Sanitary I „Authority yesterday. The meeting is held in the -offices of the Board of Guardians, at the Workhouse, and business had barely commenced when Mr. J. C. 'Sutton, clerk to the Guardians, brought into the room a boy of rather diminutive stature, who had been received into the workhouse. In reply to Mr. I Sutton, the lad said they called him John Cashon ; he was nine years of age, and belonged to Runcorn. I Both his father and mother died a few weeks I ago, and were buried in Runcorn Cemetery. He had been very fond of his parents, and was very BOITY when they died. On his death bed his father called him to his side, and said he had been a kind father to him, and he would never meet with such another. The feelings of the members of the Authority present havingbeen appropriately affected by these pathetic details, Mr. Sutton told the door- keeper to bring in the man who was wafting out- side. This man, who was decently clad and respect- able looking, was then introduced, and the lad was asked if he knew him. For a time Cas- hon speechless with surprise, but at length admitted in a crestfallen fashion that the man was his father. The boy's father then explained that his son was in the habit of leaving home. At the change of the moon it seemed as though he must have some days to himself, and he always managed to roam away from home, do as they would. The Chairman (Mr. C. Broadbent, J.P.) thought this conduct of the lad must be due to some mental affection, and, therefore, harshness to him would do no goOd. The father of the boy said he was of the same opinion, and he had only once been harsh with him,and he was sorry for it directly after. Mr. Sutton said he had brought that case before them, as Guardians, to show them what strange people the officials had to deal with some times, and Mr. Shearer, the relieving officer, who I was present, said that he had had several cases like I that. The ordinary business of the Authority was I then proceeded with, and the boy was placed in the charge of his father.

div.head: FIRE BRIGADE COMPEIITION AT WIDNES.
div.p: FIRE BRIGADE COMPEIITION AT WIDNES.

- - A competition amongst Widnes firemen, for prizes rang- ing from is to a guinea, was held on Saturday afternoon, on the Widnes market graund. The weather was anything but favourable, and in consequence an exhibition drill, which bad been arranged to be given, had to be abandoned. Mr. I. Carr, superintendent of the fire brigade, directed.- the pro- ceedings, The following members of the Local Board were present: Dr. O'Keeffe, and :lest-a. ti,enjamio 13:Own1 Eus- tace Carey, and John Houghton, ONE MAN ENGINE DRILL.—This was the fist item. The fireman had two lengths of hose-pipe, the first of which he had to couple up from the hydrant to the engine, to supply water thereto, and the second length from the engine to the delivery, which supplies water to the branch for the supposed fire. The fireman who could make all these con- moctions, and have the engine ready for working in the shortest time, received the first prize, value 21s. The second prize was la?, and the third 7s 6.1. There were ten entries in this evert, nine of whom performed the work. The fol- lowing was the result :---1, Fireman Barron. time 1 ruin. 14 sees.; 2, Fireman Carden. time 1 min. 17 2-5 secs. ; 3,• Fireman 'Harper, 1 min. 17 3-5 secs. Fireman Varley did the work in 1 MiD. 27 secs., Kayes in 1 min. 54 secs., Rowe in 1 min. 42 secs., Scott in 1 min. 31 3-5 secs., Kenrick in 1 min. 20 secs., and Bentham in 1 min. 44 1-5 secs.

Two MAN ENGINE DRILL.—With the exception that two men were engaged in the work instead of one, this was the same as the previous event. The first prize was 12s 6d each fireman, and the second 7s each. The result teas as fol- lows :-1, Firemen Welding and Harper, time 46 1-5 secs. ; 2, Welding and Scott, 47 2-5 secs. lenrick and Carden did the work in 48,1 secs., Varley and Kaves in 49 1-5 secs., Rowe and Barron, in 53 1-5 secs. Two MAN HYDRANT DRILL —ln this competition, which was the last on the programme, here was no engine used. The operAtor had to couple three lengths of hose-pipe from the hydrant direct to the branch pipe, the water being forced throuah by means of pressure from the mains, the time being taken from the commencement of the drill to the point when water was delivered. 12s 6d each fireman was the first prize, and a barn each the second. • There were five entries, four of whom performed the work. The resulr was as follows :-71, Firemen Barron and Scott, 1 min. 12 2-5 secs ; 2, Harper and Welding, 1 min. 21 3-5 secs. Firemen Varley and Rowe, and Firemen Carden and henrick did the work in 1 min. 25 4-5 secs. and 1 min, 22 secs. respec- tively.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

'ht ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Authority was bold on Tuesday aft,lnoon at Dutton Workhouse. Lieu- tenant-Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present —the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner, Thomas Whitley, and John Lockwood, and Messrs. Howitt, Knowles, Warburton, DAvies, marttyio, st‘tes, Campkio, Haofieid, Lewis, Parr, &and- reth, Hall, Forster, Percival, Pickering, Whitlow, Walling- ton, Aaron, Mounfield, H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk), Dr. Adams (medical officer of health), and James Farrington (inspector of nuisances). REGISTRATION OF MILK PURVEYORS.—A number of bye- laws with regard to the registration of sellers of miik, which had been framed by the committee appointecl for that pur- pose, were submitted. On the motion of Mr. Aaron, they were adopted and ordered to be forwarded to the Local Government Board for approval. OU'IBREAK or TYPHOID FEVER.—Dr. Adams reported that two cases of typpid fever had occurred at Norton. The cause was polluted water, which bad been analysed, and the well ordered to be closed. The well, it was stated, was within a few feet of a cesspool, privy, and pigsty. WATER ANALYSIS —The Inspector of Nuisances sub- mitted the certificate of analysis of the water supplied to certain premises in Norton. the water having been returned as being very bad and quite unfit for domestic use.—The analysis not 'being satisfactory, the inspector was directed to institute the usual proceedings for having the well closed. NEW HOUSES AT FRODSHAZI AND HELSBY.—A certificate of occupation was granted to Mr. Thomas Riley, of Prod- sham, for fert'r new houses erected by him in Main-street, Frorisharri. A similar certificate was also granted to Mr. William Booth, also of Frodaharri, for six new houses erected by him in Booth-street, Frodsham, both blocks being supplied with water from the public fountain. A like certificate was also granted to Mrs. Sarah W. Davies, of Helsbv, for four new houses erected by her at Helsby, the water supplied thereto being satisfactory.

div.head: WIDNES SOLICITOR SUING FOR PROFESSIONAL
div.p: A WIDNES SOLICITOR SUING FOR PROFESSIONAL

CHARGES. At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Collier, an action brought by Mr. W. T. Husband, solicitor, Widnes, deputy-coroner for the West Derby Hundred, against Mr. Charles Hemingway, joiner and contractor, Church-street, Widnes, and Mr. Samuel Pusill, baker, Church-street, Widnes, for £l3 17s 6d for profes- sional services rendered in the preparation of deeds for the transfer of some land, was heard. Mr. Husband conducted his own case, and Mr. Copeman, Liverpool, defended. Mr. Hemingway had paid £7 6s 6,1 into court, but that did not satisfy Mr. Husband, who stated that his charges,,XB 19d for deeds, agreements, &c., were according to scale ; he had £3 1.7 s 6d to pay Mr. Peters, solicitor to the Starr-Bowkett Building Society, who were the mortgagees of the land, and £1 Is forother services.— Defendants contonded that Mr. Husban,l arrangsd to do the work for £s.—Mr. Husband asked Mr. Hemingway if he thought he (Mr flusb aid) would prepare a lease of thirty- six folios, a cousterpart with two plans on it, four sheets of parchment, and do the work on them for £s.—Mr. Heming- wa‘, said he did. He had not had any deeds prepared be- fore. Mr. Copeman said that Mr. Peters had charged on the most exorbitant scale, and it was the duty of Mr. Hus- band to have ascertained what his charge would be, and consulted his clients. After dealing with the other items Mr. Copeman said he was sorry to meet a professional bro- ther under such circumstances. He had done his best for his clients, and he hoped he had not given pain to Mr. Husband. is Honour, after carefully reading the rule, said judgment for .£8 10d appeared to he the right. sum. He did not think sufficient information of the condition of things was given, so that defendants might understand that those costs of Mr. Peters would be incurred. He thought it right that defend- ants should have been so informed, and that some authority should have been got from one of the parties for incurring those charges. For that reason he could only give judg- ment for a 199 against Mr. Hemingway; and a nonsuit, with leave, against Mr. Pusill.

REVISION COURT AT RUNCORN. On Saturday, Mr. J. G. Foulkes, barrister, held a revi- sion court at Runcorn, in the Sessions Room. The proceed- ings passed;off very quietly. the representatives of the two political parties arranging matters amicably, somewhat on a " give and take " system.. Mr. W. Handley appeared for the Liberal party, and Mr. C. J. Hughes (Northwich) for the Conservatives. TITE CLAIMS, See.—For Runcorn North the Liberals made 13 property claims, and the Conservatives 8 ; whilst on the occupiers' list the Liberals made 13, and the Conserve.tives 6 clairns. Five Liberals ancl.6 Conservatives were objected to on the ownership list, whilst only two names were objected to on the occupiers' list. Of the 7 old imager claims 4 were Liberals and three Conservatives. There were .63 new lodger claims. The occupiers list, issued by the overseers, contained the names of 1,938 voters, and the owners list 226 names. For Runcorn South the owners list contained 75 names, and the occupiers list 500 names. In this district 7 Liberals and 2 Tories claimed the property qualification, and 7 Liberals and 1 Tory claimed to be placed on the ec3cupiers register. There were 2 old and 21 new lodger 'claims_ Three Liberals were objected to on the property list, anctone Con- servative was objected to on the occupiers list. In the out toweships of Helton, Clifton, Stockliam, Norton, and Wes- ton, there was very little change. Thera will be an increase in the number of voters of 172 in Runcorn North;and 16 in Runcorn South. AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER'S APPLICATION.—Mr. S. Col- lier, assistant overseer for the township of Weston asked the IRevising Barrister for an increase in his remnneration and expenses for work in respect of the revision for the township of Weston. The sum he received list year, he said, was .£7 17s 2d. He was only allowed the same amount as was ; allowed in respect to the toe:1104 of Halton, whereas there ' were 169 more voters on the list.—The Revisini Barrister ! said that he was not allowed -co touch a vote, and Mr. Col- -1 her said that there was more trouble in making the Bet cut. It was a very awkward township to work, one portion being two miles away from the other.—The request was not Mimed. " GENERAL" BOOTH STWOCC CXIFF THE LlST.—ObleCtiOn , was made to the name of William Booth, General' of the Salvation Army, being on the list. It was said that "General " Booth had stated in public that he only owned , property as trustee, and therefore hie right to vote in resFect of leasehOlci land and house in High-strcet, Runcorn, was objected to. The objection, which was made by the Conservatives, was sustained, and the name taken off -tlke list. At the conclueion of the eevision Mr. Handley said that in Runcorn they did the work well, and the Revising Bar- rister said that it was revision by steam. It may be stated that 35 new lodger claims were allowed to each party.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The ordinary fortnightly meeting of this Boirl was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday afternoon. Lieu- tenant-Colonel Ashton presided, and there were also present Mr. John Weir (vibe-chairman), the Revs. J.W. N. Tanner and John Lockwood' Messrs. Stokes, Hall, Brandreth, Wallington Hadfield, Whitlow, Knowles, Lewis, Speakman, Kirkham, 'Hewitt, Lowe, Warburton, Davies, Jackson, Camnkin, Parr, Forster, Percival, Pickering. Taylor High- field, Smith, Hamilton, Mounfiekl, H. Linaker (clarl), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). APPOINTMENT OF SCHOOLMISTRESS.—TiIe Clerk Btated

that in reply to the Board's advertisement for a schoolmis- tress to fill the vacancy ctused by the resio4ation of Miss Margaret Jones, six applications bad been received. The Commwee who had had the matter relegated to them had asked two of the applicants to attend there that afternoon, namely, Mary Jane Nuttall (widow), mistress of the Union Schools, Peterborough, and Frances A. Lunt, assistant mis- tress of the Union Workhouse Schools, Salford.—Mr. Whit- low said before the Board proceeded any further, he should wish to propose that the appoiutment of master and matron be taken by ballot. There were several members interested in the appointments, and he thought this would be a wise course.—The CLEux•said the matter rested entirely with the Z'oard.—The proposition was seconded and carried.— The letter from Mrs. Nuttall and her testimonials were then read, one of which, from one of her Majesty's inspectors, stated that the scholars in Mrs. Nuttall's schools, Peter- borough, had passed 100 per cent in all subjects. Miss Lunt's letter and testimonials were also read. The appli- cants were then called into the room and quationed, and having left a vote was taken, with the result that Mus..tsut- til; obtained 28 votes, and Misa Lunt 7,

APPOINTIa.NT OF MASLFEL AND Marcon. The Rev. John Lockwood read a letter with regard to th'. matter, which he said he had received that morning. Although addressed to him personally, he felt it his duty to beng it before the Board. He would make no comment upon it. The letter was from Mr. J. H. Lyon, agent for the Pru- dential Assurance Company, Preston Brook, and stated that having overlooked the advertisement in the papers as to the vacancy, he should be glad, if it was not too late, to apply for the same at a reduction of £5O per annum on the advertisement amount.—Mr. Speakman siid the letter was quite out of order, and, the Board concurring in this oninicua, the letter was laid on the table. The Clerk stated that there had been 72 applications before the committee, which, after looking through all, had selected four, who were present, to appear before the Board. These applicants' letters and testimonials were then read out, and each person attended before the Board. The names of the applicants were as fol- lows :—Edwin Preece and wife. of Salford Workhouse; Wm. Farlovr and wife, of Salford Union Infirmary; Frederick F. Nich lson and wife, of Egremont ; and Joseph Cunnah ard wife, of Frodsham. On a vote being taken 21 were for Mr. Cunnah, 10 for Mr. Preece, and 4 for Mr. Nicholson. Mr. and Mrs. Farlow, being under age, did not receive any votes. Mr. and Mrs. Cunnati were accordingly elected to the posts. A show of hands was afterwards taken, and Mr. Cunnah was elected unanimously.—The Clerk said he had refrained from saying anything with respect to Mr. Cunnah's applica- tion, but now that he was elected he would say that the Board had obtained an excellent servant, and he had lost one of the best clerks in Cheshire. (Hear, hear.) RESIGNATION.—Miss Agnes Jones sent in her resignation of the position of assistant matron. TENDERS.—On ' the motion of the Rev. J. Lockwood, seconded by Mr. Mclntyre, the following tenders were accepted :—Beef and mutton William Gill, Warrington ; groceries and flour, Samuel Collier, Runcorn ; drapery, D. H. Jones, Runcorn; wines and spirits, Thomas Price, Run- corn; coal, W. and J. Richardson, Warrington ' - coffins, John Barrow. Halton; drugs and oil, I. Speakman, Runcorn: boots, Bowcock Bros., London; potatoes, William Tickle, Keckwick ; carting, Joseph Roberts, Aston.

GAS EXHIBITION AT WIDNES. An exhibition of appliances for lighting, heating, and cooking by gas was opened in Laceyestreet schoolroom on Tuesday afternoon by Mr. Benjanin Brown. Mr. 11. Gas- kell, juur., chairman of the Gas and Water Committee of through should ChLat vbseeora performedr6du s b yillness. hthC the dtTiellhteye,eabxiuhmti btaietnaidsu detained ebWtja:i:nt e olnfraottnah heootmetle ex- hibition is set forth in the speech delivered by Mr. Brown and reported below. It may be stated that the Local Board, convinced of the advantage to be derived from a more extended use of gas, are prepared to fix gas meters and stoves free of charge, and customers may even obtain a stove on the hire system. The exhibition was of a very in- teresting character. Mr. Thomas Fletcher, of Thynne- street, Warrington, had a capital display of stores for cook- ing and heating. Of unquestioned practical ability, they were also of kilwasing designs. Of special interest to Wide nesians were eleven indestructable gas cookers. These are made of cast iron and will withstand even the corroding effects of the chemical atmosphere of Widnes. Mr. Fletcher also showed a number of his patent burners used for a variety of purposes. A patent quick washer attracted considerable attention. It is claimed that the clothes of a family may be washed in four hours by this machine without any rubbing, brushing, or dollying. Messrs. H. and C. Davies and Co., of the Metropolitan Gas Stove Works, Loadon, had an interesting and commendable collection of stoves for household use, both as regards cook- ing and heating. Messrs. John Russell and Co., Limited, of Granby-row, Manchester, exhibited a variety of chande- liers, hall lamps, and globes, whilst Messrs. Orme and Co, of Oldham, showed a variety of gas and water fittings. An interesting feature was a display of 12 burners, which Mr. Carr had taken from houses and shops during the past few days. When lighted the difference in the form and intensity of the flames was most marked, and showed the influence which bad burners had upon the illuminating power of gas, and also in causing wastefulness. There was a large com- pany of ladies and gentlemen present at the opening cere- mony, which WAS performed by Mr. Brown, who said they would all be sorry to hear that Mr. Gaskell was unfortunately detained at home through illness, being unable to leave his room. He was sure they would all sympathise with him, and join with him (Mr. Brown) in hoping that he would be speedily restored to his accustomed health. Many of them would remember that about two years ago the Local Beard held a similar exhibi- tion to that now in progress. Considerable advan- tage was experienced by the ratepayers and house- holders by that exhibition, and it had therefore been thought desirable to again bring before the public of Widnes the advantages to be derived from the use of gas, both as an illuminating agent and also as a very great help to domestic economy, especially as the price of gas in the I town was so much reduced, namely, to 2s 61 per 1,000 feet. This was a price less than any other manufacturing town in Lancashire. Notwithstanding the very great deprecia- tion there had been in the value of residuals from gas mak- ing, the Board were able through the careful and energetic' management of their manager, Mr. Carr, to reduce the , price of gas when some other companies bad bean coin- I petled to advance the since. At the present low price the Board thought a great deal more gas could be used for light- I ing purposes by the householders of Widnes than was used at present. If they would consider that the cost of the gas I supplied by the Board was much less than candles or oil, and that it did away with inconvenience and danger,a great I many persons would adopt gas in preferenct. To a good manyhe a dmt tet eddi ffit beau: tiyn oaf gfirtatai tn gmsawnyascaotgtaregaeta oi tb citgi ho nt , net i I very safe to pat in fittings, for as soon as a cottage was empty it was attacked by those who bad not much respect for property ; but still, leaving these cases out, there was a great many householders that ought to take advantage of gas. The price of fittings was seduced below former rates. The Local Board would 'find connections to the meter, fix the meter, and for 9s 6d or 103 find one light In a living room. Those who had any appreciation ot a good light and a cheerful home would .not object to that.price of fittings. With reference to the cost of gas, provided .a regulator burner was used, such as were provided by the Board, and that the time was four hours per day for the year round, the cost of gas would be 4.r1. per week. If, however, they only used gas in the same proportion as a candle, then the cost of the gas would of course be a little: reduced. The Board had many complaints that notwithstanding the reduction in the price of gas there had been an increase in the ceneumers bills. Mr. Brown ascribed this to defective burners, nal said the Gas Committee did not want to tahe advantage of the ratepayers. The gas works wece their own \property, and the Gas Committee wished to put everybody bn the best footing. Speaking of the advantages of cooking by gas instead of by coal, he said there were go serious ob- jections against gas stoves. He maintained that a good gas range could fulfil all the necessary requirements at less than half the cost of a coal range, besides being a great deal more convenient and cleaner. He had it from a person that for a family of ten people, with gas at 3s per 1.000, the cooking ,could be done at a cost of 103/4d per week. At the price of ges in Widnes, the cost would be 9d, or not quite 13/4cl per day. Then a gas stove made the meat go further. Meat ccoked by-coal yielded 60 per cent. of the raw material, while in a gas range it yielded 75 per cent. That was to say that a joint weighing ‘lolbs, cooked by a coal range, yielded Gibe, and cooked by a gas range, Whs. Referring to the objection that food cocesed be gas was prejudicial to health, Mr. Brown pointed out that most of the food in the London and other hospitals, not only for the patients but for the medical staff add attendants, was cooked by gas. This fact, and the fact that this mode of cooking had been recommended by the leaaing medical io-arntils, showed that that objection was withodt foundation. The ,use of gas would give the , best results for their labour, and the best results for their moneyt He trusted that the exhibition woula be patronised by the ratepayers, and also by the friends outside, that it would result in the Gas and Water Committee selling more gas and the ratepayers getting better advaatagees from the money they spent. (Anplanses) Mies 111uBen, lecturer on c oolsetee to the Widnes School I Board, then gave a lecture on high-class cookery, practically I illustrated.

The exhibition was also open on Wednesday, Thursday, and yesterday, and was viewed with much interest by num- bers of people. On each day Miss Mullen delivered totes on high,class and every-day cookery.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hail Yester- day. Mr. J. *Pritchard, the vice-chairman, presido.d, and th,re were present the Rev. Father Fennelly, and Messrs. Handley, Imison, and Riqby (clerk).

div.head: APFCrINTICENT OF MEMF.ER AND CHAIRMAN.

On the motion of Mr. Imison, seconded by Mr. Handley, Mr. F. A. Lake Ivas appointed a member of the Board in the' ph,ce of the late Canon Barclay.—Mr. Handley moved that Mr. Pritchard be elected chairman.—Mr. iscison seconded the motion, which was carried nnanimously.—The Chairman regretted the cause of the appointment, but he was much obliged to them for this mark of confidence, and would discharge the duties of the office to the boot of his ability.

div.head: FINANCIAL POSITION OF THE BOARD.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL POSITION OF THE BOARD.

The Clerk reported that the precept issued on the over- seers at the last meeting of £250 was met on the 18th Sept. ,This had enabled the Board to meet all their liabilities and left them with a credit balance of £lO lie. They had accounts tl meet that day amounting to LiOd. Their bal- ance would be increased by enniiry payments to £23 2s 3d.

At this time last year they had a balance against them of £5B is Bd, so that they began the year under anything but favourable circumstances. Last year they received from the overseers £l.ooo, and after deducting a balance against them of £5B 7s 83 and the £23 2s 3:1, the present balance, a nett expenditure for the year of £9lB 83 id was shown. The Clerk estimated that the liabilities of the Board 'kir the comine• half year would be something like £550. At pre- sent' they were in anything but affluent circumstances, as they had only £23 with which to pay accounts of £105. It was resolved to issue a precept for £5OO upon the over- seers.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

Mr. Hardley referred to the work of the School Atten- dance Committee, which he said would give them an ade- quate idea of the work of the Board and the results accom- plished. The attendance of every scholar on the register had been taken by the servants of the Board, He found that the certified accommodation of the 14 public elemen- tary schools in Runcorn was 3,197, the number on the rolls being 3,132, so that there was only 65 p!aces to be filled in. The average attendance, however, did not come up to this , figure, but left a margin of 778 places, the average attend- ance being 2,354 It was satisfactory to know that the new system arranged by the committee bad worked well for the I past month. which, compared with August, showed an in- crease of 7 per cent in the average attendance. The average percentage for August was 66, and for September 73. It was interesting to go into particulars to see where the increase was most marked. In the National Boys' School there was certified accommodation for 389, on the rolls 455, average attendance 357, percentage attendance 78, last mouth 74, increase 4. National Girls', accommodation 236, on the rolls 295, average attendance 229, percentage 77, last month 74, increase 3. Newtown School (mixed), accom- modation 100, on the rolls 130, average attendance 101, per- centage 77, last month 76. increase 1. Wesleyan Boys' Schools, accommodation 352, on the rolls 239, average at- ; tenclance 228, percentage 78, last month 64, Increase 12. Wesleyan Girls', accommodation 252, on the rolls 196, average attendance 147 percentage 75, last month 57, in- crease 18. Wesleyan Infants', accommodation 180, on the roll 142, average attendance 103, percentage 72, last month 58, increase 14.. Trinity Boys', accommodations 253, on the roll 265, average attendance 230, percentage 86, last month 74, increase 12. Trinity Girls' accommodation 156, on the rolls 223, average attendance 173. percentage • 77, last month 71, increase 3. Trinity Infants', accommodation, 222, on the rolls 161, average attendance 123, per- centage 76, last month 74, increase 2 per cent. Catholic School (mixed), accommodation 162, on the rolls 240, average attendance 158, percentage 65, last month 57, increase 8. Mill-brow Board school ac- commodation 124, on the roll 124, average attendance 86. per centage 69, last month 61, increase 5. Board school , girls' accommodation 207, on the roll 147, average attend- ance 90, per centage 61, last month 48, increase 13. Board school mixed accommodation 274, on the roll 170, average attendance 111, per centage 65, last month 54, increase 11. Mr. Handley expressed doubt whether these per centages were reckoned in the right way in those instances where tbe average attendance was equal or mere than the certified accommodation, and he gave a different mode showing , much improved per centages. The visitors, be said, made 600 visits a week, which showed a fair amount of work in I addition to looking after the registers. He recommended that in cases wbere the children made less than seven attendances during a week that the visitors at once send out attendance orders.-It was decided to do so. There was no other business of public interest.

div.p: BAZAAR AT ACTON. A very successful bazaar was on Thursday opened at the residence of Mr. W. Davidson, the Lower Green, Acton and it was continued yesterday. The object was to raise money towards clearing the manse in connection with Little Leigh Baptist Chapel from debt. Several rooms were stocked with the miscellaneous articles usually to be seen lat bazaars. and one room was used as a dairy sball. 'ln another room were stacked all kinds of fancy I and useful articles, and a third wast set apart for the dispensing of refreshments. The bazaar was I opened at noon on Thursday by Mrs Brunner, of Winnington Old Hall, Northwich, who was accom- panied by Mr. Brunner and friends. The stalls were in charge of the following ladies :—Mrs Lord, the Manse, Little Leigh, near Northwich ; Mrs W. Davidson, Acton ; Mrs Joseph Clarke, Cogshall ; Mrs ! Rigby, Little Leigh; Mrs James Rigby, Little Leigh; Mrs Bentley, Comberhach; • Mrs Fowles, Dutton, Preston Brook; Mrs T. Brocklehurst, Little I Leigh ; Mrs James Brocklehurst, Little Leigh; Mrs James Bowyer, Little Leigh; Miss Smith, Dutton, Preston Brook: Miss Billington, Dutton, Preston Brook; Miss Maddock, Cogshall. The refreshment lroom was in charge of Misses R. Smith, E. Billing- I ton, Jones, and E. Jones. There was a good number of people present at the opening ceremony, amongst whom were Alderman and Mrs McNeild (Crewe), Mr. and Mrs Richardson (Warrington), Mrs Hough (Ac- ton), Mrs. Deacon and friends, &c. The opening cere- mony commenced with singing and prayer, after which the Rev. W. J. M. Lord, pastor of the church, made a short business statement The land they , had purchased, he said, which was about 400 yards in extent, had, together with legal, expenses, cost £33. That they had been able to pay by a surplus that was left over from a bazaar held some time ago. The house had cost, including all expenses, £343, and they had had given and promised towards ',this the sum of £lO5, so that altogether they re- lquired £238 to clear off the debt. —Alderman Mc- iNeild congratulated the promoters •of the bazaar lupon their success. They' had, he said, been ex- tremely fortunate in securing the services of Mrs. Brunner. The object in view, as no doubt they I would all know, was to clear off the debt on the -manse. He belonged to one of the departments of Methodism that knew a good deal about chapel 'debts, and he knew that it would be a very unfor- tunate thing for their pastor—who was a -young ;man beginning the work of the ministry—to live in I a house burdened by debt. He then referred to the I energy that had been evinced by the ladies in getting together such a collection of articles for ' sale, and expressed a cordial wish that the efforts made to raise the money might be fully successful. Mr. Davidson proposed that Mrs. Brunner be accorded a vote dr thanks for attending to open the sale. Mrs. Brunner was a lady who had done a great deal of good, 'and had I assisted in many things that had resulted in good. I She was ever ready to help, and in Mr. Brunner they had a gentleman Who was almost the 'salvation of a certain district not far from there. !Had it not , I been for Brunner, Mond, find Co., there might have been great,distress in the neighbourhoods of North-, wich, Barnton, and Weaverham. Mr. James Rigby seconded the motion, which was carried with ap- plause.—Mrs. Brunner briefly declared the bazaar open, and Mr. Brunner then complied with the re- quest that he should address a few words to those assembled. It was no new thing,hesaid,Torlim to have his mind filled with good wishes for the Baptists. , ,It 'was now a good deal More than a .quarter of a 'century ago since he derived very great benefit from the teaching of a great Baptist minister—the Rev. Hugh Stowell Brown, of Liverpool. He re- membered going to that gentleman's 'Sunday after- noon lectures with rather mingled feelings, because they were always held at a time when it was neces- sary for him to hurry 'from his ffkher's house directly after dinner. The result was that Sunday with him was marked for many years by very bad indiges- tion. (Laughter.) The lectures themselves be remembered with very great ,pleasure„ and from them he had learned many a good lesson. He hoped that the bazaar -would be•succesSful, and that the Baptist community at Little Leigh would have much ptosperity. The sale WIF.3 then proceeded with.

The wocaan, who ap- peared to be in a proper state of mind, stated that shetbrew the child into the ir well, near Pomona Gardens. She was taken before the magistrates, and remanded for inquiriec. THE WELSH Maxim' STRIEB.-0111 Thursday the col- lieries in North Wales were idle, and the miners assembled, to the number of 8,030 or 10,000, in the neighbourhood of the Pies Power Collieries near • Wrexham, to prevent the men employed there from working. They have taken this step in conseqm nee of the Plas Power men raising 21cwt. to the ton to enable their employers to take contracts at a ower price. The miners indulged in some very serious ex- cesses. They smashed windows and lamps, threw the cage and a quantity of timber down the shaft, and did other damage. The assistance of police and military was asked from Wrezbem,"but the colliers dispersed after rendering the mine unworkable.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON, THURSDAY.

The current lull in political disputation is very welcome. It is long overdue, for the last two years, and more particularly the last ten months, has formed a remarkabie period of political activity. A partial indication of the state of things is f.ir- nished in the proud boast of the retiring Lord Mayor, who claims distinction above his fellows, inasmuch as during his year of office he has enter- tained three Ministries and the representatives of three Parliaments. That is certainly without a precedent. It recalls to the jadbd memory the miles of columns of speeches which the newspapers have provided within the twelve months. La-t year we practically had no recess. About this time last year the Marquis of Salisbury was setting forth at Newport the policy of the Conservative party. His speech, it will .be remembered, adumbrated a scheme of Home Rule. We are within a fortnight of the anniversary of Mr. Gladstone's penultimate Midlothian compaign. It was on the 18th of No- vember that Parliament was dissolved, and thence- forward up to the eve of Christmas the country was in the throes of a general election.

As compared with that time we are now enjoying I a period of delicious peace. It will be broken soon, 1 for Mi. Gladstone is expected to make an important , speech in receiving the deputation from Ireland, for which appointment has been made at Hawarden, and on Saturday Lord Randolph Churchill is to speak at Dartford. But these will be only tempor- ary and strictly limited interruptions of the silence. People are heartily sick of politics, and are wellj content to await the reassembling of Parliament next February before embarking npon a fresh de- ' bauch of political speech-making. There has been a good deal of talk of summoning Parliament in November, and one paper has gravely announced that instructions have been given to the officials at the House of Commons to be ready for a sitting in that month. This specific allegation is, at least, non- sense. After the explosion, the House of Commons was thoroughly renovated, and the only prepara- ations that would be necessary, supposing Parlia- ment were to meet in November, would be confined ; to dusting benches and cleaning windows. This could be done at a week's notice, and need not be ' provided for in mid-September. • I have reason to believe on other grounds that there will be no meeting of Parliament before the usual time in February. Of course, if there were an , extraordinary outbreak of outrage in Ireland, it . would be necessary to summon Parliament in order to secure exceptional powers for the executive. But ' the outbreak must be extraordinary indeed to , render necessary such a step. The powers already I vested in the Executi.ve are sufficient to meet any disturbance that is likely to arise in Ireland this ; winter. It is the policy of Mr. Parnell and his friends to discourage as sternly as possible any out- rage such as those which in Mr. Forster's time ! arrayed public opinion against the Nationalist I cause. Thus, no reasonable occasion will be fur- , nished for the meeting of Parliament, and the Go- I vernment are the last people in the world to invent occasion. Lord Randolph Churchill and his col- leagues may be safely depended upon to use every , I effort to carry on the government of Ireland with- out a winter session. The House of Commons, with its list of questions and its camp of Irish Irrecon- cileables, is inconvenient enough at periods of its ordinary sitting, and it is not a luxury which a Conservative Government would wantonly and un- necessarily indulge in. I find in a French scientific journal an interesting statement personal to Mr. Gladstone. The French people are informed that the late Premier drinks daily four glasses of claret and one of port. It is added that this is "three and half times the aver- age amount drunk by Englishmen." This is a very minute sub-division. There would, indeed, seem to be some difficulty in apportioning out for daily use a third and a half of four glasses and one of port. It makes Mr. Gladstone out by comparison a regular winebibber, whilst the average Englishman is curiousky abstemious. As a matter of fact Mr. Gladstone does not diet himself at all the matter of wine. Ile has no particular liking for it, and pro- bably in the matter of claret would not know 'one cru from another by tasting it. I once met him at a dinner party where various wines were served in successive courses. lie unresistingly permitted all his glasses to be filled, and as the dinner proceeded, and he entered into the passing conversation heart and son', as he does into everything he undertakes, he promiscuously sipped from the various glasses, evidently not filinking which was hock, which claret, er which champagne. For solid food he has an appetite wtiich to the !jaded Londoner seems enormous. Brtt he has no appreciative taste for wine. •

Apropos of wine it is satisfactocy to 'notice that I thelashion at-the best tables is growing more and more%'implified. At City banquets given by the varicras committees and guilds there the old ghafttly procession of sherry, hock,. chabilis. I claret, andt.hampagne„ with port, sherry and claret to llow. But at the Lord 'Mayor's dinners the course is 'wholesomely reduced—most practised diners-out now drink only one wine—either cham- pagne or caret. At some of the best tables, the •mess of the Horse Guards Blue for example, chant- :pugne is the only wine drunk, even the half-glass df-sherrywith the soup, and the glass of claret with the nuts, being foregone. Where claret, port; and -sherry were put on at dessert, 'fresh bottles of Champagne, usually oi 1874 vintage, now appear. 'This is a-very wholesome and desirable improve- ment, alia tends largely to that 'increased sobriety .Wrnich ii one of the marked features of society m 'the present day. There are many now living who -remember the time when fashionable men 'rose from the dinner table indubitably drunk. It is 'now the rarest thing in the 'world to see to see con- vivality carried to excess. The three bottle man is -dead and buried. Nevertheless port, his favourite liquor, is decidedly coming baak into fashion. The: ' predominance of champagne naturally swept the -port decanter off the dinner table. When men drank claret with their meat they could take port with > -their nuts. But it is only strong heads and ; 'stomachs that can stand port after champagne. At this -season of the year, when game is coming in, ;'red Wine dinners are much -in vogue, claret being ,servedthrough the dinner and port with the dessert. 'llia is all very well in cooler weather, but cham- principal beverage at the vague will remain the table ol Amphitryon. I have seen a copy of a remarkable statement on ttilie case of Crawford V. Crawford which is being privately circulated. It is in the form of notes upon theovidence at the two trials, and upon the sum- ming-up of the judge in the latter suit. It is 'done with consummate skill, not the least effective mani- festation of which appears in the judicial air pre- served throughout. It is rather the summing up of a judge 'than the plea of an advocate, and if it were possible to make it public it would, I fancy, have considerable effect in disturbing the curious unan- imity with which the public' have assumed the absoliite 'accuracy of the statements of Mrs. Craw- ford. From the construction of the notes, which deal minutely with innumerable points in the evi- dence and the summing up, it is impossible to sum- marise it. But there are one or two points that may be noted. Almost at the commencement it deals with the fatal and irrevocable error of judg- ment which kept Sir Charles Dilke out of the wit- ness box on the first trial. The statement is re- peated that upon this matter Sir Charles Dilke had "left himself in the hands of his advisers, both great lawyers and personal friends." Up to the last moment they differed as to whether he should give evidence. He expected that lie would be called, and came into court fully prepared. At the last moment they agreed, and, only on this account, he allowed himself to be dismissed from the case without going , into the box. There is no reference to the alleged
agency of Mr. Chamberlain at this delicate and critical moment.

It is pretty eertabithat the point in Mrs. Craw- ford's evidence which went further than anything in the direct :i(ya of sustaining her case, was her ability to describe the room in "the house off Tottenham Court-Toad," where, as she alleged, ,she was in the habit ~f meeting Sir Charles Dilke. It will he remembered that at the suggestion of one of the jury she arew a plan of the room. This was not disputed, and the presumption was that its accuracy 11 was admitted by Sir Charles Dilke. The amazing statement is now made for the first time that the plan was never seen until after the summing up by any one who had ever seen the room itself! So far from`being an accurate description, it was at fault in many important particulars. For example, the door was put on the wrong side of the room, and. the stairs on the wrong side of the house. The most prominent object in the room, a large Roman Catholic image, was not mentioned. Even if the plan had been correct, it did not prove the case, for it is stated that a detective named Clarke, en- gaged on behalf of Mrs. Crawford, visited Warren- street in November.

Not less striking testimony is forthcoming upon Mrs. Crawford's statements with respect to the rooms in Sloane-street. It will be remembered that one of the most revolting passages in the confession described three persons in Sir Charles Dilke's bed. It is now stated, as a matter of fact,that Sir Charles Mike's bed is a single camp bed, in which it is physically impossible for three persons to have con- gregated. Mrs. Crawford also described this room, though not accurately, and the mistake she made is very significant. Before Mrs. Crawford went into the box, and whilst she sat listening in the court, Ellen Drake, one of the servants at Sloane-street, was examined as to the appearance of the room. Subsequently, when Mrs. Crawford was put in the box, she was asked to describe the room, and fol- lowed Ellen Drake's description so minutely that she even adopted a mistake made by the girl. Ellen Drake said the room was painted all white, whereas the cupboards, which form prominent ob- jects in the room, are not white, but yel- low. It is suggested that if ,:lfrs. Craw- ford ever had seen the room she would have corrected this slip on the part of the housemaid. These are only a few of the points dealt with in this statement, the appearance of which just now in its present form is on all fours with the general conduct of the case. Had it ap- peared as the speech of Sr Charles Dilke's counsel addressed to the jury, and had the Qross-examina. flop. been conducted upon the lines it follows, the issue of the trial might have been different. Not the least effective portions of the notes are those which show how, owing to an unfortunate sequence of circumstances, beginning with the fatal abAen- tion from the witness box in the first trial, Sir Charles Dilke was practically undefended whilst his life and his character were beitsig wrecked.

div.head: BOATING FATALITY ON TEE MERSEY. A WARRINGTON POLICE-INSPECTOR DROWNED.
div.p: BOATING FATALITY ON TEE MERSEY. A WARRINGTON POLICE-INSPECTOR DROWNED.

Shortly after noon on Wednesday news reached Warrington that that morning Inspector Berry; of the Warrington Borough Police force, had been drowned in the river Mersey, in the neighbourhood of Fiddlers Ferry, while on a boating excursion in company with Mr. William Mather, who is gene- rally known as Captain Mather. The report caused much excitement, Inspector Berry being so well known, and at first it was received with incredu- lity, but doubts as to its veracity were soon dissi- pated by ample confirmation of the rumour. The exact circumstances of the sad affair are difficult to obtain before they are elicited more fully by a. coroner's inquiry, but from what can be gathered it seems that on Monday, Inspector Berry applied to his chief, Mr. Hunt, for his annual leave of absence, which was granted. On Wednesday morning he and Mr. Mather set off on the river in a boat with the intention of having a little shooting. The weather at the time was very boisterous, a strong. wind prevailing, and there was also a very high tide running. It is asserted that Captain Mather showed a disinclination to undertake the 'trip, but his scruples were overcome by the Inspector, whose mind was apparently bent on carrying out the expedition. Accordingly the party of two embarked at ..k.therton's Quay, at about seven o'clock in the morning, at which time the river was much swollen. :They proceeded in the direction of Runcorn; and nothing untoward occurred until they reached a place known as Brooks' Chevril, which is near Fiddler's Ferry. It was not in their programme for the day to proceed further than here, and they turned back and went to the Ferry Locks. It was here that the accident occurred. It is stated that at the locks two flats lay alongside each other. An attempt was made to clear them and sail past, but the high wind and strong tide prevented, and the boat, cblliding with one of the flats, capsized. Both the occupants of the boat were precipitated into the water. It is stated that the Inspector managed. to get on the keel of the boat, which then turnest , over. Seeing his companion struggling in the water,. he succeeded in getting near him, and made an en- deavour to drag him on to the boat, which over- turned: Inspector Berry lost his place of refuge, and was again thrown into the water and soon sank. Mr. Mather got hold of a small plank, and, by put- ting it under his chin, was able to keep his head above water until a boatman of the fiat Titus, . who is named White, pulled him aboard his flat. Mr. Mather was then very much exhausted, and he was soon afterwards taken home and put to bed. The time that the accident occurred was between eleven and twelve o'clock in the morning. When the sad occurrence became known efforts were at once made to recover the. body of the deceased, but it was not until evening that they were successful. As soon as recovered it was brought to the house of the deceased at War- rington. An inquest will be held this (Saturday) morning. The deceased joined the force as a con- - stable in February, 1866, when he came from Chor- ley. He was then about 22 years of age. In 1882 he became an inspector, which post he held up to to the time of his death. He leaves a widow and several children to mourn his loss. For them much sympathy is expressed by people of all classes.. In- spector Berry was known as an active and conscien- tious police officer, and his services were held in *high appreciation by the magistrates, the chief con- stable, and his fellow officers. A thorough discip- linarian, he was yet courteous and kind, and his loss will be greatly deplored. •

div.head: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES.
div.p: MAGISTERIAL REFERENCES.

At the sitting of the Borough Court on Thursday, reference was made to the sad event by the magistrates. Major Litton Sala : We cannot leave the Bench this morning without expressing our very sincere regret at the melancholy accident which occurred to Police-Inspector- Berry yesterday. He was a man who was very much es- teemed in the town, being an upright and conscientious officer, and I think from what we have seen of him in this Court that we have every right to sympathise with his. widow and family in their misfortune. lam sure from what I have seen of him that he was as good and respect- ful an officer as I ever met, and I have never heard any- thing to the contrary; in fact, all to whom I have spoken seem to be very much of the same opinion, and we sym- pathise very much with everyone who was connected with ' him, more particularly with his widow and family. It was a very, sad thing for a man in the prime of life to be cut off in this manner, but it is one of those misfortunes which do. occasionally occur. _ _ _

Alderman Webster: I coincide entirely with 'the re-- marks of the chairman; and I must say from my experi- ence of Inspector Berry that I have always found him to be a man thoroughly tb be depended upon in this court in the evidence he had to give, which was always most straight- forward and, I believe, bdnest. That is one of the greatest merits a police officer can have—that is, when his evidence can always be depended upon by the Bench. I sympathise deeply. as the chairman does, with • the widow and family upon the loss they have sustained. Inspector James (in the absence of , the Chief Constable,. who is indisposed) said Mr. Hunt, as well as the deceased's widow and family, would be glad to hear of the kind refer- ences which had been made by the Bench.

div.head: CORONER'S REFERENCE.
div.p: THE CORONER'S REFERENCE.

At an inquest held in Warrington on Thursday afternoon, Mr. Husband, the deputy-coroner, also made reference to the death of Inspector Berry. Mr. Husband said that probably there was not a gentleman in that roam that had not been deeply affected by the death of Inspector Berry. They had always found him to be an affable, -kind, and agreeable officer, and he was sure they all regretted the loss of so Nalabia an inspector. It seemed from what he (the deputy coroner had learned, that the inspector in attempting to save the life of another person had lost his own. They would all deeply sympathise with the sorrowing widow and family.

Mr.?. Davies, who was present at the inquest add ha felt strongly on the matter, perhaps more so than did the deputy coroner, seeing that he was in more con‘tant con- nection with the police. He was sure there was not a better police officer than Inspector Berry. Inspector Spinks thanked the deputy coroner and Mr. Davies for their kind remarks, and said he should brine; them under the notice of the deceased's family and rela- tives.
Ealing

div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Moerhe.Y.—Before the Mayor (alderman Harrison), Alder- man Davies, Councillor Greening, and Mr. T. Sutton. DRUNRENNESS.—Tbe follatwing people were fined for drunkenness :—William Conroy, in the Market-place on Saturday afternoon, fined 108 and costs; Martin Lyons, at Market-gate on Saturday eight, tined 10e and costa; Martin Higgins, in Church-street on Saturday night, fined se, in- cluding costs; James Jordan, in Bratermarket-street on Saturday night, fined 10e and costs; ,Margaret Sparks, in Buttermarket-street, fined 55 and costs; John Stirrup, in Winwick-street, fined 10s and costs; Eliza Smith, in Tanner's- lane, sent to prison for fourteen days. DISTURBING THE PEACE.--For committing breaches of the peace James Johnson, Walter Pridden, and Thomas Shaw were bound over and ordered to pay costs. CRUELTY TO A Cow.—Denis Finegan and Henry Mather were charged with illtreating a cow on the 20th ult. by striking it severely with a stick. Mather, a boy, was fined 5s and costs, and Finegan was fined 103 and costs. OBSTRUCTIONS.— James Leslie, B. Norman, Andrew Campbell, and Joseph Looker were summoned for causing an oustraction near Bank Quay Station by allowing hand- carts to remain longer than necessary. They were each fined 2s 6d, including cests.--John McGinn, manager of Jones's machine shop in Sankey-street, was sumeaoned for causing an obstruction by allowing three sewing machines and six boxes to remain on the footpath an unreasonable time.—Defendant sal? chat the goods were always got into the shot) as soon after arrival as possible.—He was ordered to pay 3s 6-1 costs.--William Baker was fined is and costs for wheeling a vehicle on the footpath. FIREWORKS.—John Thomas Collins and Thomas Kay, boys, were each tined is, including costs, for letting off fire- works in a public thoroughfare on the 19th ult. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Mark Flander was fined is for al- lowing the chimney 9f his house to be on fire. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. T. Sutton, and Mr. E. J. Guest. DRUNKENNESS.—Jobn Cannon was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Scotland-road on the evening previous. He was fined 5s and costs. CHARGE OF WIFE _ASSAULT.— George Bircball was charged by his wlfe Ellen with assaulting her on the previous day. Complainant said that her husband kicked her. In answer to Mr. Browne, who appeared for the defendant, she denied that she was addicted to drinking.—Prisoner said that he paid for six quarts of beer for his wife and her friends, and becauee he would not pay for any more his wife took out a warract.—The magistrates ordered him to be bound over, himself in £lO, and one surety of £5, to keep the peace for six months. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Pickmere and Mr. John Fairclough. AN ABSENTEE.—AIfred Hewitt, charged with being an absentee from the 1885 training of the Middlesex militia, at Hounslow, was fined 403 and costs. DreuerreertNese.—Helen Driscoll was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Wiuwick-street, on the previous afternoon. She was dismissed on promising to go to the Workhouse at once.—John McCoan was brought up on a warrant charged with being drunk and disorderly in Factory- yard. on the 19th ult. He was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.—Michael Morris was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bewsey-road, shortly after two o'clock the same morning. A fine of 5s and costs, or a week's imprisonment, was imposed. ALLEGED ASSAULT—James Ansbury Was charged with assaulting John Reynolds, on the 3rd of July last. Prose- cutor did not appear, and Ansbury was consequently dis- charged. Tarnspsy.—Before Major Litton and Alderman Webster. DRUNKENNESS.— Henry Wilson, a young man, was fined lOs and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Butterrner- ket-street. VAGRANCY. —Richard Jeffries was charged with begging in Sankey-street on the previous night. He received a bad character, and was sent to prison for three months. FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds and Dr. Gornall. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—AIica Bailey was SIMIIIIOned by Martha Talbot for assaulting her. Mr. A. Brewne defended. Complainant alleged that defendant struck her, but from the evidence adduced in favour of the defendant, it appeared that complainant used insulting language to her and much recrimination was indulged in by both parties. The magis- trates dismissed the case.
RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Hf-,nry Reynolds and Mr. James Hand I ey. _

JURY LISTS —The assietant overseers of the townships of Runcorn, Weston, Halton, Clifton, Norton, Scockham, and Sutton, presented lists of persons likely serve on juries, which were approved. MISCELLAREOUS.—For permitting the chimney of his dwelling-house in Mersey-street to be on tire, Patrick Coffey was fined 6,1 and costs, 9-5 61-1? or Legzing at Weston on Saturday, Owen Smith Ivas sentenced to seven days' hard la6our.—A. sentenc,‘ was passcd upon Charles Roberts for " sleepinz out."—James Flannaglian was tined lOs and costs for b,ing drunk and disorderly in I.4lers,:y-street on Saturday night.

DaRESBURY PETTY SESSIONS. TIDESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. Greenall (in the chair), W. 'Lang, C. Broadbent, H. Mama, and Neild. JURY LISTS—The jury lists for the various townships within the Petty Sessional division were presented and signed by the Bench. THE SARACEN'S HEAD, WILDERSPOOL. Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, applied for the granting of a licence to the new Saracen's Head public-house, Wilderspool, which, he said, was now finished—with the exception of some seat- ing that was being rapidly put in—at an expense of £2OOO. Be also mentioned that the tenant of the new hotel was to be Mr. George Pilling, the son of the late overseer of War- lington, and that as soon as he went in Mrs. Skinner was prepared to give up the licence of the old Saracen's Head.— Mr. W. Owen, architect, Warrington, said that the new house was practically complete now, though they still wanted the fixed seating put in. It would be finished by the 10th October.—lt was resolved to grant the new license, the new house to be opened and the old one closed on tbe 10th October. SWINE FEVER AT LITTLE LEIGH. —James Drinkwater, farmer, Little Leigh, was charged with not having reported the existence of swine fever on his premises at Little Leigh on the 13th August. Mr. P. Davies, of Warrington' defended.—Police-Sergeant Blair, lately stationed at Bud. worth, said that on the 13th Aug. as be was passing defend- ant's farmhouse a boy told him that Mr. Drinkwater wanted him. He went into the farmyard and saw Mr. Drinkwater engaged cleaning a pig which he said had died in a fit, and which he said he was preparing for the market, if passed by the sergeant. He (witness) said he could not pass the car- case, after which defendant showed him several other live pigs and told him that those were all he had. but on looking round he noticed another pig which had marks upon it. Wit- ness said that the attention of Mr. Darwell, veterinary sur- geon, Northwich, inspector under the Contagions Diseases Act, must be called to the pigs, and defendant drove him to Northwich to seek Mr. Darwell, who, however, as it was late, said he would come the next morning. The next morning Mr. Darwell savv both the carcase and the live pig, and de- clared that they were both infected with swine fever.—ln defence it was contended that, in the first place, the pigs had not peen infected with swine fever, an,i if so, that sufficient notice of the fact had been given.—In support, Mr. Willett, veterinary surgeon, was called and declared that the pigs had not been suffering from swine fever, and Mr. W. Robin- son, farmer, Antrobns, who said he had killed thousands of pigs, and wh, said he had seen the other pigs of the same litter and they were quite healthy. It was impossible, in his opinion, for one or two pigs of a litter to be infected with swine fever without the others being infected also, when they had lived together.—ln the end a fine of 108 and costs was imposed. Notice of appeal was given. AD" Irt!ILATED COFFEE .—Thomas Baxter, shopkeeper, of Walton Inferior, was fined is and costs for selling coffee adulterated with chicory, without specifying the same. ALLOWING ANIMALS TO STRAY.—Forallowing a pony and a cow to stray on the highway at Dutton, on tho sth of September, William Rutter was fined 2s and cotta.— William Sutton, for permitting a cow and two calves to stray tippleton, on the Bth inst, was fined 3s and

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. T. S. Timmis. DRUNKEN-NESS. The following persons were fined for drunkenness :—John Wickham, Michael Timmins, Robert Davies, Patrick McGuire, George Lorinson. and Richard Roach, 5s and costs, or seven days; Darby Mulligan, John Heye.s, and John Walsh, 103 and costs, or 14 day.—Mulli- gan, it wae stated, had been convicted 11 times, and the two last-named offenders seven times each, for drunkenness and other offences. .BREACH OF THE PEACE. Catherine Hynes, for com- mitting a breach of the peace by fighting. with another wo- man in water-street, on Saturday night, was, on the evi•` deuce of P.C. WINDOW BREAKER:—John 'Janina!' was charged with having been drunk at .W .. idnes on Saturday, and with doing wilful damage to a wpadow, the property of Joseph Rogers', the Ivy Green beerhouse, Pitt-street. Mr. Rogers saw the prisoner come down the road and deliberately knock his hand through the window. He went to speak to him about it, when he used foul language to him. P.C. Evans then came upon the scene, and the prisoner and another man who was with him ran away. The officer followed and captured the prisoner in Church-street, where he was making a dis- turbance with a woman about some tobacco. It appeared he went into the person's shop pretending to buy half a pound, and when he had gone out she missed a packet. It was
