TRAGIC DEATH OF A MIIRDERER.—A Portland (Oregan) telegram gives an account of the death of a murderer who had been arrested after escaping. The tragedy occurred on the 7th inst. in Grand Coulee, half way between Spokane Falls and Okanogan, in Washington Territory. A man named Paine committed a murder in Missouri several years ago, and was sentenced to be hanved. He escaped to Wash- ington Territory and settled in Okanogan county. His whereabouts having become known, a requisition for Paine was sent to Spokane Falls, and was placed in the hands of Constable J. Hubbard to serve. Hubbard took F Aiken as his deputy, and left on Sundav morning, the sth, for Paine's place, 100 miles distant. They secured Paine without trouble and put handcuffs on him. Paine asked to be al- lowed to bid farewell to his wife, and his request was granted. The two officers and the prisoner then started about noon for Spokane Falls. Towards dusk a seta of Paine, aged 25 Years, who had followed on horseback, over- took the officers and began firing from a Winchester rifle. The third r•bot hit his father, who died ten minutes after- wards. The officers opened fire with revolvers, but the range of the weapons was too short. The fifth shot from Paine struck Hubbard in the chin, and he fell to the ground dead. Young Paine then rode from the ground and made his escape. The old man, as he was dying, confessed to Aiken that when he bade his wife good-bye he told her to tell their son to rescue him, even if be had. to kill the offi- cers.

EARLESTOWN. A SLEEPY DRlVER.—Gilbert Groundp, a young man, li:ing at Orford, was summoned at the Newton Petty Ses- sions, on Saturday, for riding asleep in a cart drawn by one borse, in Warrington-road, Winwick, on the 17th ult., and was fined 2s 6d and costs.

CAUTION TO YOUNG IVIEN7—At the Newton Petty Ses- sions on Baturday, John Noon, Tbomas Judge, and John Waldren, young men, were charged with obstructing the footpath at Golborne, by jutiming thereon on Sunday, the 12th September. It was stated there had been many com- plaints of such practices, and the Bench fined each defend- ant is and costs.

OXFORD LOCAL EXAMINAT/01P8. —At the June ex- amination held at the Liverpool centre, Miss Bessie M. Smith, daughter of Mr. Alderman J. Smith, J.P., Mab's Cross, Wigan, and pupil of Miss Pennington, Halcyon House, Newton-le-Willows, passed in second-class honours. This candidate, in addition to English subjects generally, selected mathematics, music, and drawing, in all of which she was successful.

Tan JURY LISTS. —At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, the assistant overseers presented the lists of per- sons qualified to serve on juries for the under-mentioned townships, which were duly signed by the magistrates: Cnerdley, Penketh, Buttonwood, Great Sankey, Golborne, Newton, Woolston-with Martinseroft, Rixton-with-Glaze- brook, Houghton, Middleton and Arbury, Southworth-with- Croft, Poulton-with-Fearnhead, Winwick, Haydock, and Warrington. ODDIfELLOWEI DINNER. The members of the Via- duct Lodge of Loyal Order of Oddfellows held their annual dinner in the Wellington Inn, Earle-street, on Saturday evening. About 50 members and visitors sat down to an excellent repast, after which the tables were cleared and the chair was occupied by Bro. 'l'. Tunstall, the vice-chairman being Bro. Thomas Peet. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were propossd and duly honoured, and the evening was spent in a convivial manner.

A SUFFISEING DBFENDANT. At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, Michael Garry was summoned for being disorderly and refusing to quit the Old Crow Inn, Crow-lane, on the Bth September.—Superintendent Weir stated tbat since the defendant was served with the sum- mons he had been taken seriously ill and had been removed to Liverpool Infirmary. He therefore asked far the case to be remanded for five weeks.—Police-sergeant Commins said the defendant was suffering from an abscess in his face_ —The case was adjourned for five weeks.

SUNDA.Y AMUSEMENTB.—At the Newton Town Hall,. on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and W. F. Gooch, William Henry Singleton, John Brown, Thomas Gregson, and Joseph Shuttle were summoned for playing at pitch and toss at Wargrave on the 19th ult. Police-constable Hunt stated - that on Sunday afternoon he and P.C. Spencer were on duty at Wargrave, and they saw the defendants in Bradlegh-read gaming at pitch and toss. They saw money pass several times.—The defendants strongly denied the offence. The Chairman said he understood pitch and toss was becoming a great nuisance, and young men ought to know better than in- dulge in it, and especially on a Sunday afternoon.—The de- fendants were each fined 5s and costs. A. MIDNIGHT DiSTITRBANCE. Before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and W. F. Gooch, Mary Downs and her son James were charged on remand with committing a breach of the peace at Earlestown, on the 25th August.—P.C. Lee stated that about twenty minutes past twelve on the night of Friday, the date in question the defendants were drunk and disorderly in Legh- street, Earlestown. They were using bad language to a man named Bates. A crowd of people had assembled and many persons were looking through their bedroom windows. —lhe male defendant pleaded guilty, but Mrs Downs said she had never spoken a word. Her daughter and her daughter's husband were quarrelling and when she heard the baby scream she ran to her.—Each defendant was bound over to keep the peoce for six months. HARVEST FESTIVAL AT ST. JOHN'S CHURCH.—Harvest thanksgiving services were held in St. Joan the Baptiat' Church, Market-street, Earlestown, on Sunday. The sacred edifice had been tastefully decorated for the occasion, thei windows and chancel being especially noticeable for the beautiful arrangement of the roses, dahlias, and evergreens, interspersed with sprays, imitating sheaves of wheat, corn, Asc. The pulpit and choir stalls were decorated with wild flowers. grass, &c., which had been gathered in the fields by the school children. There was a fair congregation at the morning service, and at the evening service the church was crowded. Tbe collections were in aid of the funds of the church. The preacher for the day was the Rev. Elgar Hicks, of Liverpool, and appropriate sermons were delivered' The services were continued on Monday evening, when the Rev. Canon Ryecroft, of Liverpool, occupied the pulpit. GOOD TEMPLARS' ENTERTAINMENT.—About 35 mem- bers of the Pride of Earlestown Juvenile Templars enter- tained the members of the Hope of Earlestown Lodge of Good Templar i (adults) on Monday evening. There was a large attendance of the latter. Brother E. Neman, S.T.T., presided. An enjoyable programme of songs, recitations, dec., was gone through, and on the motion of Brother Geo. Clarke, seconded by Brother George E. Warburton, thanks were accorded to the entertainers. Brother Richard Wal- ton, a juvenile, responded. The weekly session of the Arial t Lodge was afterwards held, under the presidency of Brother George E. Warburton, in the absence of the W.C.T. Daring the session Sister Porter, of Liverpool, D.W.V.T., gave an interesting address on Good Templar work, and impressed upon her hearers the importance of a close union and good fellowship between the members. She also swag a solo, and selections of music were given by Brothers W. Walker and John Makin.

SMOCKING RAILWAY FATALITY AT GOLBORNE. About noon on Tuesday a shocking accident occurred at Go!borne. A clean and respectably-dressed workman was seen in the station, and shortly afterwards, having escaped the attention of the officials, be commenced walking down the line in the direction of Wigan. He had not proceeded far when he was overtaken by the 7-15 a.m. express—Lon- doe to Carlisle. The engine caught him in the back, knock- ing him a considerable distance, breaking both arms, putting out the left shoulder, and internally injuring him. The poor fellow was picked up in an unconscious state and re- moved to the waiting-room, where restoratives were applied. Medical aid was sent for, but he died just as the doctor ar- rived. The body was removed to the Manor Arms Hotel to , await an inquest. The line is being extended at Golborne, ' and it is believed deceased was walking to the spot in search of work. Deceased is said to have hailed from near Brad- ford (Yorkshire), and to be called 'Norfolk Jack," but nothing definite can be traced respecting him. He was about forty-six years of age, with dark hair and slight sandy whiskers, and woie moleskin trousers and vest and a blue pilot coat. -UNIIAPPY DOMESTIC LIFE —At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, and W. F. Gooch, James Powell, a middle-aged man, living near the bottle works of Messrs. Walton and Co., Crew-lane, was summoned for assaulting his wife, Mary, on the 3rd September. The complainant stated that her husband was "not a husband, but a brute." He kicked her several times about the body, and thumped her repeatedly about the face and head. She had a black eye as the result, and he afterwards took a strap, with the buckle end of which he thrashed her.—A, neighbour named Mrs. Deluce, and a carter nem, d Nuttall, said they saw the defendant beating his wife.—The defendant said he had no witnesses, he did not want any, and be did not care what became of him. He accused his wife of having been drunk when he came home from his work, and said she had neg- lected to "wash his shirt." and to perform other domestic duties. He concluded a pitiful story by remarking that he could take his oath that since he was married to the prose- eutrix he had never seen her sober for a week, while for a fortnight or three weeks before they were married he never saw her a day sober. He had given his wife his wages like a man, and the Bench could de with him what they liked, as he was tired of his life. He had several times slept in ' the works all night rather than be with his wife.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay a fine of 5s and costs, and advised him next time his wife was drunk to send for a policeman.

div.head: FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT SANKEY BRIDGES. THE ADJOURNED INQUEST.
div.p: THE FATAL RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT SANKEY BRIDGES. THE ADJOURNED INQUEST.

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, resumed an inquest regarding the death of William Johnson (31) a married Tian, who lived at 37, Price-street, Warrington, and who was killed on the 28th of August at a level crossing at Sankey Bridges. Deceased was an out-porter in the em- ploy of Messrs. -.Milling and Co., grocers, Horsemar- ket-st., Warrington, and on the day in question he and a lad named Robert Willans were delivering parcels, having with them a horse and trap. One of the places to be visited was Mr. B. Grimshaw's farm-house, which lies something like three hun- dred yards on the Warrington side of Sankey Bridges Station, and is reached by way of Gate- warth-street. At the end of this street, which is only a short one, there is a level crossing over the railway that runs from Warrington to Widnes and Liverpool, and at the other side of the crossing a lane, of about 200 yards in length, leads to Mr. Grimshaw's farm-house. There being no one paid or specially authorised to look after the gates of the crossing, it seems to be the common practice of lads living in the neighbourhood to open them when they see vehicles being driven in the direction of Mr. Grimshaw's farm. On the occasion in ques- tion the gates were opened by two lads, and the horse and trap passed safely over and proceeded to j the farm-house. On returning the gates were again held open by the lads, and Johnson, who had the reins in his hand, appears to have driven at a smart pace on to the crossing. Unfortunately a train, Iwhich runs between Manchester and Liverpool on Saturdays and Mondays and is due at Sankey ' Bridges shortly after half-past one o'clock in the afteincon, had • come .up in the meantime without having been noticed by either the lads at the gat-.s or the persons in the trap, and the latter had barely got on to the line when the train rushed upon them. The horse had got on the 4.1::,wn line on which the train was, but the trap was completely in front of the engine, and as a result of the terrible collision, was in a moment, as it were, smashed into splinters. The occupants of the vehicle, together with a con- siderable quantity of baskets containing groceries, were thrown with immense impetus into the air, the poor lad, Willians, being projected between twenty and thirty yards from the point of the col- lision, and Johnson, though much the heavier of the two, was carried several yards far- ther away. Both fell hi the six - foot of the line, and consequently escaped ...being mangled by the. train. So violent was the shock that Johnson, it is said, was almost lifted to the height of one of the signal posts. Singular to say, the horse was co.mparatively little hurt, the body of the cart having apparently been wrenched in- stantaneously from the shafts, and the animal gal- loped through the gateway. When the injuries of the two occupants of the cart were attended to, it was found that Johnson was killed, but Willans, though insensible, and suffering from a severe cut on the head, showed signs of .life. The body of Johnson was removed to a neighbouring cottage, while Willans was taken to the Warrington Infirm- ary. The force of the blow with which the cart was struck by the engine was vividly illustrated by the manner in which the fragments and contents were scattered for a distance of almost one hundred yards down the line. Johnson, who leaves a wife and two young children, had been in the employ of Messrs. Milling and Co. for about seven years, and was a steady . man and well thought of by his employers. Willians is fouy- teen years of age, and lived with his parents in Greenall-street. An inquest was opened on the Tuesday following the accident, when evidence was , taken that has already been reported. The enquiry was adjourned to see how the injured lad pro- gressed and to call further evidence. The adjourned enquiry was held at the Great Sankey Board Schools. The solicitors present were Messrs. T. J. Ridgway, who appeared on behalf of Messrs. Mil- ling and Co. and the relatives of the deceased; Mr. W. H. Jenkins, who represented Mr. B. Grimshaw,

div.head: HARVEST HOME FESTIVAL AND
div.p: HARVEST HOME FESTIVAL AND
CONCERT.

The most popular gathering for some years was held in the Primitive Methodist Schoolroom, Legh-street, on Tues- day evening. lhe occasion was the holding of a "Harvest Home" and concert, the proceeds of which were to be de- voted to the circuit funds. A hearty co-operation to make the gathering a success was evinced on the part of every member of the congregation, which rendered its failure almost impossible, while their individual generosity, coupled with that of other friends, added much to the gratification of the promoters. Rich and poor alike of the friends of the Primitive Methodist Chapel responded liberally to an appeal for contributions in the shape of fruit, vegetables, wheat, corn, and other emblems of the ingathering of the harvest. It is a question whether in the past history of Eailestown such a large quantity was ever gathered into a place of worship, and it is even more doubtful if ever the work of decoration was carried to a more successful issue. The walls of the schoolroom were literally covere I with choice arrangements of flowers, fruits, and vegetables, but the platform was one of the richest pieces of floral decora- tion ever seen in the district. The centre of the pl Worm was occupied by a kind of triumphal arch, covered with red baize, relieved with floral wreaths, and festooned with white curtains. A large Union Jack was an effective background. In front of the white curtains of the arch appeared a brass rod, from which hung many bunches of luscious grapes. Arranged on each side of the triumphal arch were shelves laden with fruit, vegetables, &c., and the canopy was sur- mounted with miniature necks of corn and wheat. The front portion of the Dlatform was ale() satisfactorily decorated. The window sills had been filled with the summer season's products, and along the walls were illuminated tests. The decorations had been carried out under the directions of the following committee :—Mrs. Dickens, Mr. and Mrs. Good- w n, Mr. and Mrs. T. Jackson, Mr. and Mrs, W. Worsley, Mr. and Mrs. Richard Sproston, Mr. and Mrs. F. Bagnall, Miss Carr, Miss E. Worsley, Mr. J. Sephton, Miss S. Thompson, Mr. J. Austin, and Mr. J. Sproston. The entertainment had been arranged under the supervision of Mr. 'T. Ormand, Mr. W. Banton, Mr. G. Dickens, Mr. P. Thompson, and Mr. W. Austin. The programme commenced with a pianoforte solo " Drops of dew," by Miss Sudworth, after which Mrs. Henderson and Mr. P. Hastie mere well received in the duet "Wilt thou be gone, love." As an encore they sang the Scotch piece" The crookit bawbee." Mrs. Henderson sang with taste the songs " The murmur of the shell " and " Happy be thy dreams." Mr. Peter Hestia sang "Nil Desperandum," and True till death" The song " Thou art so near and yet so far," was sung by Mr. P. El-

hot, who also gave "Alice, where art thou ?" Miss Thorni)- son sang "I dreamed a dream" and "Three fishers went :ailing." Master B. Tripp gave a violin solo, " Auld Robin Gray,' and in the second part of the programme he gave "The last rose of summer.' Miss S. Smith sang "The gate of Heaven " and the "The New Kingdom," and Mr. F. Bag- nail recited "The dying soldier" and "The burial of Moses." For the duet, " What are the wild waves saving ?" the Misses Smith were applauded. The programme was brought to a close by the singing of a quartette, "Sleep while the soft evening," by the Misses Smith, Mr. Elliott, and Mr. Smith. On Wednesday evening the fruit, flowers, ac., used in the decorations were offered for sale. Mr. William Mills was the auctioneer, and assistance was rendered by Messrs. T. Orrnand, T. Clark, Austin, Barton, dr.c.

GOLBORNE RECREATION SOCIETY. ATHLETIC FESTIVAL. div.head: _REVISION OF NEWTON VOTERS.
div.p: _REVISION OF NEWTON VOTERS.

The revision of the lists of voters for the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire was commenced before Mr. James T. Foard, revising barrister, at the Newton Town Hall, on Monday forenoon. The Liberals wore represented by Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, along with Mr. P. M. Campbell, et Barlestown, registration agent for the Nowton Division. For the Conservatives there appeared Mr. Wallhead, solicitor, Warrington, and Mr. Holbrook, Warrington. The townships taken were Newton, Button- wood, Winwick, Southworth-with-Croft, and Houghton, Middleton, and Arbary. The assistant-overseers present were Messrs. H. Houghton (Newton), T. Foster (Burton- wood), E. C. Cooper (Winwicll), and Brimelow (Croft and Houghton, &c.) Cratists AND ORP2ariows.—The number of claims and objections for the respective townships were :—Newton : Liberal objections. 52'; Conservative objections, 51; Liberal claims and re-claims, 120; Conservative claims and re- claims, 144. Bartonwood : Liberal objections. 6; Conserva- tive objections, 5 ;. Liberal claims and re-claims' 19 ; Con- servative claims and re-claims, 23. Houghton, Middleton, and Arlßtry Conservative claims, 6 ; no objections or Liberal claims. Soutliworth-with-Croft : Liberal objec- tions, 9 ; Conservative objections, 3; Liberal claims, 1 ; Conservative claims, 191 Winwick Liberal objection, 1 ; Conservative claim, 1.

QIIIISTIONABLII LODGRIZS.—Amongst the lodger claimants was John W. Glov,r, son of Mr. B. B. Glover, Newton-la- who said he paid £1 per week to his father, and had a furnished sitting-room and bedroom. In reply to the revising barrister, claimant said the sovereign included 108 for food, and was so understood when he made the arrange- ment. The Barrister : That is not good enough. Vote disallowed.—Mr. Stone, veterinary surgeon, Newton-le- Willows, claimed as a lodger paying £l5 a year. He now said he paid 12s a week, and had made a mistake. Mr. Riley urged that it was questionable whether a lodger claim should be amended,:and quoted a case. After some hesitation the barrister agreed to make the correction, but thought that such cases ahould be adjudicated'upon with the utmost discretion

LAND Olt PROPERTY ?L—Mr. John Davies claimed a vote in respect of leasehold property in Wargrave-road, and his claim was opposed by the Conservatives. He said the house had been built twelve months, and six months ago he re- moved thereto from Haydock-street, tkarlesto wn.—Mr. Well- head said his objection watt that the house had not been occupied for a sufficiently long period.—Mr. Riley explained that the claimant took the land on the 13th June, 1885, and he afterwards erected property upon it. The question was what was the property worth to him during the year; was it worth £5 ?—The Barrister held that the qualification ought to be a house or something capable of being described; in fact, it must he something in actual existence. If the land was taken alone it would not be worth £5. Thee if they took the house it was clear that it had not been in existence for 12 months. He did not think he could allow the claim this year. THE NIIVTON ASSISTAITT OVERSEER: A " Scsmi."—Mr L 91.119 F. Foulkes claimed a vote in respect of a house occu- pied by him in Bradlegh-road, Wargrave. In reply to ques- tions, he said he did not enter into tbe house until Aegust, 1885.—The Revising Barrister at once disallowed the vote, remarking that the house must be occupied for 12 months prior to July 15th.—Mr. Foulkes replied that he knew that, but his claim was made because he knew that others in a similar position to himself had been placed on the list by the Assistant Overseer —Mr. Houghton (Assistant Overseer) : I em not aware of it.—The Revising Barrister: Two blacks don't make a white.. (Laughter.)—Mr. Foulkes said he could prove his asse'rtion.—Mr. Houehton: lam net aware of anything of the kind.—Mr. Foulkes: It is so.—Mr. Houghton: Prove it.—Mr. Foulkes : I can do.—Mr. Houghton : Mention names.—Mr. Foulkes: Thomas Slater, of Crow- lane, Newton-k-Willows. He came in September, a month after me. I can give you others by a moment's reference.— The Revising Barrister : If the Overseer is anxious for them. (Laughter.)—Mr. Riley said he did not know anything about that point, but he lead the same entry, "September, 1885," against Slater's name.—The Revising Barrister said the Overseer was not bound to know exactly when a per- son entered into a house, but to enter into the rate book the names of persons whom he believed occupied premises during the year. Mr- Houghton said that his memorandum in the rate book about Slater was "Since January, 1885." He asked Mr. Ffonlkes to mention others—Mr. Ffoulkes : I have mentioned suffi- cient for Foy purpose. He afterwards asked the Revising Barrister if a person living in one parliamentary division removed into another parliamentary division could claim a vote in succession from one division to the other. He be- lieved a revising barrister in one of the districts of London bad givena decision to that effect.—The Revising Barrister did not think that was so, and did not think the decision suggested by MreFfoulkes had been correctly reported.— Mr. Riley said Mr. Ffoulkes had not claimed "in succes- sion,” or he might have argued the point for him.—The Barrister wondered if it was possible to amend the claim.— Mr. Riley : I am afraid it has been held you cannot alter it —The matter then dropped. These were the only items of public interest.

ASHTON. On Tuesday morning, Mr. J. Foard, held a court at the Local Board Rooms, Ashton, for the revision of tbe,Parlia- mentary voters' lists for the townships of Ashton-in,,Maker- held and Haydeck. Mr. H. L. Riley (St. Helens) and Mr. P. M. Campbell (registration agent) again appeared for the Literals, and Mr. Wellhead (Warrington), with Mr. Hol- brook (registration agent), represented the CODEfervtitiVeS, IMPORTANT DECISION ON LODGER CLAIMS.—A goodly number of lodger claims were set up, but at the outset the revising barrister said :—I may as well announce once and for all that wherever a person claims as a lodger in the father's or mother's house, the vote will not be allowed ex- cept there is absolute and independent proof that a fide agreement of landlord and tenant has been in existence the required time. The law never intended that two or three oersons should be put oa for a small house, and,l can- not permit any attempted manufacture of votes. here must also be a sufficient margin of rateable value to Foyer both tenant and lodger Zefore two claims can be sustained, and anything like fictitious votes I cannot and will not allow.

LORD GERARD'S COACHMAN.—Lord, Gerard's coachman claimed as an occupier of a house in his lordship's stable. yard. In reply to Mr. Riley claimant said he was absent with his master in London for three months during the qualifying period.—His Honour held that, as claimant could not return at will, the vote must be disallowed. A DOUBTFUL POINT.—The Conservatives claimed a vote under the service franchise for a caretaker respecting a large empty house belonging to Messrs. R. Evans and Co.— Mr. Riley objected on the ground that the house was not rated.—The Assistant Overseer said no rates had been Paid for four years, and applied or ,his Honour's advice.--Mr. Foard said be would give cl simant the benefit of the doubt, and allow the vote.

div.head: ST. HELENS.,
div.p: ST. HELENS.,

Mr. Foard held a court at the St. Helens Town Hall on Wednesday, for the revi3ion of the lists of voters for the townships of Ecclestcn, Sutton, Windle, Rainford, and Parr, which comprise a portion of the Newton Division. Mr. H. L Riley appeared for the Liberals, and Mr. J. 0. Swift for the Conservatives. Mr. Foarci, on taking his seat, remarked that there was a larger proportion on the list for liccleston then for any other place; and during the business he said they had a lot of claims and objections which seamed to be utterly futile, and to consider them would be a waste of public time.—Some discussion arose en the fact that " Ec- cleston-lane Ends "—a district on Present-road--had been entered to a number of names, whereas the assistant overseer had them entered as Prescot- road —Mr. Parkinson said he entered them " Pres. cot - road " on a new valuation made by the

Assessment Committee.—Mr. Foard altered the address td "krescot-road." At a later stage, when it was found that residents at all points along the thoroughfare which the assistant-oversevr had called Vrescot-road were corning for- ward with re-claims and giving local designations, the Re- vising Barrister aseepted all well-authenticated local names, and sai'd neither the overseer nor Assessment Committee had any right to make such sweeping changes unless they knew they woTaid be accepted by the Poet Office and residents themselres.

A TRADESMAN CHARGED WITH FALSE PRETENCES. EXTRAARDINARY CASH. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, a case of a Peen- liar character was heard. Thomas A. Bell, a picture frame manufacturer, and picture dealer, carrying on business in Haydock-streo, Earlestown, was charged with obtaining an albert guard, value Xes, by false pretences, from Thomas Abraham Pirnbiett, a jeweller in Market-street, Earlestown. Mr. A. Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the prisoner, who pleaded not guilty. Superintendent Weir briefly stated the charge, after which, Thomas Abraham Pimblett, the prosecutor was called. He said: lam a jeweller carrying on business at 21, Market street, Earlestown. On -Wednesday last, about half-past seven in the evening, the prisoner came to rny shop. Ile asked me if I let jewellery out on weekly payments. I said "Which way do you mean ?" He replied "To let the are ticle out at once." I said, " No, decidedly not," and he then ' asked " Upon what terms ?" I said "One half the amount being paid down, and finding a security for the other hair He went out of the shop and returned in a few minutes and asked me if I would allow him to take a gold curb chain, which he pointed out in the window, for his wife's inspection. I said I would if he would promise to return it safely in a very short time to the shop. He said, " Yes ; will return it safely to you." That was all that passed. put the chain in a little jewellery box, and gave it to hin3; 1 The chain produced is the same. He then left the shop an‘' did not bring it beck to me that night. I sent my mother to. Mr. Bell's shop about half-past eight the same night. I next saw the chain about a quarter-past two on FridaY afternoon, when Police-constable Hunt brought it tneßle. • ;nett and asked me if it was the same. lat once identi- fied it. Its value is £5. superintendent Weir % Did you notice the prisoner's condition when he calla!, to you ? Witness: He appeared to be sober.—lf you, ban known he was going to pledge the chain would you have let him have it? I should not.—ln reply to Mr. Browne? witness added; I have known Mr. Bell for about five months. I have lived in Earlestown three years, and !lave heard Mr. Bell has been a tradesman in Earlestown for eight years. I have known him by sight for more than five months —Mr. Browne: Have you ever had dealings him before ? Prosecutor: No, never.—Do you serve all- your customers this way ? He is the first who has served me this way.—Was the arrangement this—that he was 0* pay you half the money down on the following morning. and so much e week afterwards? There were no arrange- ments made at all.—lf he says he arranged to pay half the money down on the following morning and so much a week afterwards, that is not true? It is not true.—Do you know ' be was unwell on the following morning? I don't.—Do Yen know he could not get out of the house? Ido not.—Have you heard so? No.—Do you know that he expected a cheque on the following morning from a gentleman known on the bench here, at Golborne, and Intended to pay Van' with that? No, I don't know that.—Do you know he sent a boy for the cheque on the following morning and that as' the gentleman was not at home he could not pay you? I don't.—Do you mean to say that you would not have trusted Mr. Bell with ? I would not.—Would you have trusted anybody ? I would not.—Why would you not have trusted him?' I would have wanted to know something about his • character.—Then why did yo'n trust him with a guard for the approval of his wife? Because I thought he would re- turn it safely to the shop.—But there was no time stated by which. the albert must be returned ? A very short time.—According to your itatement, all he said wail " I will return it safely to you." He gave no specific time by which he would return it. No, but I thought he would return it immediately.—lt is not what you thought when he woule return it. Did he say he would return it by any particular time? No he did not.-- Would you-not have trusted him anything? I would not. —Not a penny? No.—Have you ever spoken to him be- fore ? I have not.—When did you take out the warrant? On Thursday morning.—What time? It would be abont half-past eleven o'clock.—Yet he only had it at half-past seven on Wednesday night, for inspection? That is so.— And that was before you had seen it in the hands of the police ? Yes.—Elave you any wish to press this case ? None whatever.—So long as you get the chain or the money?' Ves.—Would you prefer the money? Yes, I would prefer the money.—Prisoner (interrupting) : I ara prepared to carry out that arrangement.—Prosecutor: There was no arrangement made whatever. Thomas Baker said : I am manager of Mr. William Jones's pawnshop in Market-street, Earlestown. On the night of Wednesday, between seven and eight o'clock, the prisoner came to my master's shop. He offered the albert produced in pledge. He just asked for a sovereign upon it. He might hake had a great deal more upon it if he bad re- quired. I advanced him a sovereign. I handed the chain to the police on Friday morning.—Mr. Browne: How long have you known Mr. Bell? I have known him about two years.—Have you ever known anything against his charac- ter in any shape or kind? What I have beard about him is that he is a vary liberal man. Liberal In giving ? Yes, that is what I mean ? -- superintendent Weir : I know nothing against his character. Mr. Browne : You mean by liberal he is fend of company? Yes, sir.—Liberal, and fond of "treating Yes.—To what amount would you have given him on the chain? About £2.—Dil he give you his own name? Yes.—Was there any concealment in ani, shape or form? None whatever.—How long have you known him? Two years. I don't think he wanted to part with the chain altogether, or he would have asked more on it.—As the manager of a pawnshop, would you have trusted him £5? Yes, I would.—The Magistrates' Clerk: Without security ? Witness: Yes, sir.—Mr. Browne: He has a good' position in the town? Yes, as a picture dealer, Etc. I have never heard anything against his credit.—Did yen ask him for any explanation? No, I thought he was worth a gold albert, and I did not need to ask him anything about it,- being a tradesman.—Do you know he was bad the next day? Ido not.—Do you knew he had been drinking that night? E believe so.—Have you heard that he had been drinking? I think he had been drinking all the week. P.C. Samuel Hunt, stationed at Earlestown, said: I ap- prehended the prisoner under a warrant at five am. on Friday morning. I read the warrant over to him, and be' 'replied, "I am 'sorry. It was a drunken spree, and I in- tended to pay him for it when I got off drink." I afterwards searched him and found the pawn-ticket produced. I after-- wards went to Mr. Wm. Jones's pawnshop, and received the albert produced.—Mr. Browne: How long have you known Mr. Ball? Close on three years. Hake you known any- thing against him? No.—That is during the period you have been stationed at Earlestown? Yes.—He did not at- tempt to deny it in any way? Oh, no. He seemed Bur- prised.---Superintendent Weir: At what ?—P.C. Hunt: Bur-- prised at my coming with a warrant, when he Came down- stairs and I told him what I wanted.—Mr. Browne: He has a well-stocked shop as a picture dealer. --= P.C. Hunt: Yes. Mr. Browne then addressed the Bench on behalf of the prisoner, and said as a point of law there was no false pre- teeces. His client's tale was as good as the prosecutor's;: there was no other person present. He went into the shop, and the prosecutor said "I will let von Have it on ap- proval,!' and his client said he bought the chain out and eut and that he arranged to pay him half mine following morn- ing and the other half by weekly instalments. He then ex- pected a cheque on the following morning, with which be Intended to pay for the chain; but the gentleman had gone away, and consequently the chain was not paid for accord- ing to arrangement. He submitted there was-no false-pre- tence. The Magistrate (interposing) said:: I have studied the evidence very carefully, and I am sorry to say that I must commit him for trial. Mr- Browne again urged, as a point of law, there Shad been no,

false pretence.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Buckton) asked ,if it was usual to argue a point when a magistrate had de- cided to convict.—Mr. Browne said nabing was said at the time of the purchase when it was to be rettuned, , and the prisoner only had the chain one night, the warrant being taken out the next morning.—The Magistrate : I have really made up my mind.—Mr. Browns: Would youlike to ' hear anything as to character? I have Dr. Patterson here and a number of others.

The charge ,was then read over to the prisoner, who re- plied : I reserve my defence.—The Bench then committed him for trial at the next Liverpool Quarter Sessions.—Mr. Browne asked if the prisoner might be allowed out on bail? —The Bench: I think this is a case in which bail ought to be granted. lAm quite prepared to take two sureties of £25 each, and the prisoner himself in £so.7—Dr. J. N. Patterson and Mr. 0. Pickett were th men.

BEQUESTS TO GLASGOW INSTITUTIONS.--TTle late Mr. Andrew Cunningham, Town Clerk's deputy, Glasgow, has made some munificent bequests to Glasgow institutions. To the Glasgow University he has left £5.,000,t0 complete the tower, and £350 for an annual gold medal for mathematics, and £2 000 for bursaries connected with the University law classes; to the Glasgow Western Infirmary, £5,000; Royal Infirmary, £5,000; and the Old Man's Friendly Society, Night Asylum, Glasgow Ragged School, and Merchants' House, £5OO each. The deceased has left £250 each to six other charities, and made the Royal infirmary his resi- duary legatee. THREATENF STOPPAGE OF GOLEORNE COTTON MILS' • I —Notices have been posted at the extensive cotton mills of Messrs. S. Brawls and Co. at Golborne to the effect that at the end of the present week the hands will be at liberty ta leave without serving the usual fortnight's notice. Tbia step is regarded by the workpeople as the forerunner of the stoppage the entire concern at no distant date, and the gloomy prospect ia a serious matter for the inhabitants' The firm, hold twa large spinning mills and two weaving sheds, and formerly employed upwards of 1,200 work' people., The " New " Mill, which found employment for 500 hands, has been stanuing idle for about fifteen month% the w.orkpeople haying had to leave the neighbourhood' Owing to the de&th of Mr. John Srewis, the entire concernl together with the family residence, a large sohoolr"use. and 3.3 cottages, were, after being extensively advertised; offered for sale a few weeks ago in Manchester, but the lo had to be withdrawn without a single bid having been Trade in the locality is reported to be in a wretched cond_i: tion, but the stoppage of the remainder at the giant WOW render things far worse,

OF THIS COUNTRY IS INDIGESTION ODERN COOKING and MODERN LIVING have -IL brought it on. It comes upon US unß,wares. The patients have pains about the chest and sides and sometimes in the back. They feel dull and sleepy; the mouth has a bad taste—especially in the morn- ing. A sort of sticky slime collects about the teeth. Tne appetite is poor. There is a feeling like a heavy load on the stomach ; sometimes a faint all-gone sensation at the pit of the stomach, which food does not satisfy. The eyes are sunken, the hands and feet become cold and feel clammy. Alter a while a cough sets in, at first dry, but after a few months it is at- tended erith a greenish-coloured expectoration. The patient feels tired all the while, and sleep does not seem to afford any rest. After a time he becomes nervous, irritable, and gloomy, and has evil fore- , bodings_ There is a giddiness, a sort of whirling sensation in the head vehen rising up suddenly. The bowels become costive; the skin is dry and hot at times; the blood becomes thick and stagnant the whites of the eyes become tinged with yellow ; the kidney secretions become scanty and highly coloured, depositing a sediment after standing. There is fre- quently a spitting up of the food, semetimes with a sour taste, and sometimes with a sweetish taste; this is frequently attended with palpitation of the heart and asthmatic symptoms; the vision becomes im- paired, with spots before the eyes ; there is a feeling of great prostration and weakness. All these symp- toms are in turn present. It is thought that nearly one-half of our population has this disease in some of its varied forms. Seigel's syrup changes the fer- ments of the Digestive organs so as to convert the food we eat into a form that will give nourishment to the feebhe body, and good health is the cense- • quence. Tee effect of this remedy is simply mar- vellous: Millions upon millions of bottles have been sold in this country, and the testimonials in favour of its curative powers are overwhelming. Hundreds of so-called diseases under various names are the re- sult of Indigestion, and when this one trouble is removed the other diseases vanish, for they are but symptoms of the real malady. Good life-preserver—Food. An artist's farewell to his pictures—" You be hanged !" A philosopher says that the best way to avoid getting into debt is to die young. Why are printers' readers an incredulous body of men? Because they will not take anybody's word; they must have proofs. SOMETHING FOR DISAPPOINTED ONES.—Many a man is the architect of his own fortune, but never gets enough money to build. ANOTHER PROVERB TURNED INSIDE 017 T.—One reason why so few men are heroes to their valets is because so few men have valets. Scene—A suburban villa. Newly-married husband,: "That trellis-work wants painting badly, darling. I think I'll do it myself.' She: " Yes ;do it yourself, love, if you think it wants to be done badly." A gentleman's linen cuff, directed to the owner and stamped with a penny stamp, recently passed through ' the post-office. It bore this message :—" Please, call and pay your washing-bill.—Your Laundress." SARCASM.—Miss Sharpe: "Are you fond of waltzing, Mr. Awkward ?" Mr. Awkward: "Oh, excessively! I could waltz for ever in a dream of enchantment." Miss Sharpe: "Well, then, I wonder you don't learn !" A young lady singing a sentimental romanza displayed not only extraordinary talent, but a set of enormous teeth. " Ah," said a lady auditor to her husband, "what a grand organ !" "Perfect,' rejoined her husband, "even to the keyboArd in her mouth." A BOLD MAN.—" I consider him a bold, arrogant man." "Yes, I know he is now, but he won't be very long." "And why not, I should like to know ?" "He's to be married next week." An Orange young man took a young lady to the dance the other night, walked several squares, and didn't say but three words. Don't think that he was bashful, dear reader; he didn't have an opportunity to say any more. A THING ONE WOULD RATHER NOT HAVE SAID.— Young Featherly had been imparting to Mrs. De Towser, who has passed her first youth some information which interested that lady very; much. "I am quite surprised, Mr. Featherly," she said, "to hear of this. It only shows that—that—" "One is never too old to learn ?" prompted Featherly gallantly. If it was possible to divest man of his pride, plug hat, and starched adornments, he would become a very common-place and slouchy sort of an individual; but if it was possible to take away from lovely woman her bustle, padding, and make-up adornments, there would still be enough of her left to talk a man into convul- sions, and to make him feel as cheap as ever. A Scotch minister was paid to preach a sermon on some special occasion ir . a neighbouring town. He was informed beforehand that they could not afford to pay him more than a guinea for his discourse. When the sermon was over, he received in the vestry the.congratu- lations of the elders, who were loud in the admiration of his eloquence. He turned round upon them with a smile of contempt, and said, "Do you call that an eloquent sermon? I should just like you to hear my three-guinea one !" SOME OF HIS EARLY WORE.—A Vienna gentleman went to see Munkacsy the painter the other day, and explained that he would like to buy some pictures by him—" only," he added, "I cannot afford to pay the prices you now ask. Could you not tell me where I could find some of your early work, painted when you Were a young man in Hungary—something that I could buy cheap ?" "Certainly," said the artist; "there are two or three hundred in my native village of Munkacz —the houses I painted when I was Michael Lieb, painter and glazier." "What is thrift, after all ?" asks Mr. George Augustus Sala. "To my mind, the very best definition of the quality of frugality, or economical management of your incomings and outgoings, was that given by Mr. Henry Pulteney to an inquigitive young lady. Thrift, my dear,' he said, 'is simply this. We will suppose that the weather is very hot; that you have walked a long way; that you are very thirsty; that you like beer; that you are passing the door of an inn, and that it occurs to you that, next to a cup of nectar, a pint of beer would be about the nicest thing in the world. Have half a pint of beer. That is thrift." A raw citizen in Idaho was elected a justice of the peace, and the only law-book he had was a Cushing's Manual. The first case before him was that of a cow- boy for stealing a steer. When the case was called, the only lawyer in the little town was there to defend the prisoner. "As there is no counsel for the other side," he said, I make a motion that the case be dismissed." The justice looked over his Manual. "A motion has to be seconded," he said. "I second the motion," promptly responded the prisoner. "The motion has been made and seconded that the case be dismissed," said the Court. "All in favour will pTease say Ay." The prisoner and his attorney voted "Ay." "All opposed say 'No.'" Nobody voted. "The motion is carried, and the case is dismissed," remarked the Court. "A motion to adjourn is now in order." The prisoner made the motion, and the Court adjourned. SOUL-STIRRING ELOQUENCE.—OId Colonel Zell, at the time when Grant was up for the American Presidency, and when the Democratic watchword was "Anything to beat Grant I" was addressing an enthusiastic meeting of Republicans, when a Democrat who was hanging on to the verge of the crowd sang out, "It's easy talkin', colonel; but we'll show you something next fall." The. colonel was a Southern Union man of the ultra school and a great admirer of Grant. He at once wheeled about, and, with uplifted hands, hair bristling, and eyes flashing fire, cried out, "Build a wire fence round a winter supply of summer weather; skim the clouds from the sky with a teaspoon; catch a thunderbolt in a bladder; break a hurricane to harness; ground-sluice an earthquake ; lasso an avalanche; fix a clout on the - crater of an active volcano; hive all the stars in a nail-keg; hang out the ocean on a grape-vine to dry; put the sky to soak in a gourd, and paste To Let' on the sun and moon, but never, sir —never for a moment delude yourself with the idea that you can beat Grant !" The late Charles Dillon used to relate an amusing in- cident that occurred to him whilst travelling in Australia. ; He was due in a certain far-away city which boasted two theatres, and each of the managers, it seems, had been in tvreaty to secure him for the same date. He closed with one, and started on his way. After long and tedious journey, he arrived. The first thing that attracted his attention was a huge burly man, who, blazing with jewellery and towering above the passengers, was shouting at the top of his voice, "Which is Charles Dillon" Dillon waited till most of the crowd had dis- persed, and then, timidly approaching the glittering giant, said, "I am." "Thank Heaven !" exclaimed the man. "I was afraid you wouldn't come. I'm Manager B." In an instant Dillon felt himself hurried along as if impelled by some sudden shock, and only recovered when he had been deposited in a magnificently-appointed brougham, with the gorgeous Crummles seated opposite. ,clvell, I've got ye! The other manager tried for ye, but I've got ye !" "No doubt of it," muttered Dillon, moving uneasily. sily. "Isn't he riled too! What do you think he's going to do to spite me ?" "1 d, on't know." The Glyn Board of Guardians passecl a resolution on Sat- urday in favour of a national tribute being conferred on Mr. Gladstene, and requested Mr. Parnell's co-operation. • Two tricyclers chanced to halt by the roadside near Cambridge for a brief rest just as a group of Irish la- bourers were passing on their way home from work. Attracted by the bright new machines, two of the men paused a moment to look at them. "If you only had a tricycle, Pat," said one of the cyders to the nearest of the 'men, "you could ride to and from your employment." Said Pat, with a contemptuous look at the combination of man and wheels, "Do ye think that I came from the ould counthry to drive a donkey cart, bedad, and be me own horse?" THE SPOUTING OF WHALES.—WhaIes do not spout water. They spout vapour or breath. When a whale spoutf, his "spout hole," as whalers call it, is always above water. The enormous volume of the whale's breath, expelled suddenly into the different temperature of the air, causes the white bush-like vapour to remain suspended for a moment, like the steam from a loco- motive. The only time a whale spouts liquid is when lie has been mortally pierced by a lance, and then he spouts warm blood. The sound of a whale's spouting is like the roar of a locomotiue blowing off steam. "I've been digging over my garden," said Brown, "and I'm worn out." "Ah !" remarked Fogg, "a new kind of earthen-wear, eh ?" Fenderson, who was pre- sent, thought it was a mighty good joke, and seeing Smith a short time afterwards, of course he had to tell it. "I "say, Smith," said he, "Fogg just hit off a neat thing. Brown was saying . that lie was all worn out digging in his garden, and Fogg asked him if that wasn't a new kind of crockery-ware. What do you think of that?" "I don't see the point." "Nor do I either, now; but I thought I did when Fogg told it." Emmy' RISING.—An hour spent in the garden, or a brisk run in the green lanes, where the birds are rejoic- ing, and where sweet smells rise from every hedgerow— what earthly pleasure equals it? It lightens care, nerves the arm, clears the brain, and lifts the heart to God. Try it. "Early to bed, and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise," was the motto and practice of our forefathers; in this respect, though not in many other respects, wiser than we. Abroad the working folk are very early risers. In France, and Germany, and Switzerland the peasant farmers are up with the sun. in the towns, the sounds of busy labour begin at five _o'clock. In the heat of the day all wisely rest for two hours; and everybody, except idle, fashionable, or dis- sipated folk, goes to bed with the birds. div.head: SKIN DISEASES
div.p: SKIN DISEASES

Are of two kinds : firstly, those which are only skin deep (which are not now to be considered) ; secondly, those which are caused by a bad state of the blood, and which attack various parts of the body in different ways. Skin disease shows itself in the HEAD, sometimes in the form of Dandruff, which no amount of brushing and combieg will get rid of ; and some- times in the form of scaly eruptions, In the NECK, by an enlargement of the glands (commonly called Glandular Swell- ings), which, if unchecked, become very unsightly wounds. In the ARMPITS, and the inside of the ELBOWS, by an in- flamed roughness of the Skin, which is very paintul when washed. In the HANDS, by deep cracks or fissures, which, if healed for a few days, speedily open again, or by horny-look- ing patches. In the LEti El, by hard, shiny, and inflamed swellings, or by wounds more or less deep; and on the BODY, in red scaly patches, 'which, as often as rubbed off, form again, or in the discharge of a thin watery fluid of a very disagreeable nature. In all these cases the treatment must be twofold: An Ointment is required to relieve Itching, and to heal the surfaee, and medicine must be taken to change the state of the Blood and render it pure. Both these requirements are supplied by Dr. ROBERTS' CELEBRATED MEDICINES.

THE MAGISTRACY. Sir,—l see we have had another batch of justices appointed for the to n whose °ply recommendation seems to be that they have played a rather prominent part tn politics, and not on account of their h.ving any special advantage to mete out justice. Don't von think it is about time these apaointments were done away with, and that we had a stipendiary, one who understood his business, so that the saying of " justice's justice" might pass into an old say- ing? There are plenty of magistrates for the town without having Leen afflicted with this last lot.-1 remain, yours respectfully, .1. W. Church-street, Warrington.

div.head: STATE OF HALL-STREET.
div.p: THE STATE OF HALL-STREET.

Sir,—Ma; T call attention through the medium of your valued paper to the condition of Hall-street? Disorder of a most disgraceful kind is carried on nightly by young ruffians of both sexes, who‘e chief delight seems to be in knocking at house doors, congregating in groups, and shocking the ears of the few peaceable ratepayers who find it convenient to reside in this particular street, by brawling out the most filthy language. It is almost an im- possibility for any respectable person to pass through this thoroughfare, especially after dusk, without being grossly in- sulted and often erou;ls abused by these foul-mouthed ga,45. How long is this crying evil to exist ? It is high time something effectual was done. Let me suggest a little snore police interference, and a few of these miscreants hauled up before the bench and made a very severe example of, for the benefit of all lovers of ORDER AND DECENCY.

CLIFFORD DIX AND SANITARY MATTERS. Sir,—lt is always a source of pleasure to read the letters of " clifroTa Dix." He is always easy to understand, not infrequently- humurous, honest in intention, and often, but not always, right. His last letter would be useful if it was based upon a cor- rect knowledge of the case. It is easy to criticise and to call names, especially when you make your own "man of straw" for the purpose of knocking him down. Mr. " Dix " begins by styling the works at Longford as the "Longford Folly." It is not' English" to condemn a thing or a man untried, and while it is quite true that in the past the Long- ford Deeot as such has been a source of considerable ex- pense to the ratepayer., owing in a great measure to its in- completeness and incapacity to deal with anything like the whole of the refuse of the town, it is also true that the sanitary condition of Warrington is better than that of any town in Lancashire similarly situated as to site, Szc. How is it that while other towns are so frequently visited by epidemics of one kind or another, which sweep away, irrespective of condition or class, scores and sometimes hundreds of lives before the devastation can be arrested, Warrington, which is by no means healthily situated naturally. escapes so well. The answer is to be found at Longford and at the hospital in Aikin-street. It is true that the perambulations of the Cor- poration vans are diffusive of odours more pungent than agreeable, but there are worse things in the world than an occasional " stink." But the weekly clearance of the reface from every house in the borough is in itself the greatest possible safeguard against disease. If disease of a dangeroas and infectious character does break out and sufficient isola- tion cannot be secured at the residence of the patient so as to prevent infection, a removal can be at Once effected, and at the Fever Hospital everything that medical skill, combined with kind and efficient nursing and scrupulous cleanliness can do, is done, and many people in this town have cause to be deeply thankful for the existence of this much abused but most beneficent institution. Now as to the present Longford scheme, I am not an engineer nor a scientist. I only profess to be a common- sense man, taking a common-sense view of the scheme, and 1 believe and hope that success will attend the present under- taking. By success I mean not merely theoretical, but practical and financial. In the first place, the economy in the cost of the collection and transmission of the refuse to Longford must be very great, and secondly, the fact that we have now machinery at Longford which is capable of deal- ing with the whole of our production, instead of as formerly, with only half of it, and at very little extra cost, and so enabling us to double the quantity previously produced of a concentrated manure, admittedly of first-class quality, must inevitably lead to a great increase in the receipts. To whom do we mainly owe our present indemnity from disease, and the satisfactory sanitary position of our tewn ? To a man who, in hi a 40 years service to Warrington, has been more abused and less understood than any public man 'ln the borough, but who in spite of opposition often be- gotten of ignorance, prejudice, and self-interest, has pur- !ued.a steady, undeviating course, having only one object an view, viz., the sanitary improvement of Warrington. To Alderman Bargees our thanks are due, and I trust that in the near future those amongst us who realise the vast im- portance of the great sanitary reformation which has been quietly but vigorously accomplished in our midst, may have the opportunity of placing upon record in some per- .m,tnent form our high appreciation of his sterling werk.— Yo ars, JUNIOR.

div.head: TEE IRISH QUESTION.
div.p: TEE IRISH QUESTION.

Sir,—Your leader of last Saturday was very opportune. Now that Parliament has ceased for a time to meet we ma' expect those whose politics are something mere than a peg whereon to hang their patty social ambitions to take to the 'various local platforms. Of course I don't expect that we in Warrington have any chance of at any time hearing Sir Gilbert Greenell give ex- pression to any political opinions. If the hoeourable gentle- re 11 happens to be possessed of any, he takes good care to keep his constituents in the dark respecting them. Ido re- member, sir, and no doubt your readers will remember, that on several occasions when we have been struggling to send a man to Parliament who might fairly be said to represent the intelligence of the age, Sir Gilbert has boasted of hav- ing his friend, "plain John Roberts," to support him in whit "everyone knew to be his political opinions ;" but Sir Gilbert never by any chance ever stated how he came to be a Tory, or why he supported a Tory Government. We know well that the text and substance of what Sir Gilbert's friends call his poll. ical :Teethee have been : " How protd lam to see my friends around me,! am always proud to see my friends; you stand by me, and I'll stand by you." I have not the least doubt that I may venture to prophecy that the local press will report, as the result of a further effort on Sir Gilbert's part, the words I have already quoted from a stereotyped speech that is already stored up in the local archives in the Museum. _ _ _

What of irel-a-nd—a-ndir-e-1-a—nd's grievances? Is Sir Gilbert prepared to give to his constituents a reason why he thinks Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule measure would lead to repeal? What effect have the recently published statistics respecting Irish produce had on his mind? I aria supposing him to have read and studied these. figures as becomes a legislator. and as one who wishes to pose as a patriot. Irish produce has decreased in value, so has both Irish and English labour, yet Sir Gilbert and the party he is identified with wish to maintain rents as fixed by a land court. This action is more stupid a thous Ind times than it is for uneducated working- men to resist A falling market. Fault is found with work- ing-men when with strikes tkey enter into strife with capital, and yet Government is spending thousands of pounds of English money in trying to force, by eviction, 9 rent from Irish farmers. Nature has done little towards helping Irish farmers; bog land, and mountain land, has been converted into arable land by sheer I .bonr, and as a reward English Tories send soldiers over on'eviction errands. These Tories and dissen- tient Liberals talk of separation; why, if they have their way a twelve month longer, it will not only be Ireland that will demand, and have, Home Rule, but Scotland and Wales will have it also. Coming events are casting their shadows be-

fore; the tithe war ix Wales is destined to be the first sma‘l I cloud, no bigger than a man's hand, that will ultimately overshadow the whole land. Radicals have for years been pointing out how oar griev- ances might be remedied ; thousands of times has it been I etat,-d that the land question included within its grasp the

.. . secret of England's decadence or success. Resisted at every step by a party which had " no go" in it, we are now face to face with the most important problem we have ever been called upon to solve. In Ireland, Scotland, and Wales the cause of discontent is the land having to produce Dis- raeli's "three profits." Let the Tory working-roan, if there be such an animal, look out the names of the landlords he 1 is so proud to support, who are now demanding their rents I at the bayonet's point, and ask himself what good they ever did him or his country, or bow much worse off the world would ever have been had they never been born. It is the land question in England that now causes men's wages and employers' profits to disappear, and I am pleased to see, sir, from your report of the Warrington Farmers' Club, that at last the farmers are wakening up. It is com- mon report that Warrington tradesmen are at their wits' end on account of the neighbouring farmers, and there are not wanting men who can state with confidence that very few of the farmers who come into Warrington are solvent. Mr. John Derbyshire, at the Farmers' Club, made some sensible remarks, amongst others that were rather foolish If anyone has "talked down " the farmer it has been his landlord and his agent; the " newspaper proprietor and the reporter " have nothing to gain by doing this. abe farmer has hitherto been too happy to bow and scrape at the rent audit; his independence has been lost in the nod given by his landlord when coming out of church on Sunday, and now he is forced to acknowledge, in the words of Mr. Der- byshire, that when a man gives "from £3O to £35 a year in tithes" he might as well throw it in the river, because he " receives no benefit what- ever" from the payment. Mr. Derbyshire may rest assured that his cause and that of the Irish farmers are identical, ard that if be and his friends" remain at borne and count the cin- ders," eviction in the long run will be their doom. The Secretary (M. J. L. Stelfqx) is either a Radical or ought to be one. Referring to the rent qnestio.n, he said "he thought that in time the rent on agricultural land would he alto- gether abolished." Mr. Wright was not able to see that al- though "money had been expended on the land" it had first come out of it, consequently it was the farmer's own earnings which he was invited to submit for taxation. Both these gentlemen may ultimately be led to see that not only agricultural land, but the land upon which stands all our mills, and the minerals in the land shall be free ; that, who. ever may have given the land, it is as necessary to our exis- tence as the air we breathe, or the water we drink, and should, within certain lines, be quite as free. I may, in con- clusion, tell the members of the Farmers' Club that they can only get more for their produce when the masses earn more for their labour. No portion of the community can long live in affluence at the expense of another. So far we have had the ball in our own hands; other nations, America, = Germany, India. Australia, are now taking hold of it, or may kick it beyond us. The gulf is too wide between the " masses and the classes ;" it must be narrowed. ....... CLIFFORD DIX.

CHAMBERLAIN AND LIBERAL UNITY.—Mr. Ch.ant- berlain says, in a letter to a correspondent, that he has given sufficient proof of his desire to make all possible conces- sions in order to avoid party divisions, but the only result has been that, having gone to the furthest limit without re- sult, he has thereby incurred charges of inconsistency which are as ungenerous as they are untrue. The right bon. gen- tleman adds that the intolerant language and actions of a section of the Liberal party constitute at the present time the greatest obstacle to reunion.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 2, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, OCTOBER 2, 1886.

LYM3I. HYDROPHOEIA..—At Altrincham, on Monday morning 1 Sergeant Harrington, of the Lymm police, brought under the notice of the magistrates several cases of hydrophobia at Lyn-Im. One child, he said, had been badly bitten, but the dog was shot. A retriever beloneing to Mrs. Crosfield, valued at fifty guineas, had also been destroyed. On the application of Superintendant Leighton, an order for keep- ing dogs under control throughout Altrincham division un- til November 30th was made. A similar order had only just expired. RIFLE SHOOTING MATCH.—On Saturday a match was shot on the Lymm rifle range, between tbe shooting teams representing the A Company (Captain Mothersill) and H. Company (Captain Jones), 3rd Cheshire Rifle Volunteers ; corditions as for the Queen's Prize, first staee. The match was robbed of some of its interest, owing to the non-appear- ance of two of the Lyinrn team ; but the result was in fa- vour of the Altrincham team, their total being 754, as com- pared with the 697 of the Lycnin team. The weather was vitt and unfavourable for high scoring, the targets being almost invisible at times. PARISH CHURCH HARVEST FESTIVAL. Services of thanksgiving for the harvest were on Sunday held at Lyme(' Parish Church. In the morning the sermon was preached by the Rev. T. R. Willacy. vicar of Thorganby, Yorkshire. In the afternoon there was a service for men, which was followed by a children's service, at which an address was given by the Rev. H. A. D. Surridge, Vicar of High Legh. At the evening service the sermon was again preached by the Rev. T. R. Willacy, and an anthem was given by the choir, Mr. H. Bradburn taking the solos., The decorations had been undertaken by the Misses Jones Miss Battersby, the Misses Stubs, Mrs. Addenbrooke, the Misses Pothecary. the Misses Brabazon, and Miss King. The pillars were decorated by the Sunday school teachers and scholars, Miss Dearden, the Misses Brazendale, and Miss Evans being the chief workers. The font was again under- taken by Mr. T. P. Norris. The collections, which were in aid of the north door porch fund, amounted .o a little over £2O.
FRODSH AM•

A SUCCESSFUL STUDENT. -- Last week an examination was held at the North Wales University College at Bangor for scholarships in connection with that University. The result was declared on Tuesday, when a scholarship of .£4O a year, tenable for three years, was awarded to William Gibson Turco°, son of Mr. William Turtoo, Overton, Frod- sham. PAINFULLY SUDDEN DEATH AT FRODSHAM BRIDGE.— On Thursday between twelve and one o'clock, whilst on business at Frodsham Bridge, Mr. George Gorst, farmer, of Bradley, and assistant overseer of Sutton, was suddenly taken ill. Medical assistance was at once secured, but with- out avail, as the deceased died shortly afterwards. The cause of death is supposed to have been apoplexy. KINGSLEY CHURCH HARVEST FESTIVAL.—On Wednes- day evening a special harvest thanksgiving service was held at this church, when a large congregation assembled. The ' decorations of cern, fruit, and flowers were tastefully arranged, and those on the font and pulpit were deserving of especial note. The lessons were read by the Rev. R. M. P. Butler, M.A., of Frodsbam. The other portion of the ser- vice was performed by the Vicar, the Rev. A. P. Reynolds. The anthem, "And God said, let the earth," was sung her the choir. he sermon was preached by the Rev. J. Symons, of Southport, who delivered an impressive address from St, Luke viii. 11. A collection was made at the close, the proceeds of which will be partly devoted to the funds Of the I Chester Infirmary. STEALING FRUIT.—At Edclisbury Petty Sessions, on Mon- day, William Corker (10), Ernest Ainsworth (13), and Wil- liam Blair (13) were charged with stealing plums to the value of 7s 6d at Frodsharn. George Jones stated that on the 2nd September his sister came and told him some boys were in the garden. He went there, and saw P.C. Darrocks following some lads, who were runningbaway. Blair, whilst running, threw away some plums. The officer caught Ains- worth, and witness took hold of Blair. Corker stopped.-- P.C. Darrocks stated that from Information he received he went to the garden in question, and saw six boys coming out. They ran across a field, and he went after them. Tbe three defendants were caught, and on Corker he found 35 plums, and 18 on Ainsworth. He afterwards went to the garden, and saw a quantity ef plums on the ground.—Fined is, costs 2s 61, and damage 8a 6d each. TRINITY WESLEYAN CHAPEL—Harvest thanksgiving services were held at the Trinity Wesleyan Chapel, Feud- sham, on Sunday, when the Rev. E. Mosecrop preacbed from the following texts :—" It is a good thing to give thanks unto Thy name, 0 Most High;" "They joy before Thee according to the joy in harvest." The choir gave the harvest anthems. "Thou visitest the earth and blessest it" (W. H. Callcott), and "The earth is the Lord's" (Al- bert Lowe) under the conductorship of Mr. T. Sant. Mr. W. H. Pickering, as usual, ably presided at the organ. The decorations were of a tasteful nature. On the top of the pulpit was a fringe of oats, decked with white dahlias, lilium , and chrysanthemums, relieved with maidenhair ferns. From the bookrest hung two large bunches of black and white grapes. On the front panel of the pulpit was a beautiful anchor, composed of white dahlias, the other panels being lined with coloured roses amidst maidenhair ferns, on a groundwork of moss. On the communion table there were two pretty bouquets, three fine hunches of grapes, and two small loaves. The communion rail was wreathed with ivy and sheaflets of oats and barley ; wlaild on the standards, or pillars sustaining the Same, were four pockets filled with choice flowers, chiefly gladioli. The font was arrayed with Virginia creepers, belota lily, sprays of asparegus, and ferns. On the step of the communion the words " The earth is the Lord's" were wrought with yellow daisies on a white ground. The windows were decorated with flowers, fruit, and vegetables.—The pillars upholding the gallery were entwined with scarlet fuchsias, evergreens, nasturtiums, Jacob's ladder, sunflowers, and asters. The collections amounted to £7 3e. HARVESF FESTIVAL AV THH PARISH CHURCH.—The an- nual harvest festival service took place in Frodsharn Parish Church on Friday evening. The Rev. R. M. P. Butler, 8.A., intoned the service, which was full choral, Tallis's responses being effectively rendered by the choir. Hymns, proces- sional and recessional, were sung, and the anthem was taken from the words, "0 Lord, how manifold are thy works" (G. A. Macfarren). Special psalms were given to double chants by Goss in F and Bate in G. The chants for Magni- ficat and Nunc Dirnittis were by Goss in D and Foster in E. The first lesson was read by the Rev. E. P. Alexander, vicar of Al vanley, and the second lesson by the Rev. H. R. Whytehead, vicar of Norlev. The prayers were read by the Rev. J. M. Stevens, and the preacher was the Yen. Arch- deacon Barber, M.A., canon of Chester. The services were continued on Sunday, the sermon in the morning being preached by the lev. A. P. Reynolds, vicar of Kingsley, and in the evening by the Rev. R. M. P. Butler, 8.A., senior curate. The collections were in aid of the funds of the Chester Infirmary. A considerable amount of care bad been bestowed upon the floral decorations of the church; the pre- vailing fashion, however, of moss, yew, and dark foliage gave the decorations a somewhat sombre appearance; bat they were relieved in places by lighter treatment. An reathetic style had been adopted for the communion, sunflowers pre- dominating, with outline panels of oats and dahlias. Above the communion table were the words, "I am the bread of life," in small white flowers, with a background of moss. The vases on the communion table were, as usual, tastefully arranged with flowers, and in the centre was a beautiful cross of white chrysanthemums, with a circle of dark dahlias, the whole beine surrounded with a broad fringe of oats. On the table were bunches of grapes, dm A number of varie- gated and other plants, specimen ferns &a., were placed in t'4: sacrarium, and the communion rails were adorned with oats, dahlias, and foliage. A plentiful supply of the fruits of the season, miniature trusses of bay, cereals, ate., were displayed on the altar steps. The font was eurmounted with beautiful flowers, consisting of dahlias, Mims, etc., ar- ranged in tiers, with foliage between, a cross of coral-like appearance being fixed at the apex. The base of the font was covered with a carpet of moss, three baskets beheg placed thereon, containing chrysanthemums, geraniums, ferns, &c, the handles being entwined with ivy and maiden- hair fern. A fringe of arbor yitm, hops, egc., round the font was very effective ; while three crosses, two of which were composed of chrysanthemums, with a centre one of gladioli, gave the whole a neat and finished appearance. The pulpit was prettily decorated, the lower portion of the panels having suitable background and border, with tastefully-arranged centres of apples, grapes, flowers, cornucopia, blackberries, and miniature sheaf. A fringe of yew, dahlias, lilies, ate.. was placed round the ten of the pulpit. The choir stalls had a fringe of yew with stars of wheat, with alternate centres of lilies and gladioli, which was very effective. At the font of the east -window, in the Kingsley chapel, were de- signs emblematic of faith, hope, and charity, en a back- ground of moss.

THE CHARGE AGAINST A CLERGYMAN OF FALSIFYING A MARRIAGE REGISTER.—The Rev. John H. Latrobe Bate- man, vicar of Haile, was prosecuted by the Treasury on Monday, at Whitehaven Police Court, for feloniously insr- ting, or permitting to be inserted, in a register of marriage at Haile a certain false entry relating to a marriage, and the defendant was committed for trial at the assizes, bail being accepted, the defendant in £2OO and one surety in £2OO

A GALLANT DEED REWARDED.—It is reported from Stour- bridge that a working carpenter named Wilkinson has un- expectedly become the owner of an estate near Newcastle- me-Tyne and a considerable sum of money. Four years ago Wilkinson saved from drowning in the Tyne a well-to-do old gentleman named Willis, who, having no relatives, be- queathed the whole of his property to his rescuer. Mr. Willis died some time ago, and the efforts to find Wilkinson have only just proved successful.

. • THE ORDNANCH SCANDALS.- Speaking at the•annnal meeting of shareholders of Messrs. Armstrong, Mitchel. and Company, on Thursday, Sir William Armstrong repudiated in strong terms the allegations against the firm and Govern• ment officials. Durißg' the last 15 years, he said, they had only got twelve or fourteen hundred a year from contracts with the British Government, and on one occasion they ran the risk of injuring the shareholders' interests by letting the Government have guns made fhr the Italian Government. A CoyoNEß's DIFFICULTY.-Mr. Braxton Hicks, before opening an inquiry into the death of an infant in Soho, London, on Wednesday morning, said that his officer had had a great deal of trouble to get the body, as the parents had been drunk ever since it died, and refused to 'let the doctor make a post-mortem, or to have the body removed. It was only when force was used that they succeeded in getting it. The parents had to be sent for by the police, and then the mother said the reason the body was not given up was because she did not like to part with it.
