LAT FST NEWS.

Mr. Thomas Clark, Lord Provost of Edinburgh, is gazetted a baronet. Lord Randolph Churchill on Friday paid a long visit to the Indian (Mice. A further detachment of 70 marines, under the command of Major Peak, embarked on Friday, on board the Humber, at Portsmouth, for Tiree. FATALACCIDENT.—A wagon full of hoppickers broke down while entering Hereford on Friday afternoon, and one woman was killed and several nersons seriously injured. Tug ALLOTMENT QUESTION.—Lord Beotive has just an- nounced his willingness to let small allotments to the labourers of South Westmoreland for cultivation, at a rea- sonable rent. It is believed the offer will be readily accepted, and the experiment will be watched with great interest in the district. A NEW RAILWAY.—A cablegram, received in London from Winnipeg, on Frid-ty, states that work has been commenced upon the constinction of the Hudson's Bay Railway. and that two thousand men are now employed in connection therewith. The line will shorten by one thousand miles the distance between Liverpool and the Pacific coas.t DEATH FROM THE BITE OF A CAT. Thomas Oaks, mechanic, Rotherham, died on Friday morning from hydro- phobit, having been seized with paroxysms at a late hour the previous night. Deceased was bitten by a cat about eighteen months ago, and, until a few weeks since, no symptoms save the display of a little indifference towards his friends were apparent. AN " IMPUDENT HOAX."—The " Stourbridge County Ex- press" brands as an impudent hoax the story that a Stour- bridge carpenter named Wilkinson had been left a valuable estate and money by Mr. Willis, of Newcastle, a gentleman whose life he was said to have saved years ago. On inspec- tion the lawyer's letter informing Wilkinson of his title to the property proves to be a fraud. ATTEMPT TO UPSET A TRAIN.—On Friday morning the 9-25 train from Manchester to Macplesfield narrowly escaped being thrown off the line. The lid of an axle box and a quantity of cinders had been placed on the line. Luckily the driver observed it in time to draw up, otherwise the train, containing 30 passengers, might have been thrown down an embankment. The police are inTestigating the affair. ' SUPPOSED DEATH PROM VACCINATION.—The South Staf , fordshire coroner on Friday received information of the death of a child named Alice Harbach, aged 11 weeks, of Cradley Heath, who, it is alleged, has died from vaccine- ' iron. The deceased, prior to being vaccinated, was regarded as being very healthy, but a few days after vaccination she appeared to be in great pain, and this morning was found dead in bed. The affair has caused considerable excitement in the district. THE LAND COMMISSION. The Royal Commission on the Irish Land Act was gazetted on Friday, and consists as already announced, of Earl Cowper, Earl of Milltown, Sir James Caird, Mr. Neligan (Recorder of Loccionderry), and Mr. George Fortrell, janr., with Mr. Francis Hodder, bar- rister, as secretary. Two will form a quOrum, and the corn- miseioners are empowered to examine witnesses, and have access to books, doculente, etc. Mr. Fortrell ha e already from the Commission. SI7PPOSED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT latvEsaroot.— Shortly after midnight on Friday the canal at Liverpool was being dragged for the body of a man supposed to have com- mitted suicide, when the police recovered the body of a woman who had been in the water a short time, and identi- fied as Katherine Young., It is stated that she left home on Thursday evening with her child, aged six yeirs. The body of the child has not yet been discovered. It is be- lieved the mother murdered the child and then committed suicide. • GREAT FIRE IN LEICESTER.—J at before 12 o'clock on Toursday night fire was seen bursting through the wiedows of one of the largest boot and shoe and leather warehouses in Leicester. The fire was not extinguished until five o'clock yesterday morning, the damage being estimated at £BO,OOO. The premises of Messrs. Barrow Brothers, leather merchants ; Messrs. William Tyler and Son, leather mer- chants; Messrs. Hedges and Abel, hesiery manufacturers; and Mr. Thomas Wright, boot and shoe fector,were entirely destroyed by the fire, while two dwelling-honses and the large schoolroom of Belveir-etreet Chapel were demolished by the falling walls. The extensive factory and warehouse of Mr. William Stanyon, boot and shoe manufacturer were also greatly damaged by fire, smoke, and water. The fire originated in the premises of Messrs. Hed- ges and Abel, and spread with the utmost rapidity.

div.head: BULGARIAN QUESTION.
div.p: THE BULGARIAN QUESTION.
BIICEIAREST, FRIDAY. - The Austrian military attache has been ordered to encourage the Bulgarian Regent to re- sist Russian demands and to promise eventual assistance from Austria.
WARRING-TON UNION RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The monthly meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. Mr. C. Broad- bent, J.P. (chairman), presided, and there were also present Messrs. Jolley, Owen, Woods, Wm. Houghton, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Heaton, J. Houghton, Ku. shall, and W. Long (ex-officio): S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and Kerfoot (inspector). THE LATE ItgsrEc ron.—The CLERK said he had received a letter from the Local Government Board adverting to the fact that Mr. Rawlings, the late inspector of the Authority, had been appointed to a similar post at Rawtenstall, and asking if he had performed his duty satisfactorily to the Authority. The Clerk said he had replied, stating that Mr. Rawlings had been thirteen years in the service of the Au. thoritv, and had performed his duties satisfactorily.—The CHAIRMAN said the Clerk was perfectly justified iu saying that.

VITAL STATISTICS.—DE. SEPHTON reported that during the past month there had been 25 births and 16 deaths. The death-rate had been MI per 1.000. SURVEYOR'S REPJRT —MY. OWEN reported that he had written to the Warrington borough surveyor with regard to the sewer, bel-nging to the Authority, running down Win- wick-road to the Longford Brook, and through which the Corporation had the right of drainage, and mentioning that the Authority's ine,ector had reported that the stoppage Was occasioned hr the settling of s?climent during the time Mc Sewer was cfrsed by the tide at its month, and had alas reported that the' sediment was in his opinion of the nature of scale from iron or of some substance not venally found in sewage. Ile`therefore asked if there was any reasons why sewage containing such solid matter should be alioeved to enter the drain, that these reasons should be laid before the Authority. A letter from the borough surveyor, stating that he had received instructions to examine the sewer and report to the Pavine and Sewerage Committee, had been re- ceived, in reply, by Mr. Owen. Mr. Owen also reported that he had accepted the tender of Messrs. Hough and Sou for the sewer required in the Lovely-lane district, for £l2 10e, as instructed at their previous meeting. Mr. A. J. Heaton submitted plans for eight houses in Jockey-street, off Winwick-street, Warrington, which might be approved. —The report was adopted. LONGFORD DEPOT.—The INSPECTOR, in his report, brought under the notice of the Authcritv several alleao nuisances, and these having been disposed of, Mr. OWEN remarked that there was still no abatement of the nuisance at Longford depot. He could smell the piece four miles off. The nuisance was caused in the Authority's district, and whilst they looked after indivilual cases he thought they ought also to take the matter of Longford depot into serious consideration. He was of opinion that it was the worst of the two, both with regard to the vehicles that went be- tween the town and the depot, and the vapours arising from the depot itself.—The CHAIRMAN: You bring it before the Authority next meeting, Mr. Owen.—Mr. OWEN: Very well, sir; I will.—Mr. JOLLEY said he might explain that the Corporatton were expecting to do away with the vans, as steps were being taken to seed the material underground in a week or two.—Mr. HEATON: They will remove the nuis- ance from between here and Longford, but will give it extra vent there. (Laughter.)—Mr. OWEN: The stench is fearful. This was all the business.

At an inquest at Kilsheelan, near Clonmel, on Saturday, on the body of a child, a farm labourer named Mara stated that he found a large bull-terrier in a field with the body in its month, and with difficulty he made the animal drop it. From the medical evidence it appeared that death was not caused by violence. An open verdict was returned.

BALL CARTRIDGE- AT A SHAM FIGHT —A report was pub- lished a few days ago that during a sham fight at Aldershot ball cartridge was fired. At a court of inquiry held on Wed- nesday, the evidence showed that only one bullet was fired. How and by whom the bullet wa§ fired has not yet been ascertained, but it is generally • believed to have been the result of an accident. --

THE SUBSIDENCES AT NORTHWICII.—On Tuesday night an alarming subsidence took place in London-road, North- wich, near the Drill Hall. A man named Plumb was riding a horse, when the earth opened. The horse was carried down, but the rider escaped. A number of carriages con- veying parties home from an entertainment at the hall would soon afterwards have passed along the road.

WARRINGTON. On Thursday evening the first of three tea Parties and subsequent meetings, which had been ar- ranged to celebrate the two recent returns for War- rington of Sir Gilbert Greenall, was held at the Public Hall. About 650 persons sat down

to tea, after which a concert was given. Captain Reynolds, J.P. (chairman of the Con- servative Association), occupied the chair and he was supported by Councillors Francomb , and Sutton ; and Messrs. Mackie, J. Pier point, T. Hutchinson, and other aentlemen. Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, and the Misses Greenall were also present.—Sir GIL- BERT GREENALL, M.P., who was loudly cheered on i rising to address the meeting, spoke n eulogistic terms of Captain Reynolds services to the Con- servative cause, and the able counsel he at all times gave his supporters and workers. They had won two grand battles in less than twelve months, and if they preserved the same unity as had characterised them in the past, victory would still be theirs. (Cheers.) He thanked them for the hearty support extended to him in the past, and their kind wishes for the future.—Afterwards the room was cleared for dancing, and a pleas-

ant time was spent. A second meeting was held in the Pnblic Hall last evening, when a large number of people at- tended. The chair was occupied by Captain Rey- nolds, who was supported by Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., Lady Greenall, Miss Greenall, Mr. G. Greenall, the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Har- rison), Mr. J. E. Wright, Mr. John Pierpoint, Mr. Collins, Mr. Smethurst, and others. The CHAIRMAN said that it was a great credit to the Conservative party that the large meeting that was held on the evening previous had passed with such good order and regularity. Had it not been for a good, long pull, they should not have recov- ered Warrington from the Radical grasp. They had now doue bO, and it was left for the Conservative party in Warrington to continue the representation of the borough in the hands of the Conservative party. (Cheers.) Sir GILBERT GREENALL, who was received with loud cheers, said he rejoiced to be there that even- ing. He congratulated them upon having that second meeting an assembly as good as the meeting which it was their plea- sure to see the previous night. Well, as Cap- tain Reynolds had said, the third time generally paid for all. (Cheers.) They were to have another meeting the next evening,. arid Captain Reynolds would again be with them. (Hear, hear.) He also should rejoice to be amongst them. They were there to bear in grateful memory their great triumph. (Cheers.) He well remembered the 24th November, and should never forget the many kind- nesses which were then shown to him. He had also another day to bear in grateful memory, but on that day they had not time to make 501 into 776. (Cheers.) But only let them have another trial, and then they would have those, figures together. He should al- ways expect to see Warrington Conservative— (cheers)—and he knew Warrington would remain Conservative— (cheers) because he knew the temper of the men who lived in Warrington. He knew the righteous principles which animated them ; he knew they loved the Sovereign of this country, and he knew that they would never allow their glorious Empire to be dismembered. ("Never.") He was confident that so long as the present inhab- itants of Warrington existed, they would be found banded together to maintain the principles of the constitution. He was amongst them with very great pleasure. They were not going to forsake him . —(" No," and cheers)—and he, on his, part, would not forsake them. NT, E9I3ERT PIERPOINT, in the Mine of an ad- dress, said that through their exertions for their honoured member they had proved that the good old town of Warrington was a Conservative town, and they had shown to the rest of the electors of the kingdom that they intended tha government of this country should be a Conservative Government. They had got rid of the government that bombarded Alexandria, and that kept them always in a tur- moil. Now they had at the head of affairs a govern- ment presided over by Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill. (Cheers.) He rejoiced to hear them cheer those names. Lord Salisbury's name was known throughout the civilised world as a statesman of great ability, and he looked. upon R. Churchill as a man who had done perhaps more than any man in our age for advancing the claims ot the Conservative party to rule this country (Cheers.) They had got tired of ,the government that was always bringing forward burning questions to hide the mistakes made by the Executive, and to blind the eyes of the people to misgovernment. They had got tired of a government presided. over by a man who in his old age at last discovered that the cure for Ireland was Home Rule. Mr. Crosfield, they knew, never expressed an opinion in favour of Home Rule until it was fathered by Mr. Gladstone—until in his old age Mr. Glad- stone produced that extraordinary little son of his —Home Rule. Mr. Crosfield never hid his opinions, I whether they were the reflected ones of others, or I the few he had made himself, and he 'never thought Home Rule was the sole cure for Ireland, but rather thought that it was altogether wrong, still he with the rest gave a vote for the cause of Home Rule because it was adopted by Mr. Gladstone. The cry for Home Rule had for its end the cry of an Irish Republic, but they would say that Ireland in the future as well as in the past should remain a part of the United Kingdom: (Applause.) They must vote for men like Sir Gilbert Greenall, who were prepared to take a pride in the glorious inheritance they had received, and they might be sure that according to their best ability they would hand it down to those who came after them, still as glo- rious as when it came into their hands. (Ap- plause.) The' MAYOR (Alderman Harrison) who entered ;the,rooca some time after the meeting' commenced, said) that he had been to a private meeting of the- ttown Council, which had been held for the purjbse of practically selecting a Mayor, who would be elected on the 9th of November next. The gen- tleman who had been selected was Dr. Mackie. (Applause.) Proceeding, the Mayor said he recog- nised with sufficient gravity the important crisis through which the country had been, and was now, passing. It became every man with a true English heart to do all that he could to promote that unity between our colonies and our own land to the fullest extent in their power, and, if it were for nothing else than than that, leaving Conservatism out of the question, he was bound as an Englishman to adopt the Conservative principles of maintaining the union, dignity, and integrity of the Empire. (Cheers.) During the evening songs were given by Miss Horton, and Messrs. Benson, Taylor, Booth, and P. Davies, and afterwards the room was cleared for dancing.

Ai l ENGINE DRIVER KILLED. --- Earls' on Thursday merning an engine driver named Riehard Clemente was enga'getl in shunting trucks near the blast furnaces of the Tredegar Ron Company, at Tredegar, when he came into contact with an overhanging spout, and sustained fatal in. juries. Every day at one o'clock, 5300,000,000 sit around a little mahogany table in an upper room in the Western Union building iR New York, and eat a plain hut sub- stantial lunch. The millions belong to Jay Gould, Syd- ney Dillon, Russell Sage, and ex-Governor Alonza D. Cornell. All were country boys and wore shoes only on San. day A WIDNES MAN is TROErßLE:—lteuben Hewitt, a labouring roan living at Widnes, was brought before Mr. William PilkinAon and Mr. A. Walmesley, at the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing a pair of reins from a horse belonging to Mr. Roger Feeney, farmer. Prisoner was with other men in a trap; and at the end of Robin's-lane he cracked his whip at Mr. Fenney's horse and it galloped away in the direction of Marshall's Cross. When Miss Feeney overtook it the reins were gone. Police. constable Brooks found the reins in the house of prisoner's brother, Travis-street, Simm's-crosa, Widnes. For the de- fence it was stated that another man took them there to sell them. Prisoner was committed for two months with hard labour.

POLITICAL ECONOMY AND THE NATIONAL WELFARE _ Lord Coleridge, in a speech at a science and art school meeting at Tivarton, said he had been struck in the evidence given before the Trade Commission and the report on foreign education by Mr. Matthew Arnold by two startling facts—viz, that the nations which had systemati- cally violated the principles of political economy had suf- fered more heavily and continuously than those which had systematically maintained those principles, and that in many branches of industry and in many markets we were now being beaten by other countries which, although they started from the barriers later than we did, had stretched forward to reach the goal in the race before us. But the evidence laid before the Commission also showed that if the education which institutions such as they were engaged in supporting that day were wisely and steadily and persever- ingly used, not only was there no reason to fear, but there was every reason to hope and believe, that the Englishman, who had certain natural advantages of birth and character, would not only maintain his commercial supremacy, but would advance it into new industries and fresh markets.

WARRINGTON. , 1 TIIE "BANQUET SCENE FROM MACBETH. -- An oil painting by Mr. F. A..Essenhigh. of Warrington, representing the banquet scene from "Macbeth," has during the week been on exhibition at the Masonic Hall, Sankey-street. The dimensions of the picture, which is very creditable to the artist, are Bft. by 4ft, and nearly ninety characters are represented.

-SUDDEN DEATHS.—On Monday, the sudden death of James Henry Smith, four months old, the son of a factory hand, was reported to the bor-tgh police. , The lad had been in delicate health, and was sub- ject to convulsions. On the same day a child named Ethel Derbyshire, 15 weeks old, daughter of John 'Derbyshire, who keeps the Boar's Head, Town Hill, , also died suddenly in a fit. . PROPOSED SEARCH FOR LOCAL ANTIQUITIES.— At the meeting of the Town Council to be held 3n Tuesday evening, the General Purposes Committee will recommend that a request by Mr. Beamont that i the committee_ should cut trenches across the

vacant land in Bridge-street to discover, if possible. any relics of the Priory of the Warrington Hermit of the Order of St. Augustine be acceded to, and that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to super- intend the operations. PRESENTATION.-11fiss Townsend, a teacher at St. Paul's girls' Sunday school, was on Sunday pre- sented by the superintendent (Mr. Joseph Lawless) and the teachers with a Bible and Prayer Book. The Vicar, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, made the presen- tation; and spoke warmly of Miss Townsend's regu- larity and diligence as a teacher. He felt sure he was expressing the feelings of all present when he , said they very sincerely grieved at losing such an, lexcellent worker from the parish. Miss Townsend is leaving Warrington. THE DANGER OF PARAFFIN LAMPS.—An accident that might have had far more serious results than was actually the case, occurred in Ellesmere-street late on Monday night. The borough police were informed that a fire had broken out at 31, Elles- mere-street, where Mr. Dobson, a draughtsman, resides. An alarm was rung, and on going to the house it was discovered that Mr. Dobson, when on the point of retiring to bed, turned out a paraffin lamp, which exploded. The curtains of the room were ignited, and a dressing table also caught fire. Mrs. Dobson, who had retired to rest, was got out of the house as quickly as possible, and the fire was put out before much damage had been done. • THE PARISH CHURCH HARVEST FESTIVAL.—On Sunday, harvest thanksgiving services were con- tinued at the Parish Church. There were good congregations. In the morning the Rev. J. J. Langham, M.A. (resident clerical principal of St. Elphin's Clergy Daughters' School), preached; the sermon in the afternoon was preached by the Rev. ll.Rudge, and that in the evening by the Rev. E. H. Barry. The offertories, which go towards church expenses, amounted in all to £3O, that being the sum collected at the services on Thursday, Friday, and Sunday. Mr. W. S. Woods was the organist. On Sunday morning Oe choir sang the anthem "0, that men would praise the Lord,' in the afternoon they sang the anthem "In that day shall the Lord of Hosts," and at the evening service the anthem "0 give thanks" was. given, the bass solo being taken by Mr. C. Price. HOUSEBREAKING.—The houSe of Mr. John Hutch- inson, 19, Wilson Patten-street, is reported to have been broken into on Tuesday evening. A person who was in charge of the house, it is said, went out at about half-past eight, and, on returning, found th It in one of the rooms a desk and several -drawers had been broken open and the contents thrown labout. The police w,ere then informed of the matter. It appears that the thief effected an en- trance by taking up a grid at the back of the house and Opening the cellar window. He then ransacked the premises, but, disturbed in his operations, ap- parently made his escape by jumping from the first floor front window into the garden below. Nothing of value was missed, except a silver Geneva watch. Several petty depredations are reported to have recently taken place in the neighbourhood. WiNwicK CRICKET CLUB.—This club concluded a successful season on Saturday last with a match against Orford Barracks at Winwick, in which the home team only batted owing,to the rain, the top scorers being J. Longton (not out 19) and P. Long- ton (10). Ten matches have been won, nine lost, and two drawn. The match of the season was against Mr. George Comber's team on August 9th, on a specially prepared wicket at Myddleton when the club beat the combination, which included two of the brothers Steele, T. P. Bellhouse. Mudie, Lyon, &c., of the Whalley Range Club, both teams afterwards being entertained by Mr. Comber to dinner at the hall. The main stay of the club has been the bowling, James Harrison having had won- derful success, and claiming 63 wickets, while J. Wadsworth has taken 41 at very small cost. The best batsmen have been J. Longton (with the aver- age of 16), followed by R. Carson, J. Wadsworth, P. Lengton, D. Fergusson, and J. Dunbobbin. in addition to Mr. Comber, the Rev. Canon Hopwood has been a kind patron to the club. 1.0. OF GOOD TEMPLARS, WESLEY LODGE, NO. 409.—0 n Monday last, the members of the Juvenile Branch of this Lodge held their first tea meeting, folloWO by a distribution of prizes for the best recitations. geCit4tionF.3 were given by Sisters Keates, Woodcock, Bardford, and Ellison, Brothers Davenport, Frain, Alcock, and Griffiths, the prizes being awarded to Sister Keates and Brother Frain. The other pieces were recited in very good. style. The meeting was further enlivened by songs by Sisters Davenport, Sheath, and Brother Gallop; and a duet and glees by the children. A very pleasant meeting was brought to a close by a hearty vote of thanks to the chairman, Brother Gallop. In connection with the 13onehill Branch Lodge, 1970, of Good Templars, a grand mu- sical concert was given in the Temperance Hall, Latchford. The concert was patronised and pre- sided over by His Worship the Mayor (Mr. Harrison.) I The following members of the Manchester and district concerts kindly gave their services:— Miss Whitehouse, soprano; Miss Agnes Whitehouse, soprano; Mrs. Wilde, Contralto; Mr. Jones, tenor ; Mr. P. llankinson, bass. solo pianoforte and ac- compatiist Mr. R. HopkintOn (organist of St. Mark's, Oorton). The hall was 'Well filled with an appreciative audience, making the concert a • thorough success. Proceeds will be devoted to the hall fund: WARRigeiTON UNION ASSESSMENT Conitat. —The Monthly meeting of this commit flce was held on Friday morning, at the Work- house. There were present Mr. C. Broadbent (chairman), the Rev. G. P. Roberts, Messrs. W. Long (et-officio), W. Balharry, John Hough- ton; J. C. Sutton. (clerk), W. Owen (valuer), ' J. L. Tunstall, and other assistant overseers.— Valuer's Report: Mr. Owen reported that since the last meeting he had made the following valuations, viz.: Mr. A. E. G. Robinson, V.S., Sankey-street, Warrington, house and stables, gross £52 10s, rate- able £44 10; Penketh Tanning Co., Limited, Pen- keth, near Warrington, additions to works, gross £l6 10s, rateable £l3. Mr: Murray Douglas, Bank Quay, W arrington ; in February last he reported ithat these works were closed, but that the ware- houses were in use as stores. The assessment was then reduced to £5O gross, but he now found that the stock was reduced to almost nothing. An as- sessment of £lO gross, £8 lOs rateable, would be sufficient to cover the present occupation. Roebuck Inn, Bridge-street, Warrington : After considering the matter fully he was quite of opinion that a tem- porary assessment of £lOO gross would suffice for twelve months, subject to the overseers bringing' it forward again for re-assessment.—This report' WO' adopted. There was no other business of publie interest before the committee. ST. PAUL'S DAY SCHOOLS.—At St. Paul's Church,. on Sunday, two sermons were preached on behalf of the day schools in connection with the church, the pulpit being occupied in the. morning by the cu- rate of St.. Paul's, the Rev. R. Wood Samuels, and in, the evening by the Rev. G. D. Lyon Bennett, of. Little Leigh. Mr. Samuels, in the course of his ser- mon, spoke of the education of the young as an im- portant part of the church's work. If, he said, I more care and attention were given to Church I teaching and religious instruction in Church schools it would be a rare thing to find any falling from , their ranks, either to dissent or to any other reli- gion foreign to their own. In that parish they were especially favoured in having such superior and I well-adapted schools, an excellent staff of teachers, I and a regular course of religious instruction given to the scholars week by week. The large number ; of children attending the schools must of itself speak for the efficiency of the staff. From the Dio- cesan Calendar he found that the number of scholars upon the books was no less than 1,600, and that was higher than any other school in the dio- cese. The managers had lately incurred additional expense in the improvement of the building, for the comfort of scholars and teachers. The teaching :staff had been strengthened, extra books provided, the schoolrooms and classrooms had been fitted up .at considerable cost, the playgrounds improved, and they were asked to give liberally that day that these expenses might be met. The collections for the day amounted to about £lo'

In order to give an additional interest to the members of this Company, the Directors have decided to grant to all ori- ginal shareholders, so long as they shall continue their hold- ings, a non-transferable ticket, entitling them to travel twice to and from the island each summer and once during each winter. These tickets will be allotted as follows :—To original holders of one to four shares, a second-class ticket ; and to original holders of not less than five shares. a first- class ticket available as above. Those having the former tickets will have the privilege of travelling first-class by pay- ing the excess fare. The feillowing are some further advantages claimed for this Company. Accommodation for passengers, replete with every modern improvement. The greatest speed, with safety in c•ainparatively crowded waters. Freedom from much of the vibration usually experienced on board steamers. Reduced rate of fares, together with moderate charges for refresisments. Whilst offering the above advantages to passengers, the in- terests of the shareholders, from a dividend-paying point of view, shall be fully mainta'ned, as by the construction of first-class triple expansion screw steamers one-third only of the capital expenditure w 11 be entailed, and a corresponding saving in the working expenses will be effected as compared with large padd.e steamses. The Liverpool Journal of Commerce of September 25, com- menting on the decision to grant tickets to original share- holders, remarks : "The Directors of this Company have re- solved on making is concession to the shareholders which can- not fail to be greatly appreciated, and which marks a new departure in the management of carrying companies.' Mr. John Parry."—As rewards Llanarmon the tenant farmers will accept the offer of ten per cent on the express condition that the abatement should be extended to those persons whose goods have already been distrained upon by the rector for nonpayment of tithes. Arrangements are in progress for the holding, in Liver- pool, of a large demonstration, with a view to the inaugura- tion of 's Welsh national movement. A letter written from London by an influential Welshman, and received by the Anti-Tithe League on the subject, says :—" I should like to be down with you, to fight and suffer in the cause, but I may say that I am personally at this moment arranging for the holding. in Liverpool, of a large demonstration, with a view to the inauguration of a Welsh national movement. It has become clear that it is hopeless in the present circum- stances, and nuder our present system of Parliamentary re- presentation, to get the slightest attention paid to our wants. You know that you have never received the least shadow of encouragement from our present members ; but take heart, and work up the movement with a will. The co-operative movement is coming to your aid; we will see that you don't fight unaided; and, depend upon it, once we are represented in the House of Commons by nationalists, once we are re- presented by men drawn from the same class as they re- present, and whose interests they will have in common and mutual in ducement in promoting, you will get your grievances redressed." An important meeting of farmers was held on Wednesday evening at Caerwys, Fiintshire, Mr. John Parry, secretary of the Anti-Tithe League, presiding. Delegates were pre- sent from Ruthin, Denbigh, Holywell, Llandyraog, Llanar- mon. Henllan, Brynmawr, and other centres of the time agitation.—The Chairman, secretary of the Anti-Tithe Leagues, was enthusiastically cheered. Ho emphatically denied that the tithes were the property of the clergy, and he urged them to strive to the utmost that they might be prevented from ever becoming so. 'Dee farming classes had many channels In which their money could he used with advantage. They required a land court, and the money now paid to the Church of England should go towards the main- tenance of other institutions, of which Wales was urgently in need. (Applause.) While paying the tithes, none were more aware than themselves that they • received no benefit either temporal or spiritual. They had passively borne all the oppression of the past, they had paid the tithes that had been demanded of them, they had suffered the pangs of want to gather money together, and now they were deter- mined never to rest again until the Church of England was rooted out, disestablished, and diseadowed.—Mr. Edward Hughes, Istzlan, Holywell, said that in Whitford parish, in which he.resided, there was a tithe of £l,lOO, but of all the tithepayers only seven attended the parish church, whi.e eleven different chapels with their ministers were supported voluntarily.—Other speakers followed. The Rector of Penderyn having been petitioned to make an abatement in the tithe charge in his parish announced yesterday a reduction of 2i per cent. Other clergymen in the Principality are endeavouring to make arrangements with the farmers in order to avoid distraint, and the abatements are being offered ranging from VI to ten per cent.
